title: The Continuous Tensor Abstraction and Its High Performance Compilation
summary: This PhD thesis extends tensor programming from integer coordinates to real-valued domains. Continuous tensors reuse the language of discrete ones — convolution is the same expression over pixels on a grid or points in space — with pinpoints for isolated coordinates, intervals for regions, continuous Einsums whose reductions integrate under counting and Lebesgue measures, and a piecewise-constant representation that makes them finite and compilable. The thesis then develops format-aware reformulation, a rewrite folding format information into the expression so continuous and sparse programs become array operations executable by dense tensor infrastructure, including GPU tensor cores; native tensor-core matmul yields 2.6× over the default PyTorch compiler, and the GPU implementation is at least 5.4× faster than Finch. The thesis is the most complete treatment of the continuous tensor abstraction (OOPSLA 2025), whose first implementation extended Finch, and of Insum (ASPLOS 2026), the sparse GPU compiler supplying format-aware reformulation.
author0: Jaeyeon Won

title: Accelerating Multimedia Pipelines with Structural Specialization
summary: This M.Eng. thesis treats performance engineering as a specialization problem: identifying where a program's generality costs work, and exploiting constraints on inputs or environment that a build-time or run-time parameter makes available. It contributes a framework of specialization axes with the correctness obligation each incurs, a reproducible procedure for finding opportunities in an unfamiliar codebase, and deployability criteria for judging the result. Two case studies apply it: BuildIt-staged FFmpeg filters, where a staged geq interpreter emits straight-line C and runs up to 11× faster, and a ten-patch series for libvmaf reaching a 40% end-to-end speedup at 4K, bit-identical on integer feature paths and differing only by floating-point reassociation elsewhere. In both codebases, hardware-model specialization was already exhausted while value-range and algebraic specialization were largely untouched. The staged filters and the width-specialized convolution kernels are built with BuildIt (CGO 2021).
author0: Arjun Barrett

title: Programmatic Generation of GPU Matrix Multiplication Primitives
summary: This M.Eng. thesis generates pipelined Hopper GPU matrix multiplication kernels directly from loop nests, without asking the programmer to reason about tiling, warpgroup MMA, or the asynchronous memory model. It contributes GPU memory support in BuildIt's intermediate representation, carrying qualifiers such as __shared__ through existing passes unchanged; CuteHopperGemm, a staged helper library that lowers to CuTe so the compiler need not reason about CuTe directly; and extract_cute, an analysis pass that recognizes an annotated matmul loop nest and rewrites it. Compiler annotations extend the approach to several data types, memory layouts, and matrix dimensions. Generated kernels reach 82 to 96 percent of cuBLAS performance for square problems from 2048 to 8192, with up to 20× less user code. The work extends BuildIt (CGO 2021), adding GPU code generation to its type-based multi-stage framework.
author0: Rishab Parthasarathy

title: Accelerating Microservice Network Stacks on Kubernetes via a Unified DSL
summary: A unified DSL generates both the deployment configuration and the communication stack for Kubernetes microservices from one Python-like source file. Decorators mark which functions become microservices and which ports carry inter-container calls; the compiler emits Dockerfiles, manifests, build and deploy scripts, and NetBlocks-generated protocol code. Making custom stacks coexist with Kubernetes required a protocol identifier field and packet filter, so ARP, DNS and ICMP traffic no longer crashes the generated analyzer, and Headless Services to reach pods without NAT. On a prime-counter application, 42 input lines expand to 2,978 generated lines, and a NetBlocks UDP-over-Ethernet stack cuts median end-to-end latency against gRPC by about 330×, 41× in the communication layer alone. The unified DSL extends NetBlocks (PLDI 2024), driving its protocol stack generator and adapting it to Kubernetes, and so inherits the staging of BuildIt (CGO 2021).
author0: Ishibe, Hoku and Hu, Siyi and Brahmakshatriya, Ajay and Amarasinghe, Saman and Sato, Yukinori
booktitle: 10th cross-disciplinary Workshop on Computing Systems, Infrastructures, and Programming (xSIG)

title: Specifying, Tiling, and Fusing Complex Reductions
summary: This M.Eng. thesis extends the Halide scheduling language to complex reductions. FlashTile, backed by a theoretical framework for deriving tile-merge functions, semi-automatically performs complex tiling transformations of reductions and sliding-window aggregations that Halide otherwise forces into the function definition. Inductive functions let Halide fuse loops over recursively defined functions whose loop index is a recursive variable, as FlashAttention requires. FlashTile replicates hand-optimized schedules such as box filter pipelines and, implementing a novel optimization, produces up to an 8× speedup over PyTorch for a transformer-based time-series model. The thesis builds on the PLDI 2013 Halide compiler, into which FlashTile is integrated. Its StereoBM case study revisits limits that Zhang's 2016 stereo matching thesis met in scheduling dynamic programming and recursive filters.
author0: Steven N. Raphael

title: Towards a Flexible Python Framework for Developing Domain-Specific Languages
summary: This M.Eng. thesis develops a flexible Python framework for building domain-specific languages. It targets the redundant code DSL construction usually requires — intermediate representations such as abstract syntax trees and control-flow graphs, and the analyses over them. The framework supplies reusable components: Python abstract data types via a mypy plugin, functors for traversing IRs, control-flow-graph and SSA construction, and data-flow analyses out of the box. To avoid Python's runtime overhead, parts are compiled with Codon for comparable performance. The thesis concludes with an implementation of finch-tensor-lite on the platform and a runtime comparison. The framework builds directly on Codon (CC 2023), using its ahead-of-time compilation of Python to make a high-level DSL-building layer performant. Its finch-tensor-lite target ports the tensor programming model of Finch (OOPSLA 2025) into the Python setting.
author0: Shreya Chaudhary

title: Vectorizing Complex Programs for Modern Architectures
summary: Chen's PhD thesis revisits superword-level parallelism (SLP) as a general framework for auto-vectorization, addressing three reasons production compilers fail to vectorize real-world programs: control flow, ambiguous dependencies, and instruction complexity. It contributes SuperVectorization, a generalized SLP vectorizer whose Predicated SSA intermediate representation lets it vectorize across basic blocks and loop nests; a fine-grained program versioning framework that handles dependencies static analysis cannot resolve by inserting runtime checks; and VeGen, which targets vector instructions outside the SIMD model using only their documented semantics. This is the most complete treatment of the work published as VeGen (ASPLOS 2021, with an earlier S.M. thesis version), control-flow SLP vectorization (PLDI 2022), and fine-grained program versioning (MICRO 2024). The vectorizer builds on the superword-level parallelism of Larsen and Amarasinghe's PLDI 2000 paper.
author0: Yishen Chen
Won, Jaeyeon and Ahrens, Willow and Emer, Joel and Amarasinghe, Saman
title: Insum: Sparse GPU Kernels Simplified and Optimized with Indirect Einsums
summary: Insum is a compiler for sparse GPU kernels. It rewrites format-agnostic Einsums over sparse tensors into format-conscious indirect Einsums, which map sparse data and metadata onto dense tensor operations through indirect indexing, then lowers them to the PyTorch compiler, extended to better support Tensor-Core-enabled indirect operations. Two fixed-length sparse formats, GroupCOO and BlockGroupCOO, are designed to fit indirect Einsums naturally. Across sparse GPU applications including SpMM, equivariant tensor products, and sparse convolution, Insum achieves 1.14×–3.81× speedups while reducing lines of code by 202×–4491× compared to hand-written implementations. Won's PhD thesis (2026) gives the most complete treatment, presenting format-aware reformulation as the general form of the indirect-Einsum rewrite.
booktitle: 31st ACM International Conference on Architectural Support for Programming Languages and Operating Systems (ASPLOS)

author0: Li, Guoyu and Cao, Yang and Ng, Lucas H. L. and Charlton, Alexander and Wang, Qianzhou and Punter, Will and Papaphilippou, Philippos and Guo, Ce and Fan, Hongxiang and Luk, Wayne and Amarasinghe, Saman and Brahmakshatriya, Ajay
title: SPAC: Automating FPGA-based Network Switches with Protocol Adaptive Customization
summary: SPAC automates the generation of FPGA-based network switches co-optimized for custom protocols and application-specific traffic patterns. It combines a domain-specific language for protocol–architecture co-design, a library of modular HLS-based switch components — parsers, forwarding structures, schedulers, and buffer allocation strategies — and a trace-aware design-space exploration engine with multi-fidelity simulation that identifies Pareto-optimal designs. Across scenarios from latency-sensitive sensor and high-frequency-trading networks to datacenter fabrics, SPAC-generated designs reduce LUT and BRAM usage by 55% and 53% and cut latency by 7.8% to 38.4% relative to fixed-architecture counterparts. Developed with Imperial College London, SPAC specifies its custom protocols in syntax compatible with NetBlocks (PLDI 2024), the host-side custom-protocol compiler, carrying that work from host stacks into the switch.
booktitle: 34th IEEE Annual International Symposium on Field-Programmable Custom Computing Machines (FCCM)

author0: Bansal, Manya and Sainati, Daniel and Cutler, Joseph W. and Amarasinghe, Saman and Ragan-Kelley, Jonathan
title: Modular GPU Programming with Typed Perspectives
summary: Prism is a low-level GPU programming language that restores modularity to kernel programming. GPU programs are written per-thread, yet collective operations like Tensor Core instructions and synchronization must execute cooperatively across thread groups, making functions that encapsulate them error prone. Prism's typed perspectives materialize, at the type level, the granularity at which the programmer is controlling threads, guaranteeing that collective operations run with the compute resources they need. A core calculus, Bundl, proves type-and-perspective safety, and an implementation supporting Tensor Cores and asynchronous data movement matches hand-optimized CUDA on an H100 and a 4070 Ti Super.

title: UniTe: A Universal Tensor Abstraction for Capturing Spatial Relationships
summary: UniTe is a tensor abstraction that captures spatial relationships across the tensors of a program: tensors defined relative to a common reference coordinate system but differing in axes, spacings, origins, and shape. It contributes a mathematical model of these relationships, compiler support for reasoning about them, and two DSLs and optimizing compilers built on the abstraction, CoLa for Python and SHiM for C/C++. On image and video compression benchmarks, naive bookkeeping for spatial relationships runs up to 65× slower than reference C implementations; the UniTe compilers remove the overhead and reach performance parity. This journal article is the primary published account of UniTe. The compression abstractions first appeared in a DCC 2021 paper, and Ray's PhD dissertation gives the most complete treatment. CoLa is implemented within the Codon Python compiler, and SHiM generates code through the BuildIt staging library.

title: Sparse and Structured Tensor Programming
summary: Ahrens's PhD thesis develops sparse and structured tensor programming around the central problem of coiteration: simultaneously iterating over several tensors whose formats have different structure. It presents looplets, a language that decomposes loops over structured formats hierarchically so a compiler can coiterate over any combination of formats, capturing key mathematical properties with term rewriting, and Finch, a language that combines control flow and tensor structure in a common representation, specializing loops, ifs, and breaks to sparsity, run-length encoding, symmetry, or blocks. Case studies show speedups in linear algebra, image processing, and graph analytics. The most complete treatment of this line of work: Chapter 3 is the thesis form of the CGO 2023 Looplets paper, and later chapters appeared separately as SySTeC and the continuous tensor abstraction. The Tensor Algebra Compiler and its RLE extensions serve as evaluation baselines, and Patel's M.Eng. thesis built on Finch.
author0: Willow Ahrens

title: Democratizing High-Performance DSL Development with the BuildIt Framework
summary: Brahmakshatriya’s PhD thesis is the most complete treatment of the BuildIt project. It formalizes Re-Execution Based Multi-Staging (REMS), addressing the side-effect leak problem of imperative staging, and describes BuildIt, a lightweight type-based implementation of REMS in C++ requiring no compiler changes. The thesis details extensions that ease high-performance DSL development and three case studies — EasyGraphit, NetBlocks, and BREeze, targeting graph analytics, ad-hoc network protocols, and regular-expression matching — showing 10-100x reductions in implementation effort while performing on par with or better than purpose-built compiler frameworks on CPUs and GPUs. It closes with D2X, which adds extensible, contextual debugging to any DSL built on BuildIt. The thesis unifies the material of the CGO 2021 BuildIt paper, BuilDSL (CGO 2022), D2X (CGO 2023), and NetBlocks (PLDI 2024); BREeze is described further in Mitrovska’s M.Eng. thesis (2023), and EasyGraphit is evaluated against the original GraphIt GPU compiler (CGO 2021).
author0: Ajay Brahmakshatriya

title: WACO: Learning workload-aware co-optimization of the format and  schedule of a sparse tensor program
summary: Won's S.M. thesis presents WACO, which co-optimizes the sparse format and the schedule of a sparse tensor program for a given sparsity pattern. A sparse convolutional network, WACONet, learns features of the sparsity pattern; a SuperSchedule template embeds the coupled behavior of format and schedule in a cost model; and an approximate nearest-neighbor search retrieves the best design from the joint space. On SpMV, SpMM, SDDMM, and MTTKRP across 726 sparsity patterns, WACO achieves average speedups of 1.43×, 1.18×, 1.14×, and 1.27× over the best of four baselines. WACO chooses formats and schedules for mechanisms the TACO project built: the Tensor Algebra Compiler, its format abstraction, and its sparse iteration space transformation framework define the search space the learned cost model navigates.
author0: Won, Jaeyeon

title: Automated Finite Elements
summary: Collin's S.M. thesis introduces ElementForge, a finite element system that is parametric over the literate mathematical specification of a finite element, written in a domain-specific language. The compiler reasons about tensor spaces, tensors, and tensor bases from first principles to derive implementations of elements previously derived only by hand, and it minimally couples tensor fields, mesh topologies, sparse tensors, and assembled operators, so derived elements apply parametrically to new meshes, PDEs, and boundary conditions. The Morley, Bell, Argyris, and Hermite-like elements are each specified in under 50 lines of code and used together in a single simulation.
author0: Collin, Teodora Fields

title: On-Stack Replacement Across User-Kernel Boundaries
summary: Mohr's M.Eng. thesis contributes an on-stack replacement (OSR) mechanism that operates across the user-kernel boundary. It extends LakePlacid, a compiler-based system that inverts kernel bypass: rather than moving the network stack into user space, it migrates an application's hottest packet-handling paths into the kernel. Packets the kernel-resident code cannot handle fall back to the full user-space application; the thesis makes this fallback seamless, without re-executing side effects, by letting execution switch between code versions at any conditional and by moving the live stack from kernel to user space. The stack-switching mechanism adds only about 23 nanoseconds per call.
author0: Mohr, Katherine

title: ProgGen: Automatic Dataset Generation for the Halide Domain Specific Language
summary: ProgGen is a program generator for building the datasets that data-driven compiler cost models are trained on. Cost models for domain-specific languages usually depend on hand-written random program generators that take substantial engineering to produce realistic computation patterns. ProgGen instead borrows from genetic programming: starting from a small seed set of programs in a target domain, it evolves a dataset automatically. Against the Halide autoscheduler's random generator, ProgGen trails in the image processing and neural network domains that generator was engineered for, but is competitive in video processing and linear algebra, and reaches new domains with far less engineering time. The programs it generates and the cost models it trains target the Halide language and compiler.
author0: Holbrook, Zachary

title: Codon: A Framework for Pythonic Domain-Specific Languages
summary: This M.Eng. thesis presents Codon, a framework for building high-performance DSLs on a purely Pythonic base. It argues that dynamic languages like Python, though flexible, have ceded performance-critical domains to static languages like C++, and that a Python framework can close the gap. Codon pairs a purpose-built static type checker with a novel intermediate representation, letting developers implement analyses, optimization passes, and modular DSLs with little effort. The thesis validates the design with several Codon DSLs that achieve sizeable speedups over Python and in some cases over C++. Codon's type checker and IR derive from the Seq language (OOPSLA 2019), whose compiler it generalizes beyond genomics.
author0: Ramirez, Gabriel

title: Lightweight and Locality-Aware Composition of Black-Box Subroutines
summary: Fern is a system that fuses compositions of black-box subroutines to recover the locality lost at call boundaries. Its insight: most fusion opportunities require knowing only data production and consumption patterns, not the semantics of the computation. A lightweight enrichment of subroutine declarations exposes these patterns, and Fern generates an outer loop nest that calls the original subroutines on subsets of data. Fern is competitive with high-performance libraries with manually fused operators, fuses across library and domain boundaries, including proprietary libraries such as ArmPL and Apple's Accelerate, and delivers up to 5× speedups over unfused code.

title: Performance Analysis of the Apple AMX Matrix Accelerator
summary: This thesis empirically characterizes AMX, the matrix coprocessor in Apple Silicon that Apple exposes only through the Accelerate library. Microbenchmarks quantify load, store, and compute throughput across AMX's matrix and vector modes and data types. A case study develops an in-place matrix multiplication that handles non-multiple-of-eight sizes with masked outer products and overlapping tiles, avoiding Accelerate's scratch buffers and outperforming it. A rule-based latency model — per-instruction base time, switch latency, and data-dependency terms — is fitted on length-two instruction loops and predicts cycle counts for held-out length-three sequences.
author0: Zhou, Jonathan

title: Applied Compiler Optimizations for Proving Code
summary: Ruiz's thesis asks what happens to compiler optimizations when code is destined not for a processor but for a cryptographic prover. Working with the SP1 zkVM toolchain, which generates zero-knowledge proofs for Rust programs compiled to RISC-V, it builds a benchmarking framework for the relative proof cost of individual instructions. The central finding is that shift instructions save little over multiplication inside a prover, so strength reduction of constant multiplies, a profitable optimization for hardware execution, can lengthen proof generation. The thesis also tabulates relative proof costs across the RISC-V arithmetic instructions and investigates explicit versus implicit register loading.
author0: Ruiz, Ricardo

title: Converting PyTorch Models to StreamIt Pipelines
summary: This M.Eng. thesis makes end-to-end machine learning inference through StreamIt pipelines work. It links StreamIt graphs generated from PyTorch models against the LibTorch API, adding a StatefulFilter construct that carries per-layer weights, BuildIt custom types for tensors, expanding arrays, and layer state, and a JSON-driven generator that produces filter definitions for PyTorch operators automatically. A ResNet model converted through torch.fx compiles to an executable whose inference latencies are slightly higher than PyTorch's but comparable, leaving room for the pipeline-level optimizations the representation exposes. The work extends Dighe's 2024 thesis, which rebuilt the StreamIt language as a compiler staged through BuildIt and first converted PyTorch computation graphs to StreamIt form; this thesis completes that path from converted graph to running inference.
author0: Rajvee, Muhender

title: Eliminating Hallucination-Induced Errors in Code Generation with Functional Clustering
summary: Functional clustering is a black-box wrapper that removes nearly all hallucination-induced errors from LLM code generation. It samples many candidates per prompt, asks the model for test inputs only, runs each candidate in a sandbox, and clusters programs by input/output behavior; the mass of the largest cluster is an exact confidence score, and a threshold yields a selective coder. On LiveCodeBench it preserves baseline pass@1 while cutting the error rate of returned answers from roughly 65% to 2%, and to 0% at a threshold that still answers 15.6% of prompts. A condensed arXiv preprint (2025) presents the same method; the thesis gives the fuller treatment, adding manual audits that trace residual errors to prompt misinterpretation.
author0: Ravuri, Chaitanya

title: Automatic Conversion of C and C++ Programs to the BuildIt Multi-Stage Programming Framework
summary: This M.Eng. thesis by Aryan Kumar builds a tool that automatically converts existing C and C++ programs into equivalent BuildIt programs. Staging a program with BuildIt normally requires changing declared variable types by hand; the tool automates that step using Clang tooling together with modifications to the Clang compiler to perform type-modification rewrites, plus a stub generator and driver that handle structs, variadic functions, recursion, and global variables. The result is unstaged BuildIt code that reproduces the original program and can then be specialized by marking chosen variables static, opening existing C/C++ repositories to staging and specialization without manual rewriting. The tool targets the BuildIt framework introduced at CGO 2021, whose type-based design makes conversion a matter of type rewriting.
author0: Kumar, Aryan

title: Optimizing Scheduling for Stream Structured Programming for StreamIt
summary: This M.Eng. thesis adds a scheduler interface to the StreamIt compiler so that hardware-customized schedulers for heterogeneous and distributed machines can be written quickly. The interface models the target as a hardware graph with compute and bandwidth costs, exposes StreamIt-specific graph transformations with a dependency-breaking algorithm, and lets users pin individual filters by hand. Two schedulers exercise it — an exhaustive search-based scheduler and a heuristic min-cut scheduler — optimizing throughput and latency on synthetic benchmarks. A Split Switch extension to the language, with an inlining optimization, allows a stream graph to activate alternative branches at runtime. The original StreamIt schedulers targeted the homogeneous tiled Raw machine through the ASPLOS 2002 compiler and the coarse-grained parallelization of ASPLOS 2006; this work reopens that scheduling problem for accelerator hardware. Its cost model computes steady-state schedules with phased scheduling, and the implementation lives inside Dighe's multistage StreamIt compiler.
author0: Dow, Nicholas

title: A Framework for Fine-Grained Program Versioning
summary: This paper presents a fine-grained framework for ruling out program dependencies at run time, generalizing the loop versioning of production compilers, which works at whole-loop granularity. A client optimization specifies groups of instructions whose independence is desired but statically unprovable; the framework duplicates those instructions and guards the originals with runtime checks, executing the duplicates when a check fails. It is not tied to one optimization: extending an SLP vectorizer gives 1.17× over Clang's vectorizers on TSVC and 1.51× on PolyBench, and a more aggressive redundant load elimination gives 1.012× on SPEC 2017 floating point. The client vectorizer is the SuperVectorization system of the PLDI 2022 control-flow SLP paper, whose Predicated SSA representation it reuses to express dependence conditions; the ambiguous dependencies it targets have limited SLP since the PLDI 2000 paper. The work reappears as a chapter of Chen's PhD thesis (2026).

title: Finch: Sparse and Structured Tensor Programming with Control Flow
summary: Finch is a programming language for sparse and structured tensors with full control flow. It supports loops, if-conditions, early breaks, and affine or scatter/gather indexing over tensors whose structure may include sparsity, run-length encoding, symmetry, triangles, padding, or blocks. The compiler combines control flow and data structures in one representation and specializes programs to structure automatically, exploiting structural zeros, repeated values, and clustered nonzeros. Reported results include geomean speedups of 1.26× on SpMV and 1.30× on SpGEMM, 2.47× on Bellman-Ford with 4× fewer lines of code than GraphBLAS, and 19.5× on an image-processing workload. This is the main language paper of the Finch project. Later work builds directly on it: SySTeC generates symmetry-aware sparse kernels through Finch, and the continuous tensor abstraction extends its compiler to tensors with real-valued indices. Finch also backs the PyData/Sparse library.
abstract: From FORTRAN to NumPy, tensors have revolutionized how we express computation. However, tensors in these, and almost all prominent systems, can only handle dense rectilinear integer grids. Real world tensors often contain underlying structure, such as sparsity, runs of repeated values, or symmetry. Support for structured data is fragmented and incomplete. Existing frameworks limit the tensor structures and program control flow they support to better simplify the problem. In this work, we propose a new programming language, Finch, which supports both flexible control flow and diverse data structures. Finch facilitates a programming model which resolves the challenges of computing over structured tensors by combining control flow and data structures into a common representation where they can be co-optimized. Finch automatically specializes control flow to data so that performance engineers can focus on experimenting with many algorithms. Finch supports a familiar programming language of loops, statements, ifs, breaks, etc., over a wide variety of tensor structures, such as sparsity, run-length-encoding, symmetry, triangles, padding, or blocks. Finch reliably utilizes the key properties of structure, such as structural zeros, repeated values, or clustered non-zeros. We show that this leads to dramatic speedups in operations such as SpMV and SpGEMM, image processing, and graph analytics.
author0: Ahrens, Willow and Collin, Teodora Fields and Patel, Radha and Deeds, Kyle and Hong, Changwan and Amarasinghe, Saman

title: The Continuous Tensor Abstraction: Where Indices Are Real
summary: This paper introduces the continuous tensor abstraction, in which tensor indices take real-number values (such as A[3.14]) and tensor algebra expressions are defined over continuous domains. Under a piecewise-constant assumption, infinite iteration spaces are processed in finite time. The paper contributes a storage format for continuous tensors, reduction operations defined by integration, and a code generation technique that expresses computational geometry, genomics, point-cloud, and Neural Radiance Field computations as tensor programs. Against hand-implemented CPU libraries it reports average speedups of 9.20× on 2D radius search with about 60× fewer lines of code, 1.22× on genomic interval overlap queries, and 1.69× on trilinear interpolation. The abstraction is implemented as an extension of Finch and leverages Looplets to partition continuous iteration spaces; a chapter of Ahrens's PhD thesis presents the same material in thesis form, and Won's PhD thesis (2026) is the most complete treatment.
abstract: This paper introduces the continuous tensor abstraction, allowing indices to take real-number values (e.g., A[3.14]). It also presents continuous tensor algebra expressions, such as Cx,y = Ax,y * Bx,y, where indices are defined over a continuous domain. Our implementation supports piecewise-constant tensors, enabling infinite domains to be processed in finite time. We introduce new tensor formats for efficient storage and code generation techniques for automatic kernel generation. For the first time, domains such as computational geometry and computer graphics are expressed in the language of tensor programming. Our compiler demonstrates competitive or better performance compared to hand-optimized kernels across diverse applications, with significant speedups and reduced lines of code in tasks such as radius search, genomic interval queries, and trilinear interpolation in Neural Radiance Fields.

title: SySTeC: A Symmetric Sparse Tensor Compiler
summary: SySTeC is a compiler that automatically generates symmetry-aware code for sparse and structured tensor kernels, the first to exploit symmetry and sparsity within the same kernel. Symmetry in an order-n tensor can save up to a factor of n!, but symmetric optimizations interact awkwardly with sparse formats, which obscure where elements sit in memory. It introduces a taxonomy for symmetry in tensor kernels and transformations for each kind: restricting iteration to a canonical triangle, reusing memory reads, and filtering redundant computation and storage. Speedups range from 1.36× for SSYMV to 30.4× for a five-dimensional MTTKRP over non-symmetric implementations. SySTeC compiles to Finch, relying on its structured formats and control flow, and adopts the partial-symmetry formalism of a 2021 arXiv attempt within TACO. Patel's M.Eng. thesis is an earlier version of this work, and a chapter of Ahrens's PhD thesis presents the same methodology.
abstract: Symmetric and sparse tensors arise naturally in many domains including linear algebra, statistics, physics, chemistry, and graph theory. Symmetric tensors are equal to their transposes, so in the n-dimensional case we can save up to a factor of n! by avoiding redundant operations. Sparse tensors, on the other hand, are mostly zero, and we can save asymptotically by processing only nonzeros. Unfortunately, specializing for both symmetry and sparsity at the same time is uniquely challenging. Optimizing for symmetry requires consideration of n! transpositions of a triangular kernel, which can be complex and error prone. Considering multiple transposed iteration orders and triangular loop bounds also complicates iteration through intricate sparse tensor formats. Additionally, since each combination of symmetry and sparse tensor formats requires a specialized implementation, this leads to a combinatorial number of cases. A compiler is needed, but existing compilers cannot take advantage of both symmetry and sparsity within the same kernel. In this paper, we describe the first compiler which can automatically generate symmetry-aware code for sparse or structured tensor kernels. We introduce a taxonomy for symmetry in tensor kernels, and show how to target each kind of symmetry. Our implementation demonstrates significant speedups ranging from 1.36x for SSYMV to 30.4x for a 5-dimensional MTTKRP over the non-symmetric state of the art.

title: AskIt: Unified Programming Interface for Programming with Large Language Models
summary: AskIt is a domain-specific language, embedded in TypeScript and Python, for programming with large language models. It gives one interface to the two ways an application can use an LLM, invoking it directly at runtime or having it generate code, so developers can switch modes without rewriting. Three mechanisms enable this: type-guided output control that removes format engineering from prompts, template-based function definitions, and automatic prompt generation for both modes. Across 50 tasks AskIt shortened prompts by 16.14%, and switching from direct LLM calls to generated code brought efficiency gains on GSM8K.

title: Mechanised Hypersafety Proofs about Structured Data
summary: This PLDI 2024 paper develops the Logic for Graceful Tensor Manipulation (LGTM), a Hoare-style relational separation logic for proving that computations over compressed, structured data agree with their dense counterparts. Such specifications are hypersafety properties relating traces of k programs; LGTM's parametrised hyper-triples let k depend on program variables, so a compressed matrix-vector product is specified against the format's access functions. The logic is mechanised as a foundational Coq embedding with a soundness proof and tactic library, and validated on 13 case studies including compressed arrays and sparse tensors. Joint with the National University of Singapore, the paper gives a verification story for COMMIT's structured-data compilers: its benchmark suite adopts programs produced by the TACO tensor algebra compiler (OOPSLA 2017), and its running example follows output of Looplets (CGO 2023) — exactly the multi-loop, format-aware code LGTM specifies.

title: An Intermediate Representation for Expressing and Optimizing Computations in Lattice Quantum Chromodynamics
summary: This M.Eng. thesis develops an intermediate representation and rewrite system for correlator computations in lattice quantum chromodynamics, whose summations scale factorially with the number of quarks. The LQCD IR represents mathematical structure — sums, products, permutations — alongside algorithmic devices such as precomputation, and correctness-preserving rewrites (sum separation, loop linearization, expression partitioning, precomputation over ranges) restructure naive specifications in search of better asymptotic bounds. Baryon, dibaryon, and hexaquark case studies show up to 5× speedups on the most important problem, in hundreds rather than thousands of source lines. The work grows out of COMMIT's collaboration with lattice QCD physicists: it is measured against the hand-scheduled Tiramisu correlator codes used in results such as a variational study of two-nucleon systems, and rewritten programs are scheduled for GPUs through Halide, separating algorithmic rewriting from machine-level scheduling.

title: Variational study of two-nucleon systems with lattice QCD
summary: This Physical Review D article studies the low-energy spectrum and scattering of two-nucleon systems with lattice QCD using a variational approach. Correlation-function matrices are built from a range of interpolating operators — plane-wave dibaryons, localized hexaquarks, and quasilocal operators — computed with sparsened timeslice-to-all quark propagators and projected onto irreducible representations of the cubic group. At a pion mass of 806 MeV, the study obtains upper bounds on two-nucleon energy levels and shows that interpolating-operator dependence can produce missing energy levels, while remaining inconclusive about bound states at this quark mass. Amarasinghe and Baghdadi contributed the contraction computations: a C++ implementation whose optimizations were facilitated by Tiramisu. A 2024 M.Eng. thesis on an intermediate representation for lattice QCD later implemented these correlation-function computations as case studies.

title: Fast Multistage Compilation of Machine Learning Computation Graphs
summary: This M.Eng. thesis rebuilds the StreamIt compiler as a multistage program: the language's filters, pipelines, and split-joins are expressed as a C++ library staged through BuildIt, so that graph construction, steady-state scheduling, and flow-rate constraint solving execute at the first stage and specialized inference code is generated at the second. On top of this compiler, the thesis builds a converter that extracts PyTorch computation graphs through torch.fx, translates them into an intermediate representation, and emits StreamIt graphs — handling ResNet-style duplicate split-joins, LSTM sequence models, dead-code elimination, and fused instructions — so that machine learning models can be distributed across cores and machines. The thesis restores the abstractions of the StreamIt language on the BuildIt multistage framework, replacing the standalone compiler stack of the 2000s. Two 2025 theses continue the effort: Rajvee's links the generated pipelines to LibTorch for end-to-end inference, and Dow's adds a scheduler interface for heterogeneous hardware.

title: A System To Exploit Symmetry in Common Tensor Kernels
summary: Patel's M.Eng. thesis identifies and categorizes methods to exploit symmetry in common tensor kernels. Symmetry in an order-n tensor can save a factor of up to n! in memory accesses and operations, but hand-writing symmetric kernels nearly doubles implementation burden even for 2D BLAS. title: Looplets: A Language for Structured Coiteration
summary: Looplets is a language for describing the structure of arrays so that a compiler can generate code to coiterate over any combination of structures. Real-world arrays contain structure — sparsity, runs of repeated values, symmetry — and specializing for it yields significant speedups, but code generation is hard when arrays with different structure interact. Looplets decompose loops over structured formats hierarchically, so key properties can be captured with term rewriting. The technique enables new formats (1DVBL for irregular clustered sparsity), new iteration strategies (galloping intersections), and new operations over structured data (concatenation, convolution). Looplets grew out of the TACO line: Kjolstad, of the Tensor Algebra Compiler, is a co-author, the input language extends concrete index notation from the workspaces paper, and TACO's RLE extensions serve as an evaluation baseline. The continuous tensor abstraction later built on Looplets, and Ahrens's PhD thesis gives the most complete treatment.

title: Unified Convolution Framework: A compiler-based approach to support sparse convolutions
summary: The Unified Convolution Framework (UCF) expresses many kinds of sparse convolution — filter sparse, activation sparse, and submanifold — in one compiler abstraction. Where libraries implement each sparse convolution separately, UCF extends the Einsum language of the TACO tensor algebra compiler with affine index expressions, so convolutions can be declared and still composed with TACO's format and scheduling languages. TACO-UCF averages 1.32× and 8.3× speedups on filter sparse and submanifold sparse convolutions over specialized CPU libraries, outperforms a GPU library by 1.47× on 80%-sparse ResNet50 filter convolution, and accelerates submanifold neighbor retrieval by 2.55× and 3.34× over MinkowskiEngine and TorchSparse. The framework grows out of TACO and the format abstractions of the OOPSLA 2018 formats paper, and its core lowering generalizes the single-variable affine index expressions of the sparse array programming paper to the multi-variable case.

title: Halide in Molecular Dynamics
summary: This M.Eng. thesis evaluates Halide, a language built for image processing pipelines, as a vehicle for molecular dynamics, where complex loop structures and heavy per-timestep arithmetic make simulations expensive. title: Implementing BREeze - a High-Performance Regular Expression Library Using Code Generation with BuildIt
summary: BREeze is a regular-expression matching library built with code generation, described in Tamara Mitrovska’s M.Eng. thesis. Rather than interpreting a pattern at match time, BREeze parses the regex into a state-transition table and uses staging to generate specialized matching code for each expression, adapting Thompson’s NFA simulation to avoid catastrophic backtracking. A set of scheduling options — splitting the regex, matching multiple characters at once, dynamic grouping, interleaving, and splitting the input string — lets users tune the generated matchers. The full library takes about 1,500 lines of code yet performs comparably to production engines such as PCRE2, RE2, and Hyperscan. BREeze is implemented on BuildIt (CGO 2021), the type-based multi-stage programming framework, and extends a small staged regex compiler introduced with BuilDSL (CGO 2022); Brahmakshatriya’s PhD thesis (2025) later presents BREeze as one of its case studies.

title: Unified Compilation for Lossless Compression and Sparse Computing
summary: Donenfeld's S.M. thesis is the most complete treatment of unified compilation for lossless compression and sparse computing. It represents losslessly compressed data as generalized sparse tensors, with repeated values expressed as non-scalar, dynamic fill values, and shows how a compiler can generate code that computes on RLE- and LZ77-compressed images and video without decompressing them. title: WACO: Learning workload-aware co-optimization of the format and  schedule of a sparse tensor program
summary: WACO co-optimizes the sparse format and the schedule of a sparse tensor program for a given sparsity pattern. Its core is a cost model predicting runtime from sparsity pattern, format, and schedule: a sparse convolutional network, WACONet, learns pattern features, and a SuperSchedule template embeds the coupled behavior of format and schedule. An approximate nearest-neighbor search retrieves the best design from the co-optimization space. On SpMV, SpMM, SDDMM, and MTTKRP across 726 sparsity patterns, WACO achieves average speedups of 1.43×, 1.18×, 1.14×, and 1.27× over the best of four baselines. WACO supplies the policy for mechanisms the TACO project built: the format abstraction and the sparse iteration space transformation framework layered on the Tensor Algebra Compiler define the joint space its learned cost model searches.

title: Codon: A Compiler for High-Performance Pythonic Applications and DSLs
summary: Codon is a domain-extensible compiler and DSL framework that gives Python's syntax and semantics ahead-of-time compilation and C-like performance. It statically type-checks and compiles Python programs and exposes a purpose-built intermediate representation into which developers plug domain-specific optimizations, analyses, and language extensions. The paper builds several extensions and DSLs on this base — bioinformatics, secure multi-party computation, block-based data compression, and parallel programming — arguing that a high-level host language can reach performance usually reserved for C or C++ without giving up Python's ease. Codon is the main compiler paper of the Codon project. It generalizes the static typing and intermediate representation first developed for genomics in Seq (OOPSLA 2019), and its bioinformatics IR passes are demonstrated in a Nature Biotechnology genomics paper. Its extensible compiler was later built on by Jessica Ray's block-based compression language and Shreya Chaudhary's Python DSL framework.

title: A Universal Tensor Abstraction and its Application to and Implementation within Block-Based Compression
summary: Ray's PhD dissertation defines the Universal Tensor abstraction (UniTe), a mathematical account of tensors located in a common coordinate system and of the spatial relationships among them — projections, permutations, refinement, coarsening. It applies the abstraction to block-based compression, the core of JPEG, H.264, H.265, and H.266, where blocks represent everything from a video to a single pixel and must track location relative to other blocks. A library implementation exposes the overhead of computing spatial relationships in inner loops; two DSLs and compilers, CoLa and SHiM, remove it, reaching parity with hand-implemented C code. The most complete treatment of the UniTe line: the project began with a DCC 2021 paper on language abstractions for compression, and the material was later condensed into a journal article in ACM TACO. CoLa is built on the Codon Python compiler, and SHiM generates inlined code through the BuildIt staging library.

title: GSTACO: A Generalized Sparse Tensor Algebra Compiler
summary: GSTACO is a generalized sparse tensor algebra compiler built to support whole applications, with graph algorithms as the driving case. Its language extends tensor index notation with user-defined functions, general reduction operators, multiple-output kernels that share loops, and scheduling constructs for data-dependent format switching and loop reordering. The compiler lowers this language through an IR with cross-kernel rewrites such as memory reuse and generates sparse code through Finch. PageRank, breadth-first search, single-source shortest paths, connected components, and betweenness centrality are all expressible; PageRank is evaluated against GraphIt. The thesis responds to the gap between TACO, which optimizes individual tensor expressions, and graph DSLs like GraphIt, which handle complete algorithms and served as both proof of concept and baseline. Code generation is delegated to Finch, invoking the structured coiteration of Looplets for each tensor expression.

title: Format Abstractions for the Compilation of Sparse Tensor Algebra
summary: Chou's PhD dissertation describes how to build a sparse tensor algebra compiler that supports a wide variety of storage formats. Formats as different as CSR, COO, and DIA, and pointer-based structures like linked lists, BSTs, and C-trees, can all be expressed as compositions of per-dimension level formats, each defined through a common set of abstractions that capture how nonzeros are stored, accessed, and assembled. Implemented in TACO, the technique yielded the first compiler able to generate code for any basic tensor algebra expression with sparse tensors stored in arbitrary formats, at performance competitive with hand-optimized libraries. This is the most complete treatment of the TACO format-abstraction line, consolidating Chou's S.M. thesis, the OOPSLA 2018 formats paper, the PLDI 2020 format conversion paper, and the OOPSLA 2022 dynamic formats paper. Its code generation technique generalizes those of the OOPSLA 2017 TACO paper and the workspaces paper.

title: Compilation of Dynamic Sparse Tensor Algebra
summary: This OOPSLA 2022 paper shows how a compiler can generate efficient tensor algebra code for dynamic sparse tensors — tensors whose sparsity structure evolves during execution, as in graph analytics. It contributes a node schema language for precisely specifying recursive, pointer-based data structures, expressing formats built from block linked lists, binary search trees, B-trees, and C-trees, and a code generator that computes on tensors stored in any of them. Generated kernels perform comparably to or better than PAM, Aspen, STINGER, and Terrace, while supporting a wider range of operations, including ones that mix static and dynamic operands. The paper extends the array-based level formats of the OOPSLA 2018 formats paper to mutable, pointer-based storage, generalizing code generation techniques from the OOPSLA 2017 TACO paper. Chou's PhD thesis incorporates this material and gives the most complete treatment.
journal: ACM SIGPLAN International Conference on Object-Oriented Programming, Systems, Languages, and Applications (OOPSLA)

title: Compilation of Sparse Array Programming Models
summary: This paper shows how to compile sparse array programming languages — array languages, in the style of NumPy, that support element-wise application, reduction, and broadcasting of arbitrary functions over dense and sparse arrays with any fill value. The compiler generalizes sparse iteration spaces beyond intersections and unions, deriving them automatically from algebraic properties annotated onto functions, and supports slicing of sparse sub-arrays. Generated code runs 1.4× to 53.7× faster than PyData/Sparse on user-defined functions and at 0.56× to 3.50× the speed of hand-optimized SuiteSparse:GraphBLAS on graph kernels. The compiler generalizes the Tensor Algebra Compiler beyond addition and multiplication and extends its format abstraction, composing with the sparse iteration space transformation framework. Henry's M.Eng. thesis is an earlier version of this material, and Chou's PhD thesis incorporates the paper. It was later built on by the Unified Convolution Framework and by unified compilation for lossless compression and sparse computing.
journal: ACM SIGPLAN International Conference on Object-Oriented Programming, Systems, Languages, and Applications (OOPSLA)

title: A Deep Dive Into Understanding The Random Walk-Based Temporal Graph Learning
summary: This IISWC paper characterizes random walk-based temporal graph learning, a scalable alternative to GCNs that operates on continuous-time dynamic graphs. It builds high-performance CPU and GPU implementations of link prediction and node classification — temporal random walks feeding word2vec embeddings — and shows that the workload's irregularity, utilization, and cache hit rates differ from graph traversal, deep learning, and GCN workloads. An algorithm-level study maps the tradeoff between predictive quality and runtime and identifies a balanced hyperparameter setting, while microarchitectural analysis uncovers bottlenecks in cache misses and dependency-related stalls, yielding optimization recommendations and open-source implementations.

title: A Python-based programming language for high-performance computational genomics
summary: This correspondence in Nature Biotechnology presents Seq to the computational biology community. It frames the problem biologists face as a choice between software ecosystems that allow rapid development at the expense of performance, such as Python and R, and low-level languages that run fast but are harder to develop and maintain, such as C++ and Rust. Seq is offered as a Python-based language for high-performance computational genomics that bridges this gap, giving high-level, Pythonic code the speed usually reached only in compiled languages through a static type system and genomics-specific compiler optimizations. It presents the same Seq work first published in the OOPSLA 2019 paper, aimed here at biologists rather than compiler researchers. Seq's static typing and IR design were later generalized into the domain-configurable Codon compiler (CC 2023).

title: Parallelizing Compiler Techniques Based On Linear Inequalities
summary: Amarasinghe's Stanford PhD thesis develops a framework based on systems of linear inequalities for deriving parallelizing-compiler algorithms. A single representation captures iteration, data, and processor spaces, giving systematic solutions for code generation by scanning polyhedra, interprocedural array data-flow analysis that parallelizes loops that span procedures and hundreds of lines, communication optimization for distributed memory machines, and the first compiler to apply a full suite of data transformations — transposing, strip-mining, and padding — to combat false sharing and cache conflicts. The thesis is the most complete treatment of Amarasinghe's SUIF-era work: it consolidates the communication optimization from PLDI 1993 and the interprocedural parallelization reported at LCPC 1995 and Supercomputing '95, drawing on array data-flow analysis and implemented within the SUIF compiler system. The parallelization analyses also appear in a TOPLAS 2005 article, and later work on strength reduction of division and modulo operations builds on machinery developed here.

title: High-Performance Computational Genomics
summary: This PhD thesis is the most complete treatment of Seq, a Python-based language for bioinformatics and genomics that combines the usability of high-level languages with the performance of C and C++. It evaluates Seq across the full genomics analysis pipeline — index construction, data pre- and post-processing, read mapping and alignment, and haplotype phasing — reporting implementations up to an order of magnitude faster than existing hand-optimized tools with a fraction of the code. The gains come from genomics-specific compiler optimizations beyond the reach of general-purpose compilers, coupled with a static type system that removes Python's runtime overhead. Its Seq chapters expand the OOPSLA 2019 paper.

title: Universal Graph Framework: Achieving High-Performance across Algorithms, Graph Types, and Architectures
summary: Brahmakshatriya's S.M. thesis proposes the Universal Graph Framework (UGF), which generates high-performance graph code for CPUs, GPUs, and domain-specific accelerators from a single algorithm specification. It decouples algorithm, schedule, and backend through GraphIR, a domain-specific intermediate representation; per-architecture backends called GraphVMs; an extensible scheduling language separating hardware-independent from hardware-specific transformations; and an autotuner that finds schedules per platform. Across five algorithms and nine graphs on GPU, CPU, and Swarm backends, UGF outperforms existing frameworks by up to 5.1× and is fastest in 62 of 90 experiments. This is the thesis version of the work published as UGC at ISCA 2021, which supersedes it; its GPU material also appears in G2, and Hsu's M.Eng. thesis covers the same framework's Swarm backend.
author0: Ajay Brahmakshatriya

title: VeGen: A Vectorizer Generator for SIMD and Beyond
summary: Chen's S.M. thesis describes VeGen, a system that automatically constructs vectorizers for vector instructions falling outside the SIMD model, instructions that accelerate image processing, digital signal processing, and machine learning but that compilers otherwise reach only through ad hoc peephole optimizations. It proposes a model of vector parallelism capturing the semantics of non-SIMD instructions and a framework that extracts this parallelism automatically from the instructions' formal semantics, generating pattern matchers and lane-binding utilities offline. The thesis details the vector instruction description language, pack selection with deinterleaving and transposition heuristics, and support for x86 vector extensions and Arm Neon. The Lane Level Parallelism model here relaxes the superword-level parallelism of Larsen and Amarasinghe's PLDI 2000 paper. The S.M. thesis is an earlier form of the VeGen work that became a chapter of Chen's PhD thesis (2026).
author0: Yishen Chen

title: Unified Graph Framework: Optimizing Graph Applications across Novel Architectures
summary: Hsu's M.Eng. thesis develops the Unified Graph Framework (UGF), which lets new hardware backends plug into the GraphIt compiler without rebuilding it. It presents GraphIR, a graph-specific, hardware-independent intermediate representation; an extensible scheduling language API combining hardware-independent and programmer-defined hardware-specific optimizations; and the GraphVM backend structure. The framework is evaluated by building a GraphVM for Swarm, an architecture that speculates on fine-grained tasks, with optimizations for frontier task division, privatization of shared variables, and deduplication; on five applications and ten input graphs the generated Swarm code achieves up to 8× speedup over baseline implementations. A companion to the ISCA 2021 UGC paper, giving the fullest account of its Swarm backend; Brahmakshatriya's S.M. thesis covers the CPU and GPU sides of the same framework. The framework builds on GraphIt and the G2 GPU compiler.

title: GraphIt: Optimizing the Performance and Improving the Programmability of Graph Algorithms
summary: Zhang's PhD thesis presents GraphIt, a domain-specific language that achieves high performance across graph algorithms, inputs, and architectures while keeping programs up to an order of magnitude smaller than framework code. It develops the algorithm language; the scheduling language covering cache, NUMA, load balance, and data layout optimizations; the graph iteration space representation underlying the compiler; and the priority-based extension for ordered algorithms, reporting up to 4.8× speedup over the fastest of the shared-memory frameworks compared. This is the most complete treatment of GraphIt on CPUs. It consolidates the OOPSLA 2018 language paper, the CGO 2020 ordered-algorithms paper, and the cache optimizations first published as Cagra.

title: Towards Automated Construction of Compiler Optimizations
summary: Mendis's PhD thesis argues for moving from hand-crafted compiler optimizations toward automatically constructed ones, using auto-vectorization as its running example. It presents three systems. goSLP finds globally pairwise-optimal statement packings with an integer linear programming solver and selects vector permutations optimally with dynamic programming. Vemal, the first end-to-end learned vectorizer, formulates packing as a sequential decision process whose every step preserves correctness, outperforming hand-crafted algorithms. Ithemal, the first learned cost model for predicting the throughput of x86 basic blocks, replaces complex and incorrect hand-written performance models with a data-driven one. The thesis chapters are the fullest treatment of work published separately: goSLP (OOPSLA 2018), Vemal (NeurIPS 2019), and Ithemal, which appeared at ICML 2019 together with the BHive measurement suite (IISWC 2019).

author0: Chen, Yishen and Mendis, Charith and Carbin, Michael and Amarasinghe, Saman
title: VeGen: A Vectorizer Generator for SIMD and Beyond
summary: VeGen is a vectorizer generator that targets vector instructions beyond the SIMD model, such as the dot-product and horizontal-arithmetic instructions of AVX2 and AVX512-VNNI. It introduces Lane Level Parallelism, which generalizes superword-level parallelism by allowing non-isomorphic operations and cross-lane operand movement, and generates a target-aware vectorization pass automatically from documented instruction semantics, keeping the core vectorization algorithm target-independent. Integrated into LLVM, VeGen uses instructions that no evaluated production compiler exploits, running a TVM convolution kernel 5× faster than LLVM's output and x265's idct4 kernel 3× faster than LLVM's vectorizer. The main paper of the VeGen project. Its Lane Level Parallelism abstraction relaxes the superword-level parallelism introduced in Larsen and Amarasinghe's PLDI 2000 paper, and the material reappears as the VeGen chapter of Chen's PhD thesis (2026).

title: Taming the Zoo: A Unified Graph Compiler Framework for Novel Architectures
summary: This paper presents the Unified GraphIt Compiler framework (UGC), a graph compiler built for architectural diversity. UGC decouples architecture-independent algorithms from architecture-specific schedules and backends through GraphIR, a domain-specific intermediate representation that preserves the high-level information hardware code generators need. Backends called GraphVMs target CPUs, GPUs, the speculative Swarm architecture, and the HammerBlade manycore, while scheduling language extensions expose choices such as load balancing strategies, blocking for locality, and data structure selection. Across five algorithms, ten input graphs, and these four architectures, UGC enables optimizations that provide up to 53× speedup over straightforward implementations. This is the main paper of GraphIt's multi-architecture phase, built on the OOPSLA 2018 language paper and the G2 GPU backend. Brahmakshatriya's S.M. thesis is the thesis version of this work, and Hsu's M.Eng. thesis details the Swarm GraphVM.

title: NetBlocks: Staging Layouts for High-Performance Custom Host Network Stacks
summary: NetBlocks is a domain-specific language and compiler for designing ad-hoc network protocols and generating optimized host network-stack implementations. Users select and customize features — reliability, in-order delivery, checksumming, congestion control — and pay only for what they use; researchers can add features without compiler knowledge. Built as an aspect-oriented framework on BuildIt, it introduces a Layout Customization Layer that stages packet layouts alongside code, shrinking headers to the bits a deployment needs while preserving compatibility with existing protocols. Evaluations on three applications, from data centers to underwater acoustic networks, expose a performance-versus-features trade-off. NetBlocks extends staging from code to data layouts, building on BuildIt (CGO 2021) and the DSL-via-staging approach of BuilDSL (CGO 2022). SPAC (FCCM 2026) carries the protocol work into FPGA-based switches using NetBlocks-compatible syntax, a unified Kubernetes DSL (xSIG 2026) drives its generator for inter-container communication, and Brahmakshatriya’s PhD thesis (2025) gives the most complete treatment.

title: D2X: An eXtensible conteXtual Debugger for Modern DSLs
summary: D2X is a debugging infrastructure for domain-specific languages that generate low-level code. Conventional approaches extend compilers, debug-information formats, and the debuggers themselves; D2X instead works with standard debuggers such as GDB and LLDB without any modifications, and is easily extensible to capture the domain-specific information an end-user cares about, restoring the connection between generated code and the DSL program. Adding debugging support to the graph DSL GraphIt required changing as little as 1.4% of the compiler code base, and applying D2X to the BuildIt staging framework gives every DSL built on top of BuildIt debugging support without modification. D2X complements the DSL-construction line of BuildIt (CGO 2021) and BuilDSL (CGO 2022) by addressing the tooling those compilers still lacked, and Brahmakshatriya’s PhD thesis (2025) gives the most complete treatment of D2X alongside BuildIt.

title: GraphIt to CUDA compiler in 2021 LOC: A case for high-performance DSL implementation via staging with BuilDSL
summary: This paper makes a case for building high-performance DSL compilers by staging rather than as monolithic codebases. BuilDSL is a DSL framework on top of the BuildIt multi-stage programming framework for C++: staged types are extended to perform domain-specific data-flow and control-flow analyses and transformations, and the framework supplies GPU code generation with kernel fusion and load balancing. As the demonstration, a graph DSL written in BuilDSL generates CUDA code matching the performance of the GraphIt GPU compiler from 2,021 lines of code — 8.4% of the size of the traditional implementation. The paper joins two COMMIT lines: the GraphIt DSL, whose G2 GPU compiler sets the performance bar, and BuildIt, the CGO 2021 staging framework it builds on. The D2X debugger later built on the framework, and Brahmakshatriya's PhD thesis gives the most complete treatment.

title: Unified Compilation for Lossless Compression and Sparse Computing
summary: This CGO 2022 paper extends sparse tensor algebra compilers to compute directly on losslessly compressed data. It generalizes the fill values that sparse formats compress out from a single scalar zero to non-scalar, dynamic fills, letting variants of run-length encoding and LZ77 be described as ordinary level formats. The compiler emits kernels that compute on any mix of compressed and sparse operands without decompressing them. Generated image and video processing kernels run up to 16.3× faster than equivalent dense kernels generated by TACO and up to 16.1× faster than OpenCV. The technique builds on TACO, the level formats of the OOPSLA 2018 formats paper, and the fill-value machinery of the sparse array programming paper, and revives an observation from earlier COMMIT work on lossless video: many computations preserve repetitions. Donenfeld's S.M. thesis gives the most complete treatment, and Looplets later built on the approach.

title: BuildIt: A type based multistage programming framework for code generation in C++
summary: BuildIt is a type-based multi-stage programming framework for code generation in C++. As a pure library needing no compiler changes, it extracts next-stage programs — including data-dependent conditionals, loops, and recursion — by repeatedly executing the input program to explore every control-flow path and assemble the AST, without exponential blow-up in output size or execution time. It applies the staging to the TACO tensor compiler for custom-format IR, and stages an interpreter for an esoteric language. This is the main paper of the BuildIt project. The TACO case study stages the level-format lowering of Chou et al.’s format abstraction (OOPSLA 2018). BuilDSL (CGO 2022) rebuilt the GraphIt-to-CUDA compiler in 2,021 lines of code, D2X (CGO 2023) added extensible debugging, and NetBlocks (PLDI 2024) extended staging from code to packet layouts; later theses stage multimedia filters and Hopper GPU matmul kernels (both 2026); Brahmakshatriya’s PhD thesis gives the most complete treatment.

title: Compiling Graph Applications for GPUs with GraphIt
summary: G2 extends the GraphIt compiler to generate high-performance GPU code from the same algorithm specification used for CPUs. A GPU scheduling language expands the optimization space of GPU graph processing by combining load balancing, edge traversal direction, active vertexset creation, processing ordering, and kernel fusion. Two new optimizations complete the design: edge-based thread–warp–CTA load balancing (ETWC), and EdgeBlocking, which reorders edges so random accesses stay within the L2 cache. On five algorithms and nine graphs across Pascal and Volta GPUs, G2 achieves up to 5.11× speedup over GPU graph frameworks and is fastest on 66 of 90 experiments. G2 brings GraphIt and its ordered-algorithms extension to GPUs; Brahmakshatriya's S.M. thesis is the thesis version of the GPU work. It was later generalized into UGC and rebuilt in 2,021 lines of staged code with BuilDSL.

title: Optimizing Ordered Graph Algorithms with GraphIt
summary: This paper extends GraphIt to ordered graph algorithms such as Δ-stepping and k-core, which process vertices in a dynamic priority order to avoid redundant work. A priority-based extension of the algorithm language hides low-level bucketing details, while new program analyses, transformations, and code generation produce fast parallel implementations. It also introduces bucket fusion, an optimization that merges consecutive rounds of ordered execution to cut synchronization, yielding 1.2×–3× speedup over the fastest existing ordered implementations on large-diameter road networks. With the extension, GraphIt achieves up to 3× speedup on six ordered algorithms over Julienne, Galois, and GAPBS. The work extends the GraphIt OOPSLA 2018 paper, which handled unordered algorithms. Its priority-based abstractions were later carried to GPUs by G2 and reused in UGC, and Zhang's PhD thesis integrates ordered and unordered GraphIt into a single treatment.

title: Compiler Auto-Vectorization with Imitation Learning
summary: This paper presents Vemal, an end-to-end learned SLP vectorizer that replaces hand-written packing heuristics with a graph neural network policy. It formulates instruction packing as a sequential decision process in which every step preserves correctness, and trains the policy by imitation learning from optimal integer linear programming solutions. The learned policy achieves a 22.6% higher average cost reduction than LLVM under LLVM's own cost model, and matches the runtime performance of the ILP-based solution in 5 of 7 NAS benchmark applications. Vemal imitates the packing decisions of goSLP (OOPSLA 2018), distilling slow solver runs into a fast policy, and builds on the SLP formulation of Larsen and Amarasinghe's PLDI 2000 paper. The work reappears as a chapter of Mendis's PhD thesis.

title: BHive: A Benchmark Suite and Measurement Framework for Validating x86-64 Basic Block Performance Models
summary: BHive is a benchmark suite and measurement framework for validating x86-64 basic block performance models. Its enabling contribution is a profiler that times arbitrary memory-accessing blocks outside their program context while conforming to modeling assumptions such as L1-resident accesses; a widely used earlier script could profile only 16.65% of its blocks. The paper assembles blocks with reference timings from scientific computing, databases, compression, machine learning, compilers, and graphics, clusters them by CPU resource use, and evaluates IACA, llvm-mca, OSACA, and Ithemal, exposing per-workload strengths and weaknesses. BHive is the companion measurement paper to Ithemal (ICML 2019), supplying the systematic validation that analytical and learned throughput models had lacked. Done jointly with Google Research, it also checks the dataset against Google's Spanner and Dremel. Mendis's PhD thesis (2020) gives the most complete treatment of both systems.

title: SALSA: A Domain Specific Architecture for Sequence Alignment
summary: SALSA is a domain-specific architecture for sequence alignment, a core step in genomic data analysis. It is built from systolic arrays and programmed through the RISC-V instruction set, so users can add custom instructions; it is also configurable, letting designers tune the number of processing elements or the size of the memory port, and extensible, since each processing element combines a general-purpose ALU with custom ALUs the user can integrate. At 200 MHz, SALSA outperforms an open-source Rocket core and an Intel Xeon by factors up to 350× in performance and 790× in power efficiency.

title: Ithemal:  Accurate, Portable and Fast Basic Block Throughput Estimation using Deep Neural Networks
summary: Ithemal is the first learned tool for estimating the throughput of x86-64 basic blocks, the steady-state clock cycles they take to execute. Rather than hand-constructing an analytical model for each processor generation, it trains a hierarchical LSTM on the opcodes and operands of a block's instructions. Ithemal has less than half the error of the analytical models used in compiler backends and machine-code analyzers, LLVM's llvm-mca and Intel's IACA, predicts just as fast, and ports to a new microarchitecture by retraining rather than re-engineering. Ithemal's dataset of executed basic blocks is captured with DynamoRIO (VEE 2012), COMMIT's dynamic binary instrumentation system. The companion BHive paper (IISWC 2019) supplies the profiler and benchmark suite that validate such models, and the Tiramisu deep-learning cost model (MLSys 2021) later carried learned cost prediction to whole programs. Mendis's PhD thesis gives the most complete treatment.
author0: Mendis, Charith and Renda, Alex and Amarasinghe, Saman and Carbin, Michael
booktitle: International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML)
price: Best Paper Award (ML for Systems workshop @ISCA 2019)
abstract: Predicting the number of clock cycles a processor takes to execute a block of assembly instructions in steady state (the throughput) is important for both compiler designers and performance engineers. Building an analytical model to do so is especially complicated in modern x86-64 Complex Instruction Set Computer (CISC) machines with sophisticated processor microarchitectures in that it is tedious, error prone, and must be performed from scratch for each processor generation. In this paper we present Ithemal, the first tool which learns to predict the throughput of a set of instructions. Ithemal uses a hierarchical LSTM–based approach to predict throughput based on the opcodes and operands of instructions in a basic block. We show that Ithemal is more accurate than state-of-the-art hand-written tools currently used in compiler backends and static machine code analyzers. In particular, our model has less than half the error of state-of-the-art analytical models (LLVM’s llvm-mca and Intel’s IACA). Ithemal is also able to predict these throughput values just as fast as the aforementioned tools, and is easily ported across a variety of processor microarchitectures with minimal developer effort.

title: Domain-Specific Language Abstractions for Compression
summary: This paper introduces high-level programming abstractions for block-based data compression, the core of many compression standards including the HEVC and VVC video codecs. It identifies three recurring patterns that low-level languages like C obscure — data representation, data partitioning, and data traversal — and provides constructs for expressing the hierarchical partitions and spatial and temporal dependencies of compression algorithms, demonstrated in a Python prototype. The abstractions are presented as the basis for a domain-specific language and optimizing compiler that could generate high-performance compression code from concise algorithm descriptions. This is the first version of the work that became UniTe. Ray's PhD dissertation develops these abstractions into a universal tensor abstraction for block-based compression and gives the complete treatment; the UniTe journal paper in ACM TACO is the mature form of the same work.

title: A Deep Learning Based Cost Model for Automatic Code Optimization
summary: This MLSys 2021 paper contributes a deep-learning cost model for automatic code optimization, integrated into the Tiramisu compiler's search over code transformations. Given simple features of the unoptimized program and a candidate sequence of transformations, the model predicts the resulting speedup, letting the search rank candidates without running them. Unlike earlier models it operates on full programs and requires no heavy feature engineering. It attains 16% mean absolute percentage error predicting full-program speedups, letting Tiramisu find transformation sequences that match or outperform compilers built on hand-engineered models. The model is the automatic scheduling arm of Tiramisu (CGO 2019), whose polyhedral framework applies the transformations it scores; a 2020 arXiv paper on Tiramisu for deep learning formally describes the supported programs. It extends the learned performance modeling of Ithemal (ICML 2019) from basic blocks to whole programs, and the same group's loop interchange model (CC 2023) builds directly on it.

title: A Deep Learning Model for Loop Interchange
summary: This CC 2023 paper trains a deep-learning model that predicts, from the code representation alone, the best pair of loops to interchange in a loop nest. Cost-model-driven approaches must apply each candidate interchange and score it, so their prediction time grows with the number of loop levels; this model returns its recommendation in constant time. Implemented and evaluated in the Tiramisu polyhedral compiler, it selects the best interchange with 76.66% accuracy in one shot and 94% within two, improving on the compiler's cost-model approach by 6.66% and 14% respectively while cutting prediction time. title: Revec: Program Rejuvenation Through Revectorization
summary: Revec is a compiler pass that rejuvenates hand-vectorized code: it retargets programs written with vector intrinsics of one instruction set generation to later generations with wider registers and new capabilities. The transformation happens at the compiler intermediate representation level, restoring the performance portability that manual vectorization gives up. Revec achieves geometric mean speedups of 1.160× and 1.430× on fast integer unpacking kernels and 1.145× and 1.195× on hand-vectorized x265 media codec kernels when retargeting SSE-series implementations to AVX2 and AVX-512, and is further tested on 216 intrinsic-rich image processing and stencil implementations. Revec adapts the packing approach of superword-level parallelism (PLDI 2000) to code that is already vectorized.

title: Cimple: Instruction and Memory Level Parallelism: A DSL for Uncovering ILP and MLP
summary: Cimple is a DSL embedded in C++ for uncovering instruction-level and memory-level parallelism in pointer-heavy workloads. Its IMLP task programming model expresses computations as coroutines that yield at annotated long-latency operations — memory accesses, divisions, unpredictable branches — so independent tasks interleave on a single thread while integrating with thread parallelism and vectorization. The DSL supports exploring task scheduling, buffering, pipelining, and prefetching transformations. On in-memory database algorithms over arrays, hash tables, trees, and skip lists, Cimple reaches 2.5× throughput gains over hardware multithreading on a multicore and 6.4× single-thread speedup. Kiriansky's PhD thesis gives the most complete treatment of Cimple.

title: Sparse Tensor Transpositions
summary: This brief announcement shows that sparse tensor transposition — reordering the dimensions of a compressed tensor — can be done substantially faster than the standard approach of unpacking to coordinates and sorting from scratch. Because a lexicographically ordered tensor is already partially sorted for any target ordering, the proposed algorithm, Quesadilla, plans a minimal sequence of histogram-sort passes that exploits this sortedness. On half of all tested tensor and permutation combinations it is at least 1.19× faster than SPLATT, 1.68× faster than radix sort, and 2.76× faster than quicksort.

title: DAWG: A Defense Against Cache Timing Attacks in Speculative Execution Processors
summary: DAWG (Dynamically Allocated Way Guard) is a hardware mechanism for secure way partitioning of set-associative structures such as caches. It gives these structures protection domains and — unlike quality-of-service mechanisms such as Intel's Cache Allocation Technology — fully isolates hits, misses, and metadata updates between domains, closing the cache-state covert channel that speculative-execution attacks exploit. The paper shows DAWG fits into a processor and operating system with minimal modifications, argues a noninterference property under which Spectre variants 1 and 2 fail, and measures the cost on the cache subsystem. Kiriansky's PhD thesis (2019) gives the most complete treatment of DAWG.
