title: GraphIt: A High-performance Graph DSL
summary: GraphIt is a domain-specific language for graph analytics. It separates what is computed (an algorithm language) from how it is computed (a scheduling language), formulating edge traversal direction, data layout, parallelization, cache, and NUMA optimizations as tradeoffs among locality, parallelism, and work-efficiency. A new representation, the graph iteration space, lets the compiler model, compose, and validate optimizations, and the separation supports an autotuner. GraphIt outperforms the next fastest of six shared-memory frameworks on 24 of 32 experiments by up to 4.8×, with up to an order of magnitude fewer lines of code. This is the main language paper of the GraphIt project. Its cache and NUMA optimizations grew out of CSR segmenting in Cagra. title: Seq: A High-performance Language for Bioinformatics
summary: Seq is a programming language for bioinformatics that pairs the ease of Python with C-like performance. author0: Kjolstad, Fredrik and Kamil, Shoaib and Amarasinghe, Saman
title: Automatic Generation of Sparse Tensor Kernels with Workspaces
summary: This arXiv preprint introduces workspaces into sparse tensor algebra compilation through a compiler optimization called operator splitting, which breaks a tensor sub-expression apart at an index variable and stores intermediate results in a dense temporary. Splitting removes expensive insertions into sparse results, eliminates code that merges sparse operands, and hoists loop-invariant work. Case studies show that the transformation recreates known hand-optimized algorithms — sparse matrix multiplication by linear combination of rows, sparse matrix addition, and MTTKRP — and that generated kernels match hand-optimized code. The optimization operates on the iteration-graph representation of the OOPSLA 2017 tensor algebra compiler; Kjolstad's PhD thesis gives the most complete treatment of the workspaces material.

author0: Mendis, Charith and Amarasinghe, Saman
title: goSLP: Globally Optimized Superword Level Parallelism Framework
summary: goSLP is a superword-level parallelism (SLP) auto-vectorization framework that replaces greedy, local packing heuristics with global optimization. It encodes the statement packing problem for a whole function as an integer linear program, searching the space of pairwise packing choices with an off-the-shelf ILP solver while limiting compilation to a few minutes, and solves vector permutation selection optimally with dynamic programming. Implemented in LLVM, goSLP achieves geometric mean speedups of 7.58% on SPEC2017fp, 2.42% on SPEC2006fp, and 4.07% on the NAS benchmarks over LLVM's SLP vectorizer. The main paper of the goSLP project, it directly improves the SLP algorithm of Larsen and Amarasinghe's PLDI 2000 paper. Its ILP solutions became the training signal for Vemal, a learned vectorizer that imitates goSLP's packing decisions, and the work reappears as a chapter of Mendis's PhD thesis.

title: Format Abstraction for Sparse Tensor Algebra Compilers
summary: This paper shows how to build a sparse tensor algebra compiler that is agnostic to tensor formats. It contributes a levelization of tensor storage into hierarchies of per-dimension level formats, an interface that describes each level by its access capabilities and properties, and a modular code generator that reasons only about that interface, so new formats plug in without touching the compiler. Follow-on work includes format conversion (PLDI 2020) and dynamic sparse tensor algebra (OOPSLA 2022).

title: Tiramisu: A Polyhedral Compiler for Expressing Fast and Portable Code
summary: Tiramisu is a polyhedral compiler for expressing fast and portable code on multicores, GPUs, and distributed machines, targeting image processing, stencils, linear algebra, and deep learning. A scheduling language with commands for communication, synchronization, and memory-hierarchy mapping, together with a four-level intermediate representation, separates the algorithm from loop transformations, data layout, and communication. Generated code outperforms Intel MKL by up to 2.3× and matches or outperforms compilers and libraries across architectures. This is the main paper of the Tiramisu project. It adopts the scheduling-language approach of Halide but replaces intervals with polyhedral sets, and tightens the over-approximated communication of distributed Halide. Companion theses by Ray, Ben Romdhane, and Akkas give fuller treatments of its distributed and GPU backends, and FROST describes its FPGA backend. A 2020 arXiv paper extended Tiramisu to dense and sparse deep learning, and a deep-learning-based cost model (MLSys 2021) later gave it an autoscheduler.

title: Tensor Algebra Compilation with Workspaces
summary: This paper shows how a sparse tensor algebra compiler can introduce temporary workspaces: dense scratch arrays holding intermediate results, which hand-optimized kernels rely on but earlier compilation theory could not express. A transformation splits a tensor expression at an index variable and assigns the sub-computation to a workspace, removing expensive insertions into sparse results, eliminating merge code, and hoisting loop-invariant computation. Case studies recreate hand-written algorithms for sparse matrix multiplication, sparse addition, and MTTKRP, and generated kernels match hand-optimized code. The workspaces paper of the TACO project. It extends the iteration graphs and merge lattices of the OOPSLA 2017 tensor algebra compiler; the workspace transformation became part of the scheduling vocabulary of the sparse iteration space transformation framework (OOPSLA 2020), later searched by autoscheduling work (PLDI 2022). Kjolstad's PhD thesis gives the most complete treatment.

title: Halide: Decoupling Algorithms from Schedules for High-performance Image Processing
summary: This Communications of the ACM research highlight presents Halide to a broad audience. It argues that programming models conflate the algorithm — what a pipeline computes — with the schedule of intermediate storage and order of computation, then walks through the schedule space and the compiler that synthesizes a combined loop nest for an entire pipeline. Schedules matching or outperforming hand-written implementations often take a few lines, and small changes retarget x86, ARM, GPUs, and specialized image processors. It also reports deployment at the time of writing: four years as open source, code on tens of thousands of servers and hundreds of millions of phones, billions of images processed daily. A distillation of the same work presented in the SIGGRAPH 2012 language paper and the PLDI 2013 compiler paper; Ragan-Kelley's PhD thesis is the most complete treatment.

title: Unified Sparse Formats for Tensor Algebra Compilers
summary: Chou's S.M. thesis proposes a levelized hierarchical abstraction for sparse tensor storage: seemingly disparate formats — COO, CSR, CSC, DCSR, BCSR, CSF, CSB, ELL, DIA, and hash maps — are expressed as compositions of per-dimension levels hidden behind a common interface of capabilities and properties. A code generation algorithm emits kernels level by level for tensor algebra expressions on any combination of formats, with performance competitive with hand-implemented kernels in sparse linear and tensor algebra libraries. This is the thesis version of the material published in the OOPSLA 2018 formats paper, which supersedes it as the citable reference; both extend the OOPSLA 2017 tensor algebra compiler. Chou's PhD thesis (2022) gives the most complete treatment of the format abstraction line.

title: Efficient Memory and GPU Operations for Tiramisu Compiler
summary: Akkas's S.M. thesis develops the GPU side of the Tiramisu compiler. It adds high-level interfaces that remove manual memory management from GPU programming in Tiramisu: implicit buffers, a block API, a shared-memory interface, a cuBLAS GEMM interface, and CUDA streams support. Two benchmarks evaluate the backend: a matrix-multiplication kernel that outperforms other polyhedral compilers while approaching cuBLAS, and an LSTM recurrent network where a skew-and-interchange schedule lets Tiramisu outperform cuDNN on deep networks. The thesis is Akkas's fuller treatment of his GPU and memory contributions to the CGO 2019 Tiramisu paper, of which he is a co-author.

title: Making Caches Work for Graph Analytics
summary: Cagra is a cache-optimized in-memory graph framework. Observing that the fastest graph frameworks spend 60–80% of their cycles stalled on memory, it introduces CSR segmenting: vertices are broken into segments that fit in last-level cache, the graph is partitioned into subgraphs accordingly, random accesses are confined to one cached segment at a time, and buffered intermediate updates are combined by a low-overhead parallel cache-aware merge. Cagra achieves speedups of up to 5× for PageRank, collaborative filtering, label propagation, and betweenness centrality over the best published results from frameworks including GraphMat, Ligra, and GridGraph. This paper is a direct precursor of GraphIt: CSR segmenting became a cache optimization exposed by GraphIt's scheduling language. Zhang's PhD thesis presents the technique in its full GraphIt setting.

title: The Tensor Algebra Compiler
summary: The Tensor Algebra Compiler (taco) is the first compiler technique to generate kernels for any compound tensor algebra expression on dense and sparse tensors in any supported combination of formats. The companion ASE 2017 tool paper demonstrates the same system as web, command-line, and library tools, and a French AVANCÉES article presents it to CEA's simulation community. author0: Shoumik Palkar and James J. Thomas and Anil Shanbhag and Deepak Narayanan and Holger Pirk and Malte Schwarzkopf and Saman Amarasinghe and Matei Zaharia
title: Weld: A Common Runtime for High Performance Data Analytics
summary: Weld is a common runtime for data analytics libraries that optimizes across them. Applications mix libraries such as NumPy, Pandas, TensorFlow, and Spark SQL; each is fast in isolation, but data movement between them leaves workflows far below hardware limits. Libraries express their work in a functional intermediate representation capturing SQL, machine learning, and graph computations; a lazy runtime API collects fragments, and Weld applies cross-library optimizations such as loop fusion and vectorization. Integrated without changing user-facing APIs, Weld delivers speedups of up to 6× for Spark SQL, 32× for TensorFlow, 30× for Pandas, and 31× for applications combining libraries. The PVLDB 2018 paper later built on this vision with an automatic adaptive optimizer and a full evaluation.
booktitle: Conference on Innovative Data Systems Research (CIDR)

author0: Kiriansky, Vladimir and Zhang, Yunming and Amarasinghe, Saman
title: Optimizing Indirect Memory References with milk
summary: milk is a C/C++ language extension for memory-bound loops with indirect references, common in graph and data analytics, where random DRAM accesses leave cores stalled. Programmers add milk clauses to OpenMP directives; the compiler's DRAM-conscious clustering then collects dynamically generated indices into cache-local buffers, distributes them to DRAM-resident partitions with sequential writes, and delivers each partition's deferred updates from cache — three phases fused as coroutines to conserve bandwidth. A bulk-synchronous-style semantic model keeps parallelization simple while eliminating synchronization. On parallel graph applications, the Milk compiler demonstrates performance gains of up to 3×. Kiriansky's PhD thesis gives the most complete treatment, reporting up to 4× speedup.

title: Linear Algebra on Lattices: Simit Language Extensions with Applications to Lattice QCD
summary: Kanwar's M.Eng. thesis extends Simit, a language for linear algebra on graphs, to lattice graphs, the regular grids on which lattice QCD operates. It defines a stencil assembly construct that captures linear algebra on lattices, and a prototype compiler with a Halide backend demonstrates that the extensions capture the full structure of lattice linear algebra, are easily schedulable, and achieve performance comparable to existing methods. The thesis reviews lattice QCD as the representative application, identifies iterative inversion of the Dirac matrix as the dominant cost, and implements that computation in the extended language with competitive performance. The thesis builds on Simit, whose language paper Kanwar co-authored, and generates code through Halide.

title: Why New Programming Languages for Simulation?
summary: This ACM Transactions on Graphics perspective argues that physical simulation needs new programming languages. Performant simulations require optimizing across geometric data structures and numerical linear algebra at once, so reusability and portability are routinely sacrificed for performance, and the problem worsens as code must target multicore CPUs, GPUs, and distributed machines. Following the example of rendering and image processing, the authors contend that linguistic abstractions are the key to making simulation programmers productive, and they distill the core ideas of two simulation languages published in the same journal, Ebb and Simit. author0: Tyler Denniston and Shoaib Kamil and Saman Amarasinghe
title: Distributed Halide
summary: Distributed Halide extends the Halide compiler from shared-memory parallelism to distributed-memory execution of stencil pipelines. Its scheduling extensions compose with Halide's existing constructs, so distribution — and the tradeoff between recomputation and communication — is expressed in the schedule rather than the algorithm; existing applications distribute with minimal changes, about ten new lines even for a 200-line, 99-stage pipeline. On nine image processing benchmarks the extensions give up to 1.4× on a single node over multithreaded execution with the same cores, by mitigating non-uniform memory access, and up to 18× on a 16-node machine and 57× on 64 nodes of the NERSC Cori supercomputer. The work extends the PLDI 2013 Halide compiler with distributed scheduling. It later served as the distributed-execution baseline for Tiramisu and for Ray's 2018 M.Eng. thesis on a unified compiler backend for heterogeneous execution.
journal: ACM SIGPLAN Symposium on Principles and Practice of Parallel Programming (PPoPP)

title: Simit: A Language for Physical Simulation
summary: Simit is a programming language for physical simulation. A simulation is naturally described both locally, as a graph whose vertices hold degrees of freedom and whose edges carry interactions, and globally, in the language of sparse linear algebra; Simit's assembly construct moves cheaply between the two views, letting the compiler generate efficient in-place computation on the graph. Simit programs are typically shorter than Matlab programs, perform comparably to hand-optimized sequential simulations, and compile unchanged to GPUs, delivering 4–20× speedups over the optimized CPU code. This is the main language paper of the Simit project. A companion perspective arguing for domain-specific simulation languages appeared in the same journal, and Kanwar's M.Eng. thesis later extended the language to lattice graphs for lattice QCD.

summary: Tew's M.Eng. thesis investigates storage formats for sparse tensors in tensor libraries. title: Fourier-Motzkin with Non-Linear Symbolic Constant Coefficients
summary: This M.Eng. thesis extends Fourier-Motzkin elimination to inequalities whose coefficients are symbolic constants of arbitrary integer-polynomial degree, the non-linearity that arises when tile sizes or processor counts remain unknown at compile time. The extension lets one polyhedral framework express parametric multi-level tiling, diamond tiling, and communication-set generation for distributed machines. Suriana implements the method in a library called NFM, with simplification passes that keep the constraint systems small, and integrates it into Halide as a more robust engine for merging and intersecting iteration domains. The thesis revisits a restricted symbolic-coefficient extension from Amarasinghe's PhD thesis and generalizes it beyond degree-one coefficients; the NFM integration into Halide strengthens that compiler's bounds and interval reasoning.

title: DeepTuner: A System for Search Technique Recommendation in Program Autotuning
summary: DeepTuner is a system for recommending search techniques in program autotuning, from Wu's M.Eng. thesis. Because OpenTuner's meta-techniques learn only within a single tuning run and no one technique set suits every search space, DeepTuner adds a cross-session database of historical autotuning data with recommendation endpoints, letting a search approach explore the space of composable techniques and the program's own tuning space simultaneously. The resulting Database Initialized Recommendation Bandit meta-technique, evaluated on nine problems across three domains, matches or beats the in-situ approaches and reaches up to 3.7× improvement over OpenTuner's old default on traveling-salesman instances. The thesis builds directly on OpenTuner, generalizing its AUC bandit meta-technique with transfer learning across tuning sessions; its benchmark domains include Halide schedule tuning and PetaBricks programs.

title: Efficient and Proven Verification of Unreliable Hardware Executions of Classic Algorithms
summary: SoundCheck is a system for trusting results computed on unreliable hardware — machines run beyond their voltage and frequency guardbands, risking silent data corruption. A solver runs on the unreliable machine while an efficient checker validates its output on a reliable one; checkers for linear equations, satisfiability, linear programming, graph matching, and 3SUM run 10³–10⁶× faster than their solvers in practice. Because sound checkers are hard to write, it proves each checker sound and complete with bounded verification in the Sketch synthesis language and emits it as efficient C++. Its proofs build on the Sketch system, introduced in a PLDI 2005 paper on sketching bit-streaming programs.
author0: Yoana Gyurova
Charith Mendis and Jeffrey Bosboom and Kevin Wu and Shoaib Kamil and Jonathan Ragan-Kelley and Sylvain Paris and Qin Zhao and Saman Amarasinghe
title: Helium:  Lifting High-Performance Stencil Kernels from Stripped x86 Binaries to Halide DSL Code
summary: Helium lifts performance-critical stencil kernels from stripped x86 binaries into Halide, so that aging hand-optimized code can be regenerated for new hardware. Because such binaries resist static analysis, Helium works from dynamic traces: it reconstructs buffer structures, abstracts forests of concrete dependency trees into symbolic ones by canonicalizing and clustering them, infers higher-dimensional buffer accesses, and solves linear equations to recover high-level expressions, handling optimized kernels with input-dependent conditionals. Recompiling the lifted code makes seven Photoshop kernels 75% faster, four IrfanView kernels 4.97× faster, and a miniGMG multigrid stencil 4.25× faster; replacing eleven Photoshop filters gives a 1.12× application speedup. Helium's dynamic data flow analysis is built on DynamoRIO, its lifting target is Halide, and the recovered schedules are tuned with the OpenTuner-based Halide autotuner.

author0: Yufei Ding and Jason Ansel and Kalyan Veeramachaneni and Xipeng Shen and Una-May O'Reilly and Saman Amarasinghe
title: Autotuning Algorithmic Choice For Input Sensitivity
summary: This PLDI 2015 paper confronts input sensitivity in autotuning: the best configuration of a program often depends on the input. In algorithmic autotuning, where choices compose recursive poly-algorithms and search spaces range from 10^312 to 10^1016 configurations, tuning for every training input is infeasible. The paper's two-level input learning clusters training inputs by features, tunes a representative configuration per cluster, and uses the representatives' performance to refine input grouping, feature selection, and classifier construction. It yields up to 3x speedup over one configuration for all inputs, and 34x over a one-level input-adaptive method. The work extends PetaBricks (PLDI 2009), which made algorithmic choice a language construct; its representative configurations are built with the evolutionary autotuner (GECCO 2011), and its evaluation uses the parallel benchmarks of the variable-accuracy autotuning work (CGO 2011).

title: Helium: Lifting High-Performance Stencil Kernels from Stripped x86 Binaries to Halide DSL Code
summary: Mendis's SM thesis presents Helium, a system that recovers high-level Halide programs from performance-critical stencil kernels buried in stripped x86 binaries. It details the full lifting pipeline — dynamic tracing, buffer structure reconstruction, canonicalization and clustering of dependency trees, dimensionality inference, and the linear-equation solving that yields symbolic stencil expressions — along with the instrumentation and code generation machinery. The evaluation lifts kernels from Adobe Photoshop (75% faster), IrfanView (4.97×), and the miniGMG multigrid benchmark (4.25×), and rejuvenates Photoshop by replacing eleven filters for a 1.12× end-to-end speedup. The dynamic analysis is built on DynamoRIO; Halide is the lifting target, and the lifted code is autotuned with the OpenTuner-based Halide autotuner.

title: StreamJIT:  A Commensal Compiler for High-Performance Stream Programming
summary: StreamJIT is a Java-embedded stream programming language whose compiler demonstrates commensal compilation, a strategy for building embedded DSL compilers by reusing the host virtual machine: the host language's front-end, an autotuner in place of optimization heuristics, and the JVM JIT as the back-end code generator through MethodHandle chains. Only the domain-specific optimizations — filter fusion, static scheduling, automatic data parallelization, distribution to a cluster — must be written. The compiler runs on average 2.8 times faster than StreamIt's native code compiler with an order of magnitude less code. The language follows the structured stream graphs of the StreamIt language paper, and its parallelization draws on coarse-grained task, data, and pipeline parallelism; optimization decisions are delegated to OpenTuner. title: OpenTuner: An Extensible Framework for Program Autotuning
summary: OpenTuner is an open-source framework for building domain-specific, multi-objective program autotuners. It provides fully customizable configuration representations, an extensible library of search techniques, and a simple interface to the program being tuned. Its key mechanism runs ensembles of disparate search techniques simultaneously, with a bandit meta-technique shifting the testing budget toward whichever techniques are performing well, in search spaces of up to 10^3600 configurations. Autotuners built with the framework for seven projects and sixteen benchmarks achieve speedups up to 2.8× over each project's prior techniques. title: Decoupling Algorithms from the Organization of Computation for High Performance Image Processing
summary: Ragan-Kelley's PhD thesis is the full design and implementation of the Halide language and compiler. It argues that performance is determined not only by algorithm and hardware but by the organization of computations and data, constrained by a fundamental tension between parallelism, locality, and redundant recomputation. The thesis develops a model of schedules as loop synthesis, an algebra of schedule transformations, and the compiler passes — bounds inference, sliding-window optimization, storage folding, vectorization — that realize them, with results often many times faster than the best prior hand-tuned C, assembly, and CUDA implementations, from ARM mobile processors to GPUs. This is the most complete treatment of Halide, consolidating the SIGGRAPH 2012 paper and the PLDI 2013 paper and adding tutorial appendices. Its autotuned results used a prototype autotuner grown from PetaBricks, with a production successor built on OpenTuner; the CACM article later condensed the material.

title: Autotuning Algorithmic Choice for Input Sensitivity
summary: This technical report tackles input sensitivity in algorithmic autotuning: for many problems the best configuration depends on the input, and the features that matter are often domain-specific and expensive to extract. Its self-refining approach clusters training inputs by raw features, autotunes a landmark configuration for each cluster, refines the classes by observing how inputs perform on those landmarks, and uses supervised learning to build an input classifier that weighs feature-extraction overhead — while respecting the accuracy requirements of variable-accuracy programs. Selecting configurations per input this way yields up to a 3x speedup over one configuration for all inputs. The work extends the PetaBricks language, compiler, and autotuner and tunes benchmarks with its variable-accuracy features; the landmark configurations are constructed by the INCREA evolutionary autotuner. Ansel's PhD thesis includes text and experiments from this work.

title: Autotuning Programs with Algorithmic Choice
summary: Ansel's PhD thesis frames program optimization as a search over implementation choices and automates that search end to end. Its first half gives the full account of PetaBricks: the language, the compiler and runtime, heterogeneous CPU/GPU code generation, variable accuracy, input features, and benchmarks where autotuned poly-algorithms beat hand-written solutions. Its second half presents OpenTuner, a framework for building domain-specific multi-objective autotuners whose ensembles of search techniques — allocating more tests to techniques that perform well — handle search spaces of up to 10^3000 configurations. title: Detection of False Sharing Using Machine Learning
summary: This paper detects false sharing, the parallel-performance bug in which threads on different cores modify unshared data occupying the same cache line, using machine learning over hardware performance events. It builds a set of mini-programs in which false sharing can be switched on and off, runs them both ways to collect performance-event counts, and trains a classifier that can then analyze data from arbitrary programs. On the PARSEC and Phoenix suites the classifier detects the published false-sharing regions with zero false positives, at a performance penalty below 2%. For validation it relies on the DynamoRIO-based dynamic cache contention detection tool, whose reports of false sharing serve as ground truth in the evaluation.

title: OpenTuner:  An Extensible Framework for Program Autotuning
summary: This technical report is the first published description of OpenTuner, a framework for building domain-specific, multi-objective program autotuners. title: Halide: A Language and Compiler for Optimizing Parallelism, Locality, and Recomputation in Image Processing Pipelines
summary: Halide is a programming language for high-performance image and signal processing. Its central idea is decoupling what a pipeline computes from how its computation is organized. This paper contributes a systematic model of the fundamental parallelism–locality–recomputation tradeoff, a schedule representation that describes points in that space, and a compiler that synthesizes implementations up to 5× faster than expert-tuned code on CPUs and GPUs. This is the main compiler paper of the Halide project. The SIGGRAPH 2012 paper introduced the language and the algorithm/schedule separation, and the stochastic schedule search here is directly derived from the PetaBricks autotuner. Ragan-Kelley's PhD thesis is the most complete treatment, and the CACM article an accessible retrospective. Later systems that build on or use the compiler include OpenTuner, Distributed Halide, and Tiramisu.

title: Dynamic Expressivity with Static Optimization for Streaming Languages
summary: This DEBS 2013 paper, joint work with IBM and NYU, presents a hybrid scheduler that combines the expressivity of dynamically scheduled streaming languages with the performance of static optimization. The compiler partitions a stream program into coarse-grained subgraphs separated by dynamic-rate boundaries, then applies aggressive static optimization within each subgraph. Implemented as an extension to the StreamIt compiler, the scheduler lets a previously static language run dynamic-rate applications while outperforming three dynamic scheduling alternatives — OS-thread, demand, and no-op — on micro-benchmarks and benchmarks modeled on real applications. The work relaxes the synchronous-dataflow restriction underlying StreamIt, whose static rates enabled optimizations such as coarse-grained parallelization but excluded applications with data-dependent rates.

title: Portable Performance on Heterogeneous Architectures
summary: This paper carries PetaBricks onto heterogeneous machines, where the best mapping of work across CPUs and GPUs differs from system to system. Programs declare algorithmic choices, and the compiler generates further choices in how they map to processors and memories — OpenCL kernel generation, data movement analysis, and memory management among them — which an empirical autotuner searches at installation time. The tuner constructs poly-algorithms that mix algorithmic techniques and use CPU and GPU together, obtaining up to a 16.5x speedup over running a single program configuration on all architectures. The work extends the PetaBricks language and compiler, and its SVD benchmark uses the variable-accuracy features. The heterogeneous compiler forms a chapter of Ansel's PhD thesis.

title: SiblingRivalry: Online Autotuning Through Local Competitions
summary: SiblingRivalry is a model for always-on online autotuning that lets programs adapt to changing conditions — new microarchitectures, migration in the cloud, fluctuating load — without a separate tuning step. It divides the cores of a machine in half and processes each request twice in parallel: a known safe configuration on one half races an experimental configuration chosen by a self-adapting evolutionary algorithm on the other, and the slower copy is terminated. Although half the machine is spent on learning, this racing yields a 1.8x geometric-mean speedup when adapting to microarchitecture changes and 1.3x under moderate load. SiblingRivalry was prototyped within the PetaBricks language and uses its variable-accuracy support for quality-of-service targets. A companion bandit hyperparameter study builds on the system's mutation-operator selection, and Ansel's PhD thesis incorporates the work and gives the most complete treatment.

title: Decoupling Algorithms from Schedules for Easy Optimization of Image Processing Pipelines

Programmers explore optimizations by changing only the schedule. The companion PLDI 2013 paper supplies the systematic tradeoff model and is the main compiler paper; Ragan-Kelley's PhD thesis is the most complete treatment, and the CACM article distills both papers. title: Optimizations in Stream Programming for Multimedia Applications
summary: Eric Wong's M.Eng. thesis develops two StreamIt optimizations for multimedia workloads. It identifies induction-variable state — iteration counters that serialize otherwise data-parallel filters — as a common obstacle to scalability, and adds an iter() language construct with a modified fission transformation so that such filters can be data-parallelized. It then exploits the error tolerance of multimedia outputs through inexact memoization based on locality-sensitive hashing, with a runtime system that tunes the memoization tables to balance output quality, measured by signal-to-noise ratio, against speed. Case studies cover MPEG-2 motion estimation, FIRBank, and MPEG-2 and MP3 decoder subsets. Implemented in StreamIt, the thesis modifies the fission transformation of the ASPLOS 2002 compiler and its interaction with phased scheduling, evaluates on the parallelization path of the ASPLOS 2006 paper, takes its motivation from the PACT 2010 characterization of avoidable state, and adapts MPEG-2 code from Drake's StreamIt implementation.

title: Distributed Data as a Choice in PetaBricks
summary: This M.Eng. thesis extends PetaBricks from shared-memory multicores to clusters of distributed-memory machines by making data placement itself an autotuned choice. A RegionMatrix abstraction lets data live across nodes behind the same matrix interface, the scheduler moves computation to where most of its data resides, and the compiler generates multiple code versions so execution falls back to the shared-memory path whenever data is local. On benchmarks run on an 8-node, 96-core system and a 64-node, 512-core system, the distributed runtime scales, in some cases with linear speedups. The work extends the PetaBricks language, compiler, and runtime, making cluster-level data placement one more choice for the autotuner.

title: Transparent Dynamic Instrumentation
summary: Transparent Dynamic Instrumentation examines the central obstacle to process virtualization: an application must not be able to tell that it is running inside DynamoRIO's software code cache rather than natively, and inserted tool code must not perturb its behavior. Where transparency had been handled ad hoc as problems surfaced, this paper identifies a necessary set of transparency requirements for running mainstream Windows and Linux applications, evaluates the tradeoffs among solutions to each issue, and identifies cases where full transparency is not practically solvable. The paper consolidates a decade of DynamoRIO engineering, from the 2001 Windows dynamic optimization framework through An Infrastructure for Adaptive Dynamic Optimization and the code cache consistency work; Bruening's PhD thesis gives the most complete treatment of the same material. Among later users of the system, Ithemal relies on DynamoRIO to collect the basic-block dataset behind its throughput estimator.

title: Hyperparameter Tuning in Bandit-Based Adaptive Operator Selection
summary: Within SiblingRivalry's online autotuner, candidate configurations are generated by choosing among mutation operators using bandit-based adaptive operator selection built on the Upper Confidence Bound algorithm. This paper studies the scheme's hyperparameters, which set the exploration-exploitation balance and the length of the sliding reward window. Tuning them across benchmarks in static and dynamic environments shows that although the optimal assignment varies greatly between programs, a single assignment per context performs well regardless of the program being tuned, making hyperparameter selection feasible on a general rather than per-program basis. This is a companion to the SiblingRivalry paper, whose racing autotuner the operator selection serves. The benchmarks come from the PetaBricks language and its variable-accuracy extensions, and Ansel's PhD thesis incorporates the study into its online-autotuning chapters.

title: Aikido: Accelerating Shared Data Dynamic Analyses
summary: Aikido is a system and framework for building efficient dynamic analyses that operate on shared data in multithreaded programs. Rather than instrumenting every memory operation, it runs a custom hypervisor below the operating system that exposes per-thread hardware page protection, then applies dynamic binary rewriting only where threads actually communicate, keeping word-level accuracy at hardware-detection cost. An Aikido-enabled vector-clock race detector outperforms existing techniques of similar accuracy by up to 6.0x, and by 76% on average, on the PARSEC benchmark suite. Aikido is built directly on the group's dynamic-instrumentation infrastructure. It is implemented as an extension of Zhao's Umbra memory-shadowing framework (CGO 2010), modified to map each application address to two shadow addresses, and it ships a modified version of DynamoRIO (CGO 2003) whose changes provide the per-thread page protection at the heart of the system.

title: Optimization of Naive Dynamic Binary Instrumentation Tools
summary: Kleckner's M.Eng. thesis speeds up naive dynamic binary instrumentation tools, those that instrument code through clean calls: callbacks into ordinary C that require a stack switch, a full register save, and argument materialization at every call site. It adds to DynamoRIO a partial inlining optimization for instrumentation routines with conditional fast paths, a call coalescing optimization that batches calls into fewer context switches, and supporting machine-code optimizations such as redundant load elimination and flags avoidance. On SPEC CPU2006 benchmarks the thesis reports speedups of up to 54.8x for an instruction-counting tool and 3.7x on average for a memory-alignment checker. The work extends the tool interface of DynamoRIO, building on an inlining prototype by Qin Zhao, and narrows the gap between easy-to-write clean-call tools and hand-optimized instrumentation; Bruening's PhD thesis describes the runtime and the general tool interface the thesis optimizes.

title: Can Silhouette Execution mitigate VM Boot Storms?
summary: This M.Eng. thesis asks whether a hypervisor can exploit the overlap between the instruction streams of virtual machines booting concurrently — an idea named silhouette execution — to relieve the CPU pressure of boot storms. Using dynamic instrumentation, it profiles nondeterminism in the user-space instruction streams of Linux services and catalogs the causes of divergence. Simulations show naive silhouette execution would increase CPU pressure by 13% for 100 VMs, but with strategies that remove synthetic differences between executions it reduces CPU pressure by 8x for 100 VMs and 19x for 1000 VMs. The instruction-stream profiles were gathered with Pin and DynamoRIO, run independently to verify the accuracy of the measurements.

title: An Efficient Evolutionary Algorithm for Solving Bottom Up Problems
summary: INCREA is an evolutionary algorithm for problems whose small instances embed within larger ones, as they do in program autotuning. It derives its initial population by recursively running itself on smaller problem instances, expands and shrinks the population each generation, cuts off candidates that stop looking fruitful, and resolves noisy fitness measurements on small, cheap-to-evaluate instances before scaling up. Compared with a general-purpose evolutionary algorithm on PetaBricks autotuning benchmarks, INCREA usually reaches the same solution in significantly less time. The autotuners in the paper operate on programs written in the PetaBricks language. Later input-sensitivity work — a 2014 technical report and a PLDI 2015 paper — built on the evolutionary autotuner to construct landmark configurations, and Ansel's PhD thesis incorporates INCREA as its evolutionary-autotuning chapter.

title: Language-Independent Sandboxing of Just-In-Time Compilation and Self-Modifying Code
summary: This paper extends software-based fault isolation (SFI), traditionally a static technique, so that just-in-time compilers and self-modifying code can run safely inside a sandbox. It contributes language-independent constraints and mechanisms under which runtime code creation, modification, and deletion preserve the sandbox's safety guarantees, implemented in both the x86-32 and x86-64 variants of Google's Native Client. The authors port two production language runtimes, the Mono common language runtime and the V8 JavaScript engine, and measure sandboxing overheads that are generally moderate and close to zero for some benchmark and platform combinations.

title: Scaling Deterministic Multithreading
summary: This workshop paper at WoDet 2011, the Workshop on Determinism and Correctness in Parallel Programming, takes up the question its title states: how deterministic multithreading behaves as parallel machines grow. Kendo had shown that a reproducible order of lock acquisitions can be enforced in software with a geometric-mean overhead of 16% on four processors; this paper examines what it takes for such weak-determinism guarantees to remain efficient as core counts rise. It continues the line begun with Kendo (ASPLOS 2009), by the same authors, whose deterministic logical time is the mechanism being scaled. No copy of the paper is available on the publications site, so this description draws on the title, venue, and surrounding work.

title: Dynamic Cache Contention Detection in Multi-threaded Applications
summary: This paper presents a tool that detects true and false sharing in multi-threaded applications without simulating the memory hierarchy. Its key insight is that while the slowdown caused by cache contention depends on thread-to-core binding and machine parameters, the amount of data sharing is primarily a function of cache line size and application behavior. Using memory shadowing and dynamic instrumentation, the tool determines thread correlation and pinpoints the sources of significant false sharing at an average slowdown of 5x over native execution, far below detailed cache simulation, and guided fixes that improved some applications by up to 12x. The tool is built on Umbra's shadow memory framework and DynamoRIO, using the EMS64 mapping scheme on 64-bit address spaces. A machine-learning false sharing detector presented at SC 2013 later used the tool as ground truth and baseline in its evaluation.

title: Practical Memory Checking with Dr. Memory
summary: Dr. Memory is a memory checking tool that finds memory-related errors, including use of freed or uninitialized memory, corruption, and leaks, in unmodified applications on both Windows and Linux. The paper describes how it copes with the complex and incompletely documented Windows environment, avoids the false positive leak reports that plague traditional leak-locating algorithms, and keeps overhead down with efficient instrumentation. In a direct comparison, Dr. Memory is twice as fast as Valgrind's Memcheck on average and up to four times faster on individual benchmarks. Dr. Memory is built on DynamoRIO, whose design and tool interface Bruening's PhD thesis describes in full.

title: Language and Compiler Support For Auto-Tuning Variable-Accuracy Algorithms
summary: This paper makes accuracy a tunable dimension of PetaBricks programs. Language extensions let programmers define accuracy metrics, accuracy variables, and target requirements for variable-accuracy algorithms — approximation algorithms, iterative methods, heuristics — including when such algorithms nest. The compiler performs fully automatic compile-time and install-time autotuning, using a structured genetic algorithm to search algorithm and accuracy choices through recursion and sub-calls, so a library user states a target accuracy and gets an optimized implementation. Across a new benchmark suite, relaxing accuracy yields speedups from 1.1x to orders of magnitude. The extensions build on the PetaBricks language and generalize the accuracy-aware multigrid autotuner. Later work built on them: the heterogeneous compiler tunes variable-accuracy benchmarks, and the input-sensitivity work selects accuracy-respecting configurations per input. Ansel's PhD thesis incorporates the material and gives the most complete treatment.

title: PetaBricks:  Building adaptable and more efficient programs for the multi-core era
summary: A magazine article, written for ACM's student magazine XRDS, that introduces PetaBricks to a broad audience. It explains how transforms and rules let a program define not a single algorithmic path but a search space of paths, walks through a k-means example whose initial conditions and iteration strategies are all choices, and argues that empirical autotuning over such spaces gives programs portable performance — and longer useful lifetimes — across architectures. Sort configurations moved between three machines slowed by 1.68x on average, making the case for per-machine tuning. The article is a magazine presentation of the system described in the PLDI 2009 language paper and Ansel's S.M. thesis; his PhD thesis later absorbed the material and gives the most complete treatment.

title: An Empirical Characterization of Stream Programs and its Implications for Language and Compiler Design
summary: This PACT 2010 paper characterizes stream programs as written natively in a stream language, rather than inferred from legacy C, C++, or FORTRAN implementations. Using the StreamIt benchmark suite — 65 programs and 33,600 lines of code — it quantifies the bottlenecks to parallelism, data-reference patterns, input/output rates, use of filter state, and scheduling behavior, and draws out the implications for the design of streaming languages, compilers, and architectures. Among the findings: most filters are stateless, and much of the state that does occur is avoidable. The study distills a decade of application development around StreamIt; the same material forms a chapter of Thies's PhD thesis. The suite includes Aziz's motion-estimation application, and phased scheduling and the ASPLOS 2006 parallelizer are among the techniques it assesses. The avoidable-state finding motivated Wong's M.Eng. thesis, and the suite became the comparison baseline for StreamJIT.

title: Compiler Techniques for Scalable Performance of Stream Programs on Multicore Architectures
summary: Michael Gordon's PhD thesis demonstrates that when algorithmic parallelism is expressed as a stream graph, a compiler can manage granularity, load balancing, synchronization, and communication automatically. Working on static-rate regions, the compiler coarsens granularity, then exploits data, task, and pipeline parallelism holistically; it data-parallelizes filters with sliding windows by translating serializing state into minimal inter-core communication, and applies coarse-grained software pipelining to the stateful filters that remain. On the 12-application StreamIt Core suite it reports a 14.9x mean speedup on the 16-core Raw machine, 14x on a 16-core SMP, and 52x on a 64-core distributed shared-memory multicore. The most complete treatment of StreamIt's parallelization line, the thesis subsumes and updates earlier versions of this work — his S.M. thesis, the ASPLOS 2002 stream compiler and its technical-report form, and the ASPLOS 2006 paper — and evaluates on the benchmark suite described in Thies's companion thesis.

title: Distributed Functional Programming in Scheme
summary: This M.Eng. thesis presents a framework for distributed programming in Scheme built on simple future semantics: a program written for a single computer can run on a cluster with very little modification, and the structure of the computation need not be specified in advance. A system of job-execution servers transparently runs arbitrary Scheme code written in a functional, mostly side-effect-free style, which removes most data-consistency concerns. Demonstrations include a distributed SAT solver, and measured performance grows roughly linearly with the number of servers.

title: Efficient Memory Shadowing for 64-bit Architectures
summary: EMS64 is a memory shadowing scheme for 64-bit architectures. Direct mapping schemes fail on 64-bit machines because operating system layout constraints leave no single contiguous region that can shadow the whole address space, while segmented schemes pay a table lookup on every translation. EMS64 instead exploits application reference locality and the large unused regions of the 64-bit address space to translate addresses with a simple displacement in the common case. The paper proves feasibility conditions for a valid mapping, gives a randomized layout algorithm, and reduces average translation overhead to 81%, nearly halving that of the fastest 64-bit scheme known to the authors. EMS64 is implemented on top of Umbra, whose CGO 2010 paper introduced the framework at a 133% average translation overhead, and runs on DynamoRIO. The cache contention detector later adopted the EMS64 mapping to shadow 64-bit address spaces.

title: Umbra: Efficient and Scalable Memory Shadowing
summary: Umbra is a framework for memory shadowing, the technique shadow-value tools use to track metadata about every application data location at instruction granularity. Its translation scheme maps application addresses to shadow metadata for both 32-bit and 64-bit applications without relying on platform features or fixing the shadow memory size, removing the limitation that kept earlier tools from monitoring the full 64-bit address space. Combined with mapping optimizations and general instrumentation optimizations, Umbra reduces shadow translation overhead to 133% on average, demonstrated on a real shadow-value tool. Umbra is built on DynamoRIO. The companion EMS64 paper at ISMM 2010 lowers the 64-bit translation overhead further, to 81%; the cache contention detector is built directly on Umbra's framework, and Aikido extends it to accelerate dynamic analyses of shared data.

title: PetaBricks: A Language and Compiler for Algorithmic Choice
summary: This S.M. thesis presents the PetaBricks language and compiler, in which transforms compute outputs through multiple alternative rules and the compiler autotunes over the resulting choice space. It describes the compiler's code generation, the work-stealing runtime, the autotuning system and its choice configuration framework, automated consistency checking between alternative implementations, and evaluations on Poisson's equation, the symmetric eigenproblem, sort, and matrix multiply, including experiments on how tuned configurations shift between architectures. The thesis is the graduate-thesis version of the PLDI 2009 paper, with text drawn in part from the SC 2009 multigrid paper. The same system is presented for students in an XRDS magazine article, and Ansel's PhD thesis subsumes the material and gives the most complete treatment.

title: Autotuning Multigrid with PetaBricks
summary: This paper autotunes multigrid solvers written in PetaBricks, where algorithmic choice recurs at every level of recursion: at each grid resolution a cycle may coarsen, refine, apply iterative methods such as Jacobi or successive over-relaxation, or switch to a direct solver. Because these choices trade accuracy against time, the autotuner uses a dynamic programming method that builds tuned algorithms bottom-up from tuned sub-algorithms, each meeting a target accuracy, yielding customized multigrid cycle shapes for a given problem, machine, and accuracy requirement. The multigrid work was developed in the PetaBricks language, and its accuracy-aware tuning was generalized in the CGO 2011 variable-accuracy paper. Its text is shared with Ansel's S.M. thesis, and his PhD thesis presents the multigrid autotuning in fullest form.

title: Computer-Aided Design for Microfluidic Chips Based on Multilayer Soft Lithography
summary: Computer-Aided Design for Microfluidic Chips Based on Multilayer Soft Lithography brings design automation to chips where fluids flow along channels controlled by pressurized valves, a substrate earlier CAD work had ignored in favor of droplet devices. It focuses on the control layer: designers specify a device's Instruction Set Architecture, from which the tool infers the valve locations that implement it. It contributes algorithms for minimizing the control lines that drive the valves and for routing valves to control ports while sharing lines. These are packaged as Micado, a free AutoCAD plug-in, demonstrated on three realistic chips. It builds on the microfluidic-ISA notion set out in the Natural Computing abstraction-layers paper.

title: Manipulating Lossless Video in the Compressed Domain
summary: This ACM Multimedia 2009 paper presents a general technique for transforming data compressed with sliding-window Lempel-Ziv (LZ77) without decompressing it, extending compressed-domain processing — previously limited to lossy formats such as JPEG and MPEG — to the lossless formats used in video production. Applied to the Apple Animation format, the technique supports color adjustment, compositing, and other editing operations directly on compressed video. A compiler transformation makes it automatic: users write a StreamIt program over uncompressed data, and the compiler maps it to operate on compressed data. Across 12 benchmark videos, speedups are roughly proportional to the compression factor, ranging from 1.1x to 471x with a median of 15x. The compiler transformation is built on StreamIt, and a chapter of Thies's PhD thesis subsumes this material. The approach of computing directly on LZ77-compressed data was later built on by a CGO 2022 compiler that unifies lossless compression with sparse computing.

summary: PetaBricks is an implicitly parallel language and compiler that makes algorithmic choice a first-class construct. A programmer writes multiple rules for producing the same data — different algorithms, decompositions, and base cases — and the compiler and autotuner assemble them into poly-algorithms, tuning parallelization, data distribution, and blocking alongside the algorithms themselves. title: DMTCP: Transparent Checkpointing for Cluster Computations and the Desktop
summary: DMTCP (Distributed MultiThreaded CheckPointing) is a transparent, user-level checkpointing package for distributed applications. Requiring no kernel modules, patches, or special privileges, it can be bundled with the applications it checkpoints, and it automatically handles threads, sockets, pipes, terminals, shared memory, and ssh-spawned processes. The paper demonstrates checkpoint and restart for over 20 applications, including MATLAB, Python, OpenMPI, and the 680 MB runCMS image from the Large Hadron Collider's CMS experiment; on 128 distributed cores, checkpoint and restart typically take 2 seconds, falling to 0.2 seconds with forked checkpointing. Written with Arya and Cooperman of Northeastern University, DMTCP became a widely used open-source checkpointing tool.

title: Language and Compiler Support for Stream Programs
summary: William Thies's PhD thesis is the most complete treatment of the StreamIt language. It defines the abstractions — hierarchical single-input single-output streams, composable primitives for data reordering, and teleport messaging for precise event handling — and validates them by characterizing the 34,000-line StreamIt benchmark suite, spanning MPEG-2 codecs to GMTI radar. The thesis consolidates the CC 2002 language paper, teleport messaging, the MICRO 2007 legacy-C work, and the compressed-domain paper; the benchmark characterization later appeared at PACT 2010. title: Kendo: Efficient Deterministic Multithreading in Software
summary: Kendo is a software-only system that provides deterministic multithreading: given the same input, a lock-based parallel program always sees the same interleaving of lock acquisitions and specially declared unprotected reads. A dynamically load-balanced scheduling algorithm constructs a deterministic logical time from hardware performance counters, so the schedule is reproducible yet still balances work on commodity hardware. On the SPLASH-2 benchmarks Kendo incurs a geometric-mean overhead of 16% on four processors, low enough to leave determinism enabled after deployment. This is the main paper of the Aikido/Kendo project; Scaling Deterministic Multithreading (WoDet 2011), by the same authors, later examined how its guarantees hold up as core counts rise.

title: Static Deadlock Detection for Java Libraries
summary: This ECOOP paper develops static deadlock detection for Java libraries, determining whether any client calling pattern can deadlock a library so its writer can guarantee deadlock freedom. A flow-sensitive, context-sensitive analysis computes a lock-order graph representing the order in which the library acquires locks; cycles in the graph indicate deadlock possibilities, and the tool reports all of them. Applied to 18 libraries comprising 1,245 kLOC, the analysis verified 13 libraries to be free from deadlock and found 14 distinct deadlocks in three of them.

summary: Abstraction Layers for Scalable Microfluidic Biocomputing is the journal treatment of the BioStream/Fluidic ISA work and its most complete account. It presents BioStream, a portable language for biology protocols, and the Fluidic ISA, a stable interface for chip designers, arguing that, as with silicon, such layers must decouple software from a device technology whose complexity rises like Moore's Law. A novel algorithm translates microfluidic mixing operations from the BioStream layer down to the Fluidic ISA. To demonstrate, the authors build two chips that execute the same BioStream code despite significant device-level differences. It and the extended technical report present the same material in different form. The programmable chip it relies on is described in Digital microfluidics using soft lithography. title: Tiled Microprocessors
summary: Tiled Microprocessors is Michael Taylor's PhD thesis on the class of physically scalable processors that Raw exemplifies: arrays of replicated tiles joined by a Scalar Operand Network optimized for low-latency, low-occupancy transport of operands between ALUs on different tiles. The thesis identifies seven criteria for physical scalability, develops the study of scalar operand networks — introducing the 5-tuple performance metric and the AsTrO taxonomy — and details the design, implementation, and analysis of the Raw prototype, built at MIT in 180 nm technology. This is the most complete treatment of the architecture side of the Raw project, consolidating Taylor's earlier publications on the same work: the scalar operand networks paper of HPCA 2003, the IEEE Micro chip description, the ISSCC 2003 implementation paper, and the ISCA 2004 evaluation.

title: Software orchestration of Instruction Level parallelism on Tiled Processor Architectures
summary: Walter Lee's PhD thesis examines how a tiled processor architecture distributes its resources — instructions, registers, control flow, data memory, and wires — over a pipelined interconnect, and how a compiler can orchestrate instruction-level parallelism across them. Its centerpiece is Rawcc, the ILP compiler for Raw, which partitions operations among tiles, places them for locality, and programs the routes that carry operands between them. Evaluated on a cycle-accurate simulator and the 16-tile Raw chip, Rawcc obtains speedups on fine-grained applications, with performance scaling up to 64 tiles. This is the most complete treatment of the Rawcc space-time scheduling work, earlier versions of which appeared as a 1997 technical report and the ASPLOS 1998 space-time scheduling paper.

author0:
Blaise Gassend and Charles W. O'Donnell and William Thies and Andrew Lee and Marten van Dijk and
                  Srinivas Devadas
title:
Learning Biophysically Motivated Parameters for
                  Alpha Helix Prediction
summary: This RECOMB 2006 poster sketches a method for predicting protein secondary structure from an intuitive, biophysically-motivated energy model. A protein's structure is taken to minimize a free-energy function computed as a sum of elementary free-energies — for example, the cost of a residue sitting in an alpha helix — which dynamic programming minimizes once the parameters are fixed. The elementary free-energies are learned with a structured Support Vector Machine trained on a database of known structures, using margin maximization and slack variables, iterating until predictions are correct. On all-alpha proteins, a 302-parameter model reaches a Qα of 77.6% and SOVα of 73.4%. The companion PRIB 2006 paper presents the same 302-parameter model as a Hidden Markov Support Vector Machine.
booktitle: International Conference on Research in Computational Molecular Biology (RECOMB), Poster Session

title:
Learning Biophysically-Motivated Parameters for
                  Alpha Helix Prediction
summary: This journal article develops a protein secondary-structure predictor built on an intuitive, biophysically-motivated energy model. It treats prediction as an optimization problem: a parameterizable cost function of biological pseudo-energies is minimized, and machine-learning methods estimate the parameters so that known structures are predicted correctly. Focusing on alpha helices, the authors show that a model with 302 parameters achieves a Qα value of 77.6% and an SOVα value of 73.4% — among the best for techniques that do not rely on external databases such as multiple sequence alignments. With so few parameters the model's biological significance is easier to extract, and the method extends beyond the all-alpha case. This article expands the PRIB 2006 paper, which casts the same 302-parameter model as a Hidden Markov Support Vector Machine.

author0:
Blaise Gassend and Charles W. O'Donnell and William Thies and Andrew Lee and Marten van Dijk and
                  Srinivas Devadas
title:
Predicting Secondary Structure of All-Helical
                  Proteins Using Hidden Markov Support Vector
                  Machines
summary: This PRIB 2006 paper predicts the secondary structure of all-helical proteins using Hidden Markov Support Vector Machines. Hidden Markov Models give a natural representation of secondary structure with fewer parameters than neural networks — hundreds rather than ten thousand — aiding interpretability and reducing overlearning, though standard training limits accuracy. HM-SVMs keep the HMM prediction structure while replacing expectation-maximization with a discriminative learner that offers a soft-margin criterion and bidirectional influence of features on parameters. Applied to a 7-state, 302-parameter HMM for alpha helices and coils, the method reaches a Qα of 77.6% and SOVα of 73.4%, among the best for methods avoiding external databases. It shares its 302-parameter model and headline numbers with the RECOMB 2006 poster; the expanded BMC Bioinformatics 2007 journal article gives the most complete treatment of the same work.

author0: Somani Patnaik and Emma Brunskill and William Thies
title:
Evaluating the Accuracy of Data Collection on Mobile
                  Phones: A Study of Forms, SMS, and Voice
summary: This paper reports the first quantitative evaluation, to its authors' knowledge, of data-entry accuracy on mobile phones in a resource-poor setting. Thirteen users in Gujarat, India, reported structured data through three interfaces: electronic forms, SMS composed from printed cue cards, and live voice calls to an operator. Error rates per datum were 4.2% for forms, 4.5% for SMS, and 0.45% for voice — a gap that led the authors to move their own tuberculosis-treatment program in rural India from forms to voice. The finding was later built on by a DEV 2010 study of IVR interfaces, which asked whether an automated voice system, rather than a live operator, could serve untrained rural users.
booktitle: International Conference on Information and Communication Technologies and Development (ICTD)

title: Programming by Sketching for Bit-Streaming Programs
summary: This PLDI paper introduces programming by sketching: the programmer writes a clean bit-level reference program, then sketches only the outline of an efficient word-level implementation, and the compiler fills in the missing details while guaranteeing that the completed sketch stays faithful to the reference. StreamBit realizes the methodology for bit-streaming programs such as ciphers, where buggy optimizations become security holes. In a user study, given the same time budget, novice StreamBit programmers produced ciphers 2.5× faster than experienced C programmers, and DES and Serpent implementations competitive with hand-optimized public code. Reference programs are written in the StreamIt dataflow language, whose synchronous dataflow model StreamBit's intermediate representation and sketch semantics build on. The Sketch synthesis approach begun here was later used to prove checkers correct in a 2015 M.Eng. thesis on verifying executions of classic algorithms on unreliable hardware.
author0: Armando Solar-Lezama and Rodric Rabbah and Rastislav Bodik and Kemal Ebcioglu

title: How to do a million watchpoints: Efficient Debugging Using Dynamic Instrumentation
summary: EDDI, Efficient Debugging using Dynamic Instrumentation, shows that dynamic instrumentation applied on demand can accelerate software debuggers where hardware support is lacking. Its centerpiece is the data watchpoint: where debuggers relying on x86 debug registers are limited to four watched locations, EDDI inserts checking code into the running application and can monitor more than a million data locations with a slowdown of less than 3x compared to native execution. That overhead is low enough for interactive debugging, and the framework extends to other debugging features beyond watchpoints. EDDI is implemented as an extension of DynamoRIO, the runtime code manipulation system described in Bruening's PhD thesis.

author0: Nada Amin
title: Computer-Aided Design for Multilayer Microfluidic Chips
summary: Computer-Aided Design for Multilayer Microfluidic Chips is Nada Amin's M.Eng. thesis and the most complete treatment of the Micado design-automation work. It targets multilayer soft-lithography chips, whose growing component counts had outrun a manual design methodology, and automates the control layer. The thesis defines an Instruction Set Architecture as a hierarchical composition of flows, infers and generates the logic and control signals that drive the chip, and gives a routing algorithm connecting control channels to peripheral I/O ports. The techniques ship as Micado, an AutoCAD plug-in evaluated on real chips used by designers. It builds on the microfluidic-ISA notion set out in the Natural Computing abstraction-layers paper.

author0: Pratik Kotkar and William Thies and Saman Amarasinghe
title: An Audio Wiki for Building Local Repositories of Knowledge in the Developing World
summary: The Audio Wiki is a repository of spoken content that a community can build and browse using ordinary telephones. All content is stored as audio recordings of users' experience and knowledge, so the system serves illiterate users and any local language; callers navigate menus by speech or keypad to search, listen to, and edit entries. This poster paper presents the design and implementation of the server that supports it, motivated by cell-phone penetration in the developing world far outpacing computer ownership. A companion CHI 2008 workshop paper is another version of the same work, emphasizing publishing rather than only consuming information.
booktitle: Wireless Systems: Advanced Research and Development (WISARD)

author0: Pratik Kotkar and William Thies and Saman Amarasinghe
title: An Audio Wiki for Publishing User-Generated Content in the Developing World
summary: This workshop paper argues that the Web's power came from making everyone a publisher, yet its interfaces demand literacy and computer access that much of the world lacks. It proposes the Audio Wiki as a remedy: a repository of spoken content that can be created, edited, and played back in audio over a low-cost telephone. Because no reading is required at any stage, the system is open to illiterate users and supports any local language, with envisioned applications in agriculture, health, government, and entrepreneurship. The paper is a companion version of the WISARD 2008 poster, which details the same system's design and implementation.
booktitle: HCI for Community and International Development (HCI4CID Workshop at CHI)
venue: HCI for Community and International Development (HCI4CID Workshop)

title: PiPA: Pipelined Profiling and Analysis on Multi-core Systems
summary: PiPA, Pipelined Profiling and Analysis, parallelizes dynamic program profiling on multicore systems. The overhead of instrumentation-based tools comes both from the instrumentation itself and from the user-defined analysis; PiPA attacks the second, less-studied component by having the instrumented application record compact execution profiles that a pipeline of helper threads decodes and analyzes in parallel. A prototype built on DynamoRIO performing full cache simulation slows applications by only 10.5x on an 8-core system, compared with more than 100x for Cachegrind and 32x for Pin's dcache tool. The prototype's runtime, DynamoRIO, is described in An Infrastructure for Adaptive Dynamic Optimization.
author0: Qin Zhao and Ioana Cutcutache and Weng-Fai Wong
booktitle: 6th International Symposium on Code Generation and Optimization (CGO)

author0: Xin David Zhang and Qiuyuan J. Li and Rodric Rabbah and Saman Amarasinghe
title: A Lightweight Streaming Layer for Multicore Execution
summary: This dasCMP 2007 paper specifies a multicore streaming layer: an intermediate layer between a stream program and its target that presents a common abstraction across multicore architectures, manages filter computation, and orchestrates and optimizes communication automatically where appropriate. The authors implement an instance of the layer for the Cell processor in the context of StreamIt and report greater than 88% utilization on all benchmarks with relatively small amounts of code; the design applies to other architectures and stream languages as well. The Cell backend is built in the context of StreamIt, on the compiler infrastructure and software-pipelining techniques of the ASPLOS 2006 paper. Zhang's M.Eng. thesis is the complete account of the same framework, covering the Cell runtime library and the dynamic scheduling framework built on it.
booktitle: Workshop on Design, Architecture and Simulation of Chip Multi-Processors (dasCMP)

author0: Xin David Zhang
title: A Streaming Computation Framework for the Cell Processor
summary: Xin David Zhang's M.Eng. thesis implements a runtime library for the Cell processor designed to support streaming applications and streaming-language compilers. The library abstracts Cell's DMA-based on-chip communication network behind filter, buffer, and command constructs; handles data movement among the PowerPC core and the SPEs; and simplifies the scheduling of stream actors. On top of it the thesis builds a dynamic scheduling framework and compares scheduler programmability with and without the library, finding that it adds no significant overhead while greatly reducing the code a high-level scheduler requires. The thesis is the full account of the framework summarized in the dasCMP 2007 paper on the multicore streaming layer. It is designed around StreamIt and its ASPLOS 2002 compiler, and implements on Cell the coarse-grained software-pipelining execution pattern of the ASPLOS 2006 paper.

author0: William Thies and Vikram Chandrasekhar and Saman Amarasinghe
title: A Practical Approach to Exploiting Coarse-Grained Pipeline Parallelism in C Programs
summary: This MICRO 2007 paper offers a pragmatic route to coarse-grained pipeline parallelism in legacy C programs. The programmer marks candidate pipeline-stage boundaries in a loop; a dynamic analysis records all communication crossing those boundaries during training runs and emits both a stream graph of the algorithm and macros that fork the stages into processes communicating through pipes. The transformation is deliberately unsound — it assumes the observed communication pattern is stable, as it typically is in streaming applications — with errors caught by ordinary testing. Across six case studies, including MPEG-2 and MP3 decoding, GMTI radar processing, and three SPEC benchmarks, it reports a 2.78x mean speedup on a four-core machine. The same material appears, in very similar form, as a chapter of Thies's PhD thesis.
booktitle: 40th Annual IEEE/ACM International Symposium on Microarchitecture (MICRO)

author0: Abdulbasier Aziz
title: Image-Based Motion Estimation in a Stream Programming Language
summary: Abdulbasier Aziz's M.Eng. thesis contributes a computer-vision case study of StreamIt: an image-based motion estimation application — feature extraction, putative matching, and RANSAC — ported from a MATLAB reference implementation. The thesis examines how well filters, pipelines, split-joins, feedback loops, and messaging preserve the block structure of the original algorithm, reports the StreamIt version running 2% faster than the MATLAB reference, proposes language extensions suggested by the porting experience, and discusses the further speedups available from parallelizing subroutines within the program. The application is written in StreamIt, exercising the language's abstractions on irregular, feedback-heavy code. Later work drew on it: Thies's PhD thesis counts the evaluation among StreamIt's application studies, and its Mosaic implementation became one of the benchmarks characterized at PACT 2010.

author0: Saman Amarasinghe
title: The Looming Software Crisis due to the Multicore Menace
summary: This talk argues that multicore processors set off a third software crisis. The first crisis was resolved by high-level languages such as FORTRAN and C; the second by object orientation and better tools. Both let programmers ignore the processor while Moore's law supplied speedups. With sequential performance stalled and vendors adding cores instead, that abstraction fails: existing programs stop getting faster, and performance again becomes the programmer's problem. The talk argues for languages and compilers that expose parallelism naturally, with streaming as a leading example. The argument frames the motivation for the StreamIt project, presented in the CC 2002 language paper; the response it sketches is the task, data, and pipeline parallelism of the ASPLOS 2006 paper, whose results the talk presents as its evidence.

author0: Saman Amarasinghe
title: StreamIt – A Programming Language for the Era of Multicores
summary: A talk surveying the StreamIt project as an answer to the multicore era. The slides trace the end of uniprocessor performance scaling, frame the parallel programmer's dilemma between productivity and performance, and lay out the project's layered agenda: language semantics and the Eclipse programming environment; scheduling and cache optimization; domain-specific linear and state-space optimization; teleport messaging and compilation to communication-exposed architectures; and applications ranging from DSP benchmarks and MPEG to cryptography. The slides condense the project's publications into one narrative: the language (CC 2002), teleport messaging (PPoPP 2005), and coarse-grained parallelization (ASPLOS 2006), framed by the question posed in the CGO 2005 keynote abstract. This entry is a slide deck rather than a paper.

author0: Qin Zhao and Rodric Rabbah and Saman Amarasinghe and Larry Rudolph and Weng-Fai Wong
title: Ubiquitous Memory Introspection
summary: Ubiquitous Memory Introspection (UMI) is an online, lightweight methodology for obtaining fine-grained memory behavior profiles while a program runs. It identifies frequently executed code regions, selectively instruments them to record short memory access traces, and periodically runs fast mini-simulations over those traces to derive instruction-level profiles that would otherwise require lengthy offline cache simulation. A prototype has 14% average runtime overhead, only 1% more than plain binary instrumentation, across 32 benchmarks; it predicts delinquent loads with 88% accuracy for applications with many cache misses, and drives a runtime software prefetching strategy achieving up to a 64% speedup. The UMI prototype is built by extending DynamoRIO.
booktitle: 5th International Symposium on Code Generation and Optimization (CGO)

author0: Qin Zhao and Joon Edward Sim and Larry Rudolph and Weng-Fai Wong
title: DEP: Detailed Execution Profile
summary: DEP, the Detailed Execution Profile, captures a program's complete dynamic control flow, data dependences, and memory references in one compact profile. Its key insight: because memory is addressed register-relatively, a coupled record of control flow and register value changes suffices to recover every memory reference. Profiles are collected in a single pass by Adept, an instrumentation infrastructure built on DynamoRIO that covers shared libraries and multiple threads. DEP incurs a 5x average slowdown with 10MB of intermediate buffering per thread, versus 23x and 500MB for eWPP, with profiles about 60% the size of traditional ones. The DynamoRIO runtime beneath Adept is described in An Infrastructure for Adaptive Dynamic Optimization.
booktitle: 15th International Conference on Parallel Architectures and Compilation Techniques (PACT)

author0: Michael I. Gordon and William Thies and Saman Amarasinghe
title: Exploiting Coarse-Grained Task, Data, and Pipeline Parallelism in Stream Programs
summary: This paper demonstrates an end-to-end stream compiler that exploits task, data, and pipeline parallelism in a unified manner, so that multicore performance holds up across applications whose dominant form of parallelism differs. It coarsens the stream graph, fissions stateless filters for data parallelism, and software-pipelines stateful filters. Mapping StreamIt programs to the 16-core Raw architecture, the compiler attains an 11.2x mean speedup over a single-core baseline and a 1.84x speedup over the earlier StreamIt backend. This is the main multicore-parallelization paper of the StreamIt project. Gordon's PhD thesis (2010) gives the most complete treatment of these techniques, and much subsequent stream-compiler work builds on the paper, including an empirical characterization of stream programs (PACT 2010), StreamJIT (OOPSLA 2014), and Gloss (ASPLOS 2018).
booktitle: 12th International Conference on Architectural Support for Programming Languages and Operating Systems (ASPLOS)

author0: Mark Stephenson
title: Automating the Construction of Compiler Heuristics Using Machine Learning
summary: Stephenson's PhD thesis is the most complete treatment of meta optimization, the methodology of constructing compiler heuristics by machine learning rather than by hand. Arguing that compiler writers should concentrate on correctness while learning algorithms design policy, it develops machine-learned heuristics for three optimizations (hyperblock formation, register allocation, and loop unrolling) that outperform their hand-crafted counterparts by as much as 3× in some cases, combining genetic-programming policy search with supervised classification. The experiments culminate in collaborative compilation, which lets ordinary users transparently train compiler heuristics simply by running their applications. The thesis consolidates the PLDI 2003 Meta Optimization paper, its EuroGP 2003 companion, and the supervised study Predicting Unroll Factors; the pass-ordering results of Adapting Convergent Scheduling, joint work with Diego Puppin, appear here as dissertation research as well.
