author0: Sie Hendrata Dharmawan
title: Understanding Program Structure and Behavior
summary: Dharmawan's M.Eng. thesis presents LogiView, an algorithm that recovers the logical organization of a program from its call graph. Computing dominator trees and identifying phase-marker functions, LogiView groups functions into logical tasks, exposing structure that documentation and code inspection rarely reveal. A second analysis mines function names, building dictionaries of semantically related names and measuring how similar two programs are. A final chapter uses the identified phase markers to explain abrupt changes and repetitions in observed behavior, such as cache miss-rate phases.

author0: Matthew Drake
title: Stream Programming for Image and Video Compression
summary: Drake's M.Eng. thesis argues that multimedia compression is a natural fit for the streaming model, through a case study of MPEG-2. It contributes a clean, malleable, and portable StreamIt implementation of both an MPEG-2 encoder and decoder, an analysis of how a streaming language improves programmer productivity and enables scalable parallel execution, and an enumeration of the language features needed to express compression algorithms cleanly and to support large-scale application development with portability and reuse. The thesis is the expanded treatment of the IPDPS 2006 paper, which covers the decoder; the thesis adds the encoder and the language-design analysis. The codec is written in the StreamIt language (CC 2002), and its parallel execution rests on the ASPLOS 2002 stream compiler and the Raw architecture it targets (ISCA 2004).

author0: Samuel Larsen
title: Compilation Techniques for Short-Vector Instructions
summary: Larsen's PhD thesis develops compiler techniques for targeting the short-vector instructions of multimedia extensions automatically and transparently. Its two main contributions are selective vectorization, a software-pipelining formulation on a low-level intermediate representation that balances computation between scalar and vector resources and manages operand transfer between them, and a range of techniques for detecting and enforcing memory alignment, the most practical of which aligns roughly 75% of dynamic references. On a realistic VLIW model, selective vectorization yields whole-program speedups of up to 1.35x on SPEC FP benchmarks, and up to 1.75x on individual loops. This is the most complete treatment of the SLP line, consolidating the PLDI 2000 paper that introduced superword-level parallelism (first circulated as a 1999 technical report and expanded in Larsen's S.M. thesis), the alignment and congruence work, and the MICRO 2005 selective vectorization paper. Its compiler passes were built on the SUIF infrastructure.

title: Abstraction layers for scalable microfluidic biocomputers (Extended version)
summary: This technical report is the extended version of the abstraction-layers work on microfluidic biocomputing. It presents BioStream, a portable language for biology protocols, and the Fluidic ISA, a stable interface for chip designers, together with an algorithm that translates BioStream mixing operations to the Fluidic ISA and two fabricated chips that run the same BioStream code despite device-level differences. One of its two fabricated chips is the soft-lithography device from Digital microfluidics using soft lithography.

author0: Matthew Drake and Henry Hoffman and Rodric Rabbah and Saman Amarasinghe
title: MPEG-2 Decoding in a Stream Programming Language
summary: This paper presents an implementation of the MPEG-2 decoder in StreamIt and uses it to argue that video codecs are a good match for the stream programming model. The decoder's stages map naturally onto filters, pipelines, and split-joins, exposing the data and pipeline parallelism inherent in the standard. The paper illustrates the malleability of the implementation with a simple modification supporting alternate color compression formats, and shows how modular stream components increase reuse and can be verified independently. Drake's M.Eng. thesis (2006) is the fuller treatment, adding an MPEG-2 encoder and a language-design analysis. Control messages of the kind MPEG-2 requires are handled by teleport messaging (PPoPP 2005), and the decoder is written in the StreamIt language (CC 2002). The MPEG-2 work is extended in a 2012 M.Eng. thesis on optimizations for multimedia applications.

title: Digital microfluidics using soft lithography
summary: Digital microfluidics using soft lithography is the hardware paper of the programmable-microfluidics line. It presents an approach for programmable, scalable control of discrete fluid samples in a PDMS system using multiphase flows: an immiscible fluid phase separates aqueous samples, and a novel "microfluidic latch" realigns a sample after long-distance transport. To show scalability it introduces a general-purpose chip with a rotary mixer and addressable storage cells, where every operation is expressed over unit-sized aqueous samples. A software library lets users specify experiments as variables (fluids) and operations (mixes) without knowledge of the device architecture. This chip and its software library provided the substrate that the abstraction-layers work built on, serving as one of the two demonstration chips in the DNA 2006 paper, its extended technical report, and the Natural Computing journal version.

author0: Benjamin Wagner
title: Collaborative Compilation
summary: Wagner's MEng thesis observes that optimizing compilers are tuned “at the factory” against standard benchmarks, so applications outside the benchmark suite never get the heuristics tuned for them. Collaborative compilation closes that gap: it exploits the repeated compilations a Java virtual machine already performs to gather profiling information from the programs a user actually runs, then shares profile data and tuning results across users, so no individual pays the profiling overhead but everyone benefits from the tuning. The thesis works through the measurement-bias and data-quality challenges of aggregating profiles collected on users' machines and shows performance improvements on several compilation problems. The work applies the group's machine-learning-for-compilers agenda, begun with Meta Optimization, to profiles collected collaboratively at deployment time rather than at the factory.

author0: Zhao, Qin and Rabbah, Rodric and Wong, Weng-Fai
title: Dynamic memory optimization using pool allocation and prefetching
summary: This paper describes a dynamic memory optimizer built with DynamoRIO. It replaces heap allocation requests in a running binary with custom pool allocators that group data by requesting context, improving spatial locality, and exploits the resulting regularity of access patterns to insert prefetch instructions at runtime — all on unmodified programs without source code. The optimizer measures a 17% speedup over gcc -O3 on an Athlon MP and 13% on a Pentium 4. The optimizer is implemented in the DynamoRIO framework described most completely in Bruening's PhD thesis.

author0: Samuel Larsen and Rodric Rabbah and Saman Amarasinghe
title: Exploiting Vector Parallelism in Software Pipelined Loops
summary: This paper presents selective vectorization, an algorithm for exploiting short vector instructions in software-pipelined loops. Rather than vectorizing every data-parallel operation, it partitions a loop's operations between scalar and vector resources to minimize the initiation interval of the modulo schedule, manages operand communication between the two, handles misaligned vector memory references, and backs off when vectorization would reduce performance. Operating in the compiler backend, where costs are measurable, it achieves speedups of up to 1.38x, and 1.11x on average, over software pipelining alone on nine SPEC FP benchmarks. The compiler uses the SUIF infrastructure as its frontend, which supplies the memory dependence information the algorithm relies on. Larsen's PhD thesis is the complete version of this work, developing selective vectorization in the most detail and reporting loop speedups of up to 1.75x on a realistic VLIW model.
booktitle: 38th Annual IEEE/ACM International Symposium on Microarchitecture (MICRO)

author0: Sitij Agrawal and William Thies and Saman Amarasinghe
title: Optimizing Stream Programs Using Linear State Space Analysis
summary: This paper introduces linear state space analysis, a framework for streaming filters whose outputs and state updates are linear combinations of inputs and internal states — IIR filters, linear difference equations, and similar DSP kernels. It contributes extraction of a state space representation from each filter, rules for combining adjacent blocks in sequential, parallel, and cyclic configurations, removal of redundant states, and parameter reduction to decrease the operations per execution. Implemented in the StreamIt compiler, the framework is shown to be more general than linear optimization alone. The work generalizes linear analysis (PLDI 2003) and Lamb's M.Eng. thesis, which handled only stateless filters, and condenses Agrawal's M.Eng. thesis (2004), where the framework was first developed. Thies's PhD thesis (2009) also presents this material, and the HPEC 2005 overview summarizes it alongside the project's other compiler thrusts.

title: A Reconfigurable Architecture for Load-Balanced Rendering
summary: This paper attacks load imbalance in graphics processors, whose fixed allocation of vertex and pixel pipelines leaves resources idle under mismatched workloads. author0: Janis Sermulins
title: Cache Optimizations for Stream Programs
summary: Sermulins's M.Eng. thesis develops cache optimizations for stream programs, using the statically known communication rates of synchronous dataflow to model caching behavior. It presents four transformations: cache aware fusion, which combines adjacent actors under instruction and data cache constraints; execution scaling, which repeats actor executions to improve locality; scalar replacement, which turns data buffers into register-allocatable scalars; and optimized buffer management, which reduces memory accesses. Over a streaming benchmark suite the optimizations yield 257% speedup on a StrongARM 1110, 154% on a Pentium 3, and 152% on an Itanium 2. The thesis is the expanded version of the LCTES 2005 paper, adding optimized buffer management; the conference paper is the primary reference. The fusion machinery builds on phased scheduling (LCTES 2003) and operates on the StreamIt language (CC 2002). Thies's PhD thesis (2009) carries the cache work into the full StreamIt compiler.

author0: William Thies and Michal Karczmarek and Janis Sermulins and Rodric Rabbah and Saman Amarasinghe
title: Teleport Messaging for Distributed Stream Programs
summary: Teleport messaging is a language construct for precise handling of control events in parallel stream programs, where low-bandwidth messages such as coefficient changes or frequency hops must arrive at exact points relative to the high-bandwidth dataflow. Leveraging static synchronous dataflow properties, the paper defines a stream dependence function, sdep, capturing ordering constraints between actor executions, and treats a control message as an asynchronous method call delivered when the receiver sees the effects of the sender's current execution. Implemented in the StreamIt compiler with a cluster backend, teleport messaging yields a 49% performance improvement on a software radio benchmark. Control messaging appeared in the design of the StreamIt language (CC 2002); this paper supplies its semantics and implementation, building on the ASPLOS 2002 stream compiler. The construct is exercised in MPEG-2 decoding in StreamIt (IPDPS 2006), and Thies's PhD thesis (2009) gives the most complete treatment.

author0: Saman Amarasinghe
title: Multicores from the Compiler's Perspective: A Blessing or A Curse?
summary: The published abstract of a CGO 2005 keynote asking what multicore processors mean for compiler writers. Amarasinghe traces the technology and business forces that ended uniprocessor scaling, then reviews the facets of the multicore compilation problem through three case studies: coarse-grain parallelism from the perspective of the SUIF parallelizing compiler, instruction-level parallelism with the Raw ILP compiler, and language-exposed parallelism with the StreamIt language and compiler. It closes by asking whether multicores can finally deliver pervasive, scalable parallelism. The three case studies correspond to three bodies of work by the group: the SUIF parallelizing compiler, space-time scheduling on Raw (ASPLOS 1998), and the StreamIt language (CC 2002). The argument is developed at greater length in a 2006 talk, StreamIt – A Programming Language for the Era of Multicores.

title: A Productive Programming Environment for Stream Computing

author0: Diego Puppin and Mark Stephenson and Walter Lee and Saman Amarasinghe
title: Convergent Scheduling
summary: This journal article presents convergent scheduling, a framework for instruction scheduling and cluster assignment on spatial architectures such as clustered VLIWs and Raw. Its passes, one per constraint (load balancing, communication, register pressure, preplaced instructions), share one interface: each adjusts soft spatial and temporal preferences for every instruction, and successive passes converge on a schedule satisfying most constraints. It reports an average 14% improvement over UAS on a clustered VLIW and 21% over the Raw space-time scheduler, while genetic-programming search finds architecture-specific pass orderings gaining a further 12% to 95% over the hand-selected baseline order. The Raw comparison builds directly on space-time scheduling: convergent scheduling is implemented inside the RawCC compiler and evaluated against its space-time scheduler.
journal: Journal of Instruction-Level Parallelism

author0: Mark Stephenson and Saman Amarasinghe
title: Predicting Unroll Factors Using Supervised Classification
summary: This CGO paper shows that supervised classification can replace hand-built models inside a compiler, with loop unrolling as the case study. From more than 2,500 loops drawn from 72 benchmarks, it trains near-neighbor and support-vector-machine classifiers to predict the unroll factor for a novel loop in the Open Research Compiler on Itanium 2. The best classifier picks the optimal unroll factor for 65% of the loops, and the optimal or second-best factor 79% of the time, yielding a 5% overall speedup over ORC's heuristic on SPEC 2000 and 9% on its floating-point benchmarks. Stephenson's PhD thesis gives the most complete treatment of this work, as one of its three case studies.
booktitle: 3rd IEEE/ACM International Symposium on Code Generation and Optimization (CGO)

author0: Derek Bruening and Saman Amarasinghe
title: Maintaining Consistency and Bounding Capacity of Software Code Caches
summary: This paper presents efficient schemes for keeping a software code cache consistent with the original code and for dynamically bounding cache size to match an application's working set. On IA-32, code can be modified without any explicit application action, so consistency events — library unloading, rebasing and rebinding, re-use of memory for generated code, and self-modifying code — must be detected and handled; the schemes here do so in the presence of multiple threads, and are implemented and evaluated in DynamoRIO on SPEC CPU, SPEC JVM, and large Windows desktop applications. The algorithms extend the DynamoRIO system of Bruening's PhD thesis, which gives the fullest treatment of this material, and the VEE 2012 paper on transparent dynamic instrumentation builds on the consistency machinery developed here.
booktitle: 3rd IEEE/ACM International Symposium on Code Generation and Optimization (CGO)

author0: Juan C Reyes
title: A Graph Editing Framework for the StreamIt Language
summary: Reyes's M.Eng. thesis presents the StreamIt Graph Editor, a prototype graphical programming tool that exploits the hierarchical, structural nature of the StreamIt language. Built on Eclipse and JGraph, the editor visualizes a program as its stream graph and offers editing, overview, and hierarchy perspectives, direct graphical editing with property modification, automatic graph layout, merging, image export, and generation of StreamIt code from the drawn graph. The aim is to let developers work at the level of stream topology rather than low-level textual details, automating parts of the development process. The editor rests on the structured stream graph representation defined by the StreamIt language (CC 2002).

author0: Derek Bruening
title: Efficient, Transparent, and Comprehensive Runtime Code Manipulation
summary: Bruening's PhD thesis presents DynamoRIO, a fully-implemented system for general-purpose runtime code manipulation that supports code transformations on any part of a program while it executes. author0: Diego Puppin and Mark Stephenson and Saman Amarasinghe and Una-May O'Reilly and Martin C. Martin
title: Adapting Convergent Scheduling Using Machine Learning
summary: Convergent scheduling assembles instruction schedules from independent passes that express soft spatial and temporal preferences through a common interface, so passes may run in any order, any number of times. This paper uses genetic programming to search the resulting space of pass orderings, evolving s-expressions that can make the sequence conditional on properties of the code being compiled. In under two days on a cluster of workstations, it finds architecture-specific orderings for a range of clustered VLIW machines, yielding 12% to 95% speedups over the earlier hand-tuned ordering and generally outperforming UAS and PCC. The paper extends Convergent Scheduling (MICRO 2002), whose hand-tuned pass order is its baseline, and the scheduler detailed in Puppin's S.M. thesis; Stephenson's PhD thesis gives the most complete treatment, where these results appear as joint dissertation research.

author0: Jeremy Wong
title: Modeling the Scalability of Acyclic Stream Programs
summary: Wong's M.Eng. thesis asks how much speedup stream programs can gain from parallelization, introducing two analytical models that predict the scalability of stateless acyclic stream programs. The models, a basic cost metric and one adding synchronization overhead, are evaluated by comparing predicted speedups for StreamIt benchmarks against actual runs on the Raw machine and an idealized Magic network. Programs with low communication data rates gain up to a tenfold speedup from data parallelization, those with high rates approximately twofold, and the synchronization-aware model is the more accurate predictor. The study quantifies the filter fission tradeoffs in the StreamIt-to-Raw backend of the ASPLOS 2002 compiler paper, targeting the Raw microprocessor (IEEE Micro 2002).

author0: Michael Taylor and Walter Lee and Jason Miller and David Wentzlaff and Ian Bratt and Benjamin Greenwald and Henry Hoffman and Paul Johnson and Jason Kim and James Psota and Arvind Saraf and Nathan Shnidman and Volker Strumpen and Matthew Frank and Saman Amarasinghe and Anant Agarwal
title: Evaluation of the Raw Microprocessor: An Exposed-Wire-Delay Architecture for ILP and Streams
summary: This ISCA paper evaluates the fabricated Raw microprocessor, asking how well an exposed-wire-delay architecture serves instruction, data, thread, and stream parallelism. Raw exposes gate, wire, and pin resources through a tiled ISA and routes operands over a point-to-point scalar operand network. Using a cycle-accurate simulator validated against the 180 nm chip, Raw runs within 2x of a same-generation Pentium-III on low-ILP sequential code, 2x to 9x better at higher ILP, and 10x to 100x better on highly parallel applications coded in a stream language or by hand. It proposes a versatility metric. This is the capstone of the Raw project, begun with Baring it all to Software. The chip is described in IEEE Micro, its operand transport in the scalar operand networks paper. The ILP results use Rawcc — space-time scheduling, Maps, convergent scheduling — the stream results the StreamIt compiler; Taylor's thesis is the most complete treatment.
booktitle: 31st Annual International Symposium on Computer Architecture (ISCA)

author0: Chris Yu
title: Characterizing Function Inlining with Genetic Programming
summary: Yu's MEng thesis turns genetic programming loose on one of the classic judgment calls in an optimizing compiler: which function calls to inline. Working in the Trimaran compiler, it evolves inlining heuristics over thousands of compilation runs, producing decision rules that outperform the compiler's default heuristic, and then reads the evolved population back to characterize which properties of a call site actually matter to the decision. The thesis applies the group's Meta Optimization approach — using machine learning to construct compiler heuristics rather than hand-tuning them, introduced in the PLDI 2003 paper — to the inlining problem.

author0: Timothy Garnett
title: Dynamic Optimization of IA-32 Applications Under DynamoRIO
summary: Garnett's MEng thesis presents two uses of DynamoRIO for optimizing applications at runtime. The first is a set of optimizations for interpreters running under the logical program counter extension — annotation-driven constant propagation, dead code removal, call-return matching, and stack adjustment — yielding 20 to 60 percent performance improvements on instrumented interpreters. The second is a proof of concept that accelerates IA-32 applications on the Itanium processor by dynamically translating hot traces into IA-64 assembly while colder code runs in Itanium's IA-32 hardware emulation, with speedups of almost 50 percent on small loop-intensive benchmarks. The interpreter optimizations run under the logical-PC extension introduced in the IVME 2003 paper, and the work builds on the DynamoRIO platform presented in the CGO 2003 infrastructure paper, which Garnett co-authored.

author0: Matthew Frank
title: SUDS: Automatic Parallelization for Raw Processors
summary: SUDS, the Software Un-Do System, is Matthew Frank's PhD thesis on automatically parallelizing imperative programs with unstructured control flow for Raw processors. Its core transformation, scalar queue conversion, makes scalar renaming an explicit operation, in the manner of closure conversion. A transactional runtime checkpoints machine state, executes speculatively, and commits or rolls back, so threads can issue memory operations concurrently even when the compiler cannot prove independence. On three such applications, SUDS running in software on Raw achieves speedups equivalent to, or better than, an idealized hardware model of Tomasulo's algorithm. The work grew out of the Raw project's search for concurrency beyond static scheduling (Baring it all to Software), and an earlier version of the memory-dependence speculation system appeared as a 1999 technical report.

author0: Gleb A. Chuvpilo and Saman Amarasinghe
title: High-Bandwidth Packet Switching on the Raw General-Purpose Architecture
summary: This ICPP paper proposes using the Raw processor as both the network processor and the switch fabric of a multigigabit Internet router, work conventionally done by ASICs or custom hardware. Because Raw's tiled architecture and software-exposed on-chip networks give programs a direct interface to the chip's internal and external bandwidth, a general-purpose part can sustain routing rates otherwise reserved for special-purpose designs, with the economies of scale and flexibility that follow. The paper describes the router design and shows how packet switching maps onto Raw's static and dynamic networks. This is the conference version of a line that began with the Gigabit IP Routing on Raw workshop paper in 2002; Chuvpilo's S.M. thesis gives the most complete treatment, including the rotating-crossbar design and a measured 26.9 gigabits per second for a 4-port edge router. The Raw processor itself is introduced in Baring it all to Software.
booktitle: International Conference on Parallel Processing (ICPP)

author0: Iris Baron
title: Dynamic Optimization of Interpreters using DynamoRIO
summary: Baron's SM thesis builds a single software dynamic optimizer that can be applied to different interpreters, avoiding the engineering cost of a per-language JIT. DynamoRIO-with-LogPC modifies DynamoRIO's trace creation so that traces correspond to frequent bytecode sequences of the interpreted program, guided by simple interpreter annotations, then applies constant propagation, dead code elimination, and partial evaluation, with two techniques for keeping native loops from unrolling into overlong traces. On the Kaffe and TinyVM interpreters the system outperforms base DynamoRIO and runs 50–90% faster than native execution. The thesis is the longest treatment of the system introduced in the IVME 2003 paper, the primary publication of this work. The underlying framework is described in the 2001 workshop paper, and Leger's MEng thesis generalized the logical-PC extension into an API for dynamic partial evaluation.

author0: Vladimir Kiriansky and Derek Bruening and Saman Amarasinghe
title: Execution Model Enforcement Via Program Shepherding
summary: This technical report employs program shepherding to enforce a program's execution model — the ABI, rules from the source programming language, and program-specific components such as the values a function pointer may take. Static analyses, which need source access but no recompilation, and dynamic analyses automatically build a custom security policy with no user interaction; the resulting policy is strict enough to prevent all deviations from the program's control flow graph and nearly all violations of the calling convention, closing off the unintended actions that most attacks depend on, with minimal or no performance overhead. The report extends the USENIX Security 2002 paper from its three original building blocks toward automatically constructed, program-specific policies. The same material is covered in Kiriansky's MEng thesis, the most complete treatment, and the implementation is built as an extension of the DynamoRIO dynamic optimizer.

author0: Gregory Sullivan and Derek Bruening and Iris Baron and Timothy Garnett and Saman Amarasinghe
title: Dynamic Native Optimization of Interpreters
summary: This paper presents dynamic native optimization of interpreters, an approach that removes much of the interpretive overhead of a language implementation without building a JIT compiler. The interpreter writer adds lightweight annotations identifying a logical program counter; DynamoRIO then forms traces that follow frequent paths of the interpreted program rather than the interpreter's dispatch loop, and specializes them with partial evaluation, constant propagation, and dead-code elimination. The approach is demonstrated on the TinyVM and Kaffe interpreters. This is the main paper of the interpreter effort within DynamoRIO, built on the framework of the 2001 workshop paper; Baron's SM thesis gives the fullest treatment of the same work. Garnett's MEng thesis built further optimizations on the logical-PC extension, Leger's MEng thesis generalized it into an API for dynamic partial evaluation, and Bruening's PhD thesis includes the technique as a demonstration of DynamoRIO.
booktitle: Workshop on Interpreters, Virtual Machines and Emulators (IVME)

author0: Andrew Lamb
title: Linear Analysis and Optimization of Stream Programs
summary: Lamb's M.Eng. thesis is the complete treatment of linear analysis in the StreamIt compiler. It presents the linear extraction analysis that detects filters whose outputs are affine combinations of their inputs, procedures for combining adjacent linear filters and translating them to the frequency domain, and the dynamic-programming optimization selection algorithm. It also develops a redundancy elimination pass — a specialized caching strategy that removes computations repeated across filter firings. Over the benchmark suite, the optimizations remove an average of 86% of the floating point instructions required, with an average execution time decrease of 450% and 800% in the best case. The line continued with linear state-space analysis (CASES 2005), which extends the approach to filters with state, and Thies's PhD thesis draws its linear-optimization results from here.

author0: Michal Karczmarek and William Thies and Saman Amarasinghe
title: Phased Scheduling of Stream Programs
summary: Phased scheduling addresses a classic synchronous-dataflow problem — the tradeoff between the code size of a stored schedule and the buffer space it requires — for StreamIt's hierarchical stream graphs, which add single-input, single-output structure and a peek operation to SDF. The paper contributes fundamental techniques for building hierarchical schedules, a method for computing initialization schedules required by peeking, and a parameterized algorithm that executes each hierarchical unit as a set of phases, spanning a continuum from single-appearance to minimum-latency schedules. The minimal-latency instance reduces buffer requirements, contains code growth, and avoids deadlock in any valid feedback loop. Karczmarek's S.M. thesis is the fullest treatment of the same work, adding constrained scheduling for control messages. The schedules feed the Raw backend of the ASPLOS 2002 paper; cache aware optimization (LCTES 2005) later built on these schedules, and Thies's PhD thesis revisits phased scheduling in its experience report.

author0: Mark Stephenson and Saman Amarasinghe and Martin C. Martin and Una-May O'Reilly
title: Meta Optimization: Improving  Compiler Heuristics with Machine Learning
summary: Meta Optimization is a methodology for improving compiler heuristics automatically with machine learning. Its key observation is that a heuristic's policy often concentrates in a single priority function, such as the one a register allocator uses to pick spill candidates, so machine learning can search priority-function space directly, relieving compiler writers of trial-and-error tweaking. Applying genetic programming to hyperblock formation, register allocation, and data prefetching, application-specific hyperblock heuristics average 23% speedup (up to 73%), and the best general-purpose heuristic gains 25% on its training set and 9% on an unrelated test set. This is the main paper of Stephenson's machine-learned-heuristics line. A companion EuroGP 2003 paper presents the same system and experiments to the evolutionary-computation community, and Stephenson's PhD thesis gives the most complete treatment.
booktitle: 24th ACM SIGPLAN Conference on Programming Language Design and Implementation (PLDI)

author0: Andrew Lamb and William Thies and Saman Amarasinghe
title: Linear Analysis and Optimization of Stream Programs
summary: This paper automates, inside the StreamIt compiler, algorithmic DSP transformations traditionally hand-tuned by experts. A filter is linear if each output is an affine combination of its inputs; FIR filters, expanders, compressors, FFTs, and DCTs all qualify. It contributes a linear dataflow analysis that extracts this representation from C-like filter code, transformations that combine neighboring linear filters and translate them into the frequency domain, and a selection algorithm that picks the most beneficial sequence. The implementation yields an average speedup of 450% and a best case of 800% over the benchmark suite. One of the main optimization papers of the StreamIt project, it builds on the CC 2002 language paper and is implemented in the compiler of the ASPLOS 2002 paper. It was extended to stateful filters by linear state-space analysis (CASES 2005), and Chapter 4 of Thies's PhD thesis summarizes the same work.
booktitle: 24th ACM SIGPLAN Conference on Programming Language Design and Implementation (PLDI)

author0: Vladimir Kiriansky
title: Secure Execution Environment via Program Shepherding
summary: Kiriansky's MEng thesis presents program shepherding — restricting execution by code origins, restricting control transfers, and uncircumventable sandboxing — and extends it into execution model enforcement. Static and dynamic analyses automatically build a custom security policy specifying a program's execution model, from the ABI down to which values a particular function pointer may take: indirect calls are allowed only to known targets and returns only to known callers, preventing all deviations from the control flow graph and nearly all calling convention violations. The system runs on unmodified binaries with minimal overhead. The execution-model-enforcement material also appears in a 2003 technical report, with the thesis the fuller treatment of that work; the implementation is built in the DynamoRIO runtime code modification system presented in the CGO 2003 paper.

author0: Saman Amarasinghe
title: Defying the Speed of Light: Wire-Exposed Architectures and Spatially-Aware Compilers
summary: This short overview argues that as wire delay becomes a dominant constraint on microprocessor design, wire-exposed architectures need a programming model that circumvents the von Neumann bottleneck. It presents StreamIt in that role: a language that abstracts away a target's granularity, memory layout, and network interconnect while capturing the notion of replicated processing units communicating in regular patterns. It sketches the compiler analyses required — fission and fusion to adjust stream-graph granularity, layout to map the graph onto a network topology, and scheduling to generate a fine-grained static communication pattern — as implemented in the compiler for the Raw processor. The paper condenses two threads: the language case of the CC 2002 paper and the compiler of the ASPLOS 2002 paper, with the Raw processor as the wire-exposed target. It presents the same material as A Common Machine Language for Grid-Based Architectures (2002).
booktitle: GOMACTech Conference

author0: Michael Taylor and Walter Lee and Saman Amarasinghe and Anant Agarwal
title: Scalar Operand Networks: On-chip Interconnect for ILP in Partitioned Architectures
summary: This HPCA paper names and analyzes scalar operand networks: the interconnects, implicit in the bypass paths and multiported register files of conventional processors, that route operand values among ALUs. As designs partition their register files, caches, and pipelines in search of scalability, operand transport becomes an explicit network problem with unusual requirements — latencies of a few cycles rather than tens, and very fast operation-operand matching. The paper examines alternative implementations, details the point-to-point network of the Raw microprocessor, and measures how sensitive ILP performance is to network latency and occupancy. The network it details is the one programmed by the space-time scheduling compiler and built into the chip of IEEE Micro 2002, with data placed by Maps. The ISSCC 2003 paper and the ISCA 2004 evaluation build on the concept; Taylor's PhD thesis gives the most complete treatment, adding the 5-tuple metric and the AsTrO taxonomy.
booktitle: IEEE International Symposium on High-Performance Computer Architecture (HPCA)

author0: Diego Puppin
title: Convergent Scheduling: A Flexible and Extensible Scheduling Framework for Clustered VLIW Architectures
summary: Convergent scheduling is a framework for instruction scheduling and cluster assignment on spatial architectures. Instead of a fixed phase order, independent passes — addressing parallelism, locality, register pressure, load balancing, and preplaced instructions — share a simple interface of weighted spatial and temporal preferences, each pass adjusting them until a schedule emerges. Puppin's S.M. thesis presents the framework, implementations for the Raw processor and a clustered VLIW machine, and a genetic-programming method that evolves the pass sequence for a new architecture. The framework improves on Rawcc's space-time scheduler by a reported 21%, and was implemented in two systems: the Raw microprocessor and the Chorus clustered VLIW infrastructure of Mazur's M.Eng. thesis. Both compilers use memory address congruence analysis to create the preplaced instructions the framework exploits. The approach was later built on in an LCPC 2003 paper that uses machine learning to adapt the pass sequence to new architectures.

author0: Mark Stephenson and Una-May O'Reilly and Martin C. Martin and Saman Amarasinghe
title: Genetic Programming Applied to Compiler Heuristic Optimization
summary: This EuroGP paper argues that genetic programming has a natural niche in optimizing small but high-payoff software heuristics, demonstrated on the priority functions inside two compiler heuristics: predicated hyperblock formation and register allocation. Evolved application-specific heuristics for hyperblock selection average 23% speedup (up to 73%); a general-purpose heuristic evolved over several benchmarks improves the predication algorithm by 25% on the training set and 9% on an unrelated test set. For register allocation, specialized heuristics average a 6% speedup and the general-purpose heuristic 3%. A companion of the PLDI 2003 Meta Optimization paper, addressed to the evolutionary-computation community; the PLDI version adds data prefetching and the fuller compiler framing and is the primary reference for the work, while Stephenson's PhD thesis gives the most complete treatment.
booktitle: European Conference on Genetic Programming (EuroGP)

author0: Derek Bruening and Timothy Garnett and Saman Amarasinghe
title: An Infrastructure for Adaptive Dynamic Optimization
summary: This is the main infrastructure paper of the DynamoRIO project, a runtime code manipulation system for IA-32 that executes applications out of a software code cache while retaining complete control. It contributes an interface for building external clients — dynamic optimizations, instrumentation, profiling, and translation tools — that hides the runtime system's low-level details behind a lightweight API, achieved by restricting optimization units to linear streams of code and representing instructions at adaptive levels of detail. Sample optimizations improve some applications by as much as 40% over native execution, averaging 12% over base DynamoRIO. DynamoRIO grew out of porting Hewlett-Packard's Dynamo optimizer to IA-32 Windows, first described in a 2001 workshop paper. Instrumentation tools from Umbra to Dr. Memory were built on the system, and Bruening's PhD thesis gives the most complete treatment.
booktitle: 1st IEEE/ACM International Symposium on Code Generation and Optimization (CGO)

author0: Michal Karczmarek
title: Constrained and Phased Scheduling of Synchronous Data Flow Graphs for StreamIt Language
summary: Karczmarek's S.M. thesis develops the scheduling theory behind the StreamIt compiler. For hierarchical stream graphs that extend synchronous dataflow with single-input, single-output structure and a peek operation, it shows how to compute minimal steady states, how to construct the initialization schedules that peeking requires, and how to schedule pipelines, split-joins, and feedback loops hierarchically. Its phased scheduling technique represents each hierarchical unit as a sequence of single-appearance phases, giving a controlled tradeoff between stored schedule size and buffer requirements, and its constrained scheduling accounts for the latency semantics of StreamIt's control messages. The phased scheduling material was published as the LCTES 2003 paper; the thesis is the fuller treatment of the same work and the only one covering constrained scheduling, whose messaging model builds on the 2001 compiler technical report.

author0: Walter Lee and Diego Puppin and Shane Michael Swenson and Saman Amarasinghe
title: Convergent Scheduling
summary: Convergent scheduling is a framework for cluster assignment and instruction scheduling on spatial architectures, where placing an instruction is both a temporal and a spatial decision. A convergent scheduler is a series of independent passes, each a heuristic for one constraint — parallelism, load balancing, communication, preplaced instructions — sharing one interface: a map of confidence-weighted spatial and temporal preferences for each instruction, which passes adjust rather than overwrite. Applied to Raw and a clustered VLIW machine, it improves performance by 21% over Raw's space-time scheduler and 14% over existing clustered-VLIW assignment and scheduling techniques. Co-author Swenson's M.Eng. thesis is an earlier version of this work. Convergent scheduling improves on the space-time scheduler of Rawcc, and the clustered-VLIW results use the Chorus infrastructure. An LCPC 2003 paper applied machine learning to tune the pass sequence, and the ISCA 2004 Raw evaluation ran it as part of the Rawcc toolchain.
booktitle: 35th Annual IEEE/ACM International Symposium on Microarchitecture (MICRO)

author0: Michael I. Gordon
title: A Stream-Aware Compiler For Communication-Exposed Architectures
summary: Gordon's S.M. thesis describes the StreamIt compiler backend for Raw at thesis length. It develops the three stages of mapping a high-level, architecture-independent stream program onto a communication-exposed processor: a partitioning algorithm that employs fission and fusion transformations to adjust the granularity of the stream graph, a layout algorithm that maps the graph onto Raw's network of tiles, and a scheduling strategy that generates a fine-grained static communication pattern for each computational element. The fully functional compiler includes several load-balancing transformations, and cycle-accurate simulation shows the high-level stream abstraction mapped to Raw without losing performance. The compiler implements the language of the CC 2002 paper on the Raw machine, and Gordon's PhD thesis (2010) gives the most complete treatment of the same compilation line for multicores.

author0: Gleb A. Chuvpilo
title: High-Bandwidth Packet Switching on the Raw General-Purpose Architecture
summary: Chuvpilo's S.M. thesis works out, in full, a single-chip router built on the Raw processor. It contributes three things: a 4-port edge router design in which a 250 MHz Raw chip switches 3.3 million packets per second — 26.9 gigabits per second with 1,024-byte packets; a demonstration that the dynamic communication pattern of a router's switch fabric can be mapped efficiently onto Raw's compile-time static interconnect, via a Rotating Crossbar design; and a proposal to fold computation into the switch fabric itself, so routers can operate on packet payloads. The thesis is the most complete treatment of the Raw router work: it expands the workshop paper written with Wentzlaff earlier in 2002, and was condensed into the ICPP 2003 paper. The Raw processor it builds on is introduced in Baring it all to Software.

author0: Michael I. Gordon and William Thies and Michal Karczmarek and Jasper Lin and Ali S. Meli and Christopher Leger and Andrew Lamb and Jeremy Wong and Henry Hoffman and David Maze and Saman Amarasinghe
title: A Stream Compiler For Communication-Exposed Architectures
summary: This is the main compiler paper of the early StreamIt project. It describes a compiler that maps the architecture-independent StreamIt language onto Raw, a tiled architecture with fine-grained, software-exposed communication, through three general techniques: partitioning, which applies filter fission and fusion to adjust the granularity of a stream graph to its target; layout, which maps the graph onto a given network topology; and communication scheduling, which generates a static communication pattern for each tile. On the cycle-accurate Raw simulator, the compiler maps the high-level abstraction to Raw without losing performance. The companion of the CC 2002 language paper, it supplies the compiler story for the Raw machine. The ISCA 2004 evaluation of Raw later drew on this compiler for its stream workloads, and Gordon's PhD thesis gives the most complete treatment of the compilation path.
booktitle: 10th International Conference on Architectural Support for Programming Languages and Operating Systems (ASPLOS)

author0: Samuel Larsen and Emmett Witchel and Saman Amarasinghe
title: Increasing and Detecting Memory Address Congruence
summary: A static memory reference is congruent when all of its dynamic addresses share a residue with respect to some non-trivial modulus, the property that determines which memory bank or cache-line offset a reference touches. This paper contributes transformations that force congruence, achieving a five-fold increase in congruent memory operations without interprocedural analysis and with almost no overhead, and a compiler algorithm that then detects 95% of them. Fed to a vectorizing compiler, the information improves G4 AltiVec performance by up to a factor of two and cuts data-cache energy by as much as 35%. This is the conference version of a 2001 technical report on memory alignment, and it grew out of the SLP compiler's need for aligned superword loads and stores. Larsen's PhD thesis gives the fullest treatment, aligning roughly 75% of dynamic references, and the congruence transformation was later employed in the convergent scheduling compilers.
booktitle: 11th International Conference on Parallel Architectures and Compilation Techniques (PACT)

author0: Samidh Chakrabarti
title: Low-Bandwidth Web Access with Tandem Proxies
summary: This M.Eng. thesis develops Tandem Proxies, a pair of cooperating Web proxies placed on either side of a poor-quality bottleneck link, combining caching, diffs, and compression to reduce the data that must cross it. The thesis analyzes an aggressive caching procedure for its efficacy, details a method of computing diffs against an entire database of files rather than a single file, and specifies an image-compression algorithm built on large dictionaries.

author0: William Thies and Michal Karczmarek and Michael I. Gordon and David Maze and Jeremy Wong and Henry Hoffman and Matthew Brown and Saman Amarasinghe
title: A Common Machine Language for Grid-Based Architectures
summary: This position paper argues that StreamIt can serve as a common machine language for grid-based architectures, playing the role C played for von Neumann machines: abstracting away the idiosyncratic differences between targets while encapsulating the properties they share. For processors built from replicated tiles with software-exposed communication, it proposes representing a program not as a single instruction stream over a monolithic memory but as a composition of autonomous filters, each with private state, communicating with neighbors through high-bandwidth data channels and non-locally through a low-bandwidth control messaging system. The paper distills the portability argument of the CC 2002 language paper for an architecture audience, with the Raw machine as the concrete example; the ASPLOS 2002 compiler paper supplies the supporting implementation. The overview Defying the Speed of Light (2003) re-presents the same material, and Thies's PhD thesis gives the most complete treatment.
booktitle: ACM SIGARCH Computer Architecture News

author0: Vladimir Kiriansky and Derek Bruening and Saman Amarasinghe
title: Secure Execution via Program Shepherding
summary: This paper introduces program shepherding, a method for monitoring control flow transfers during program execution to enforce a security policy. Shepherding provides three building blocks: restricting execution privileges by code origins, so that malicious code masquerading as data is never executed; restricting control transfers by instruction class, source, and target, for example entering shared libraries only through declared entry points; and sandboxing checks that can never be bypassed. It is implemented with minimal or no performance penalty on unmodified native binaries on IA-32 Linux and Windows, with no special hardware support. This is the main paper of the Program Shepherding project, built on the IA-32 Dynamo port of a 2001 workshop paper. A 2003 technical report extended shepherding to execution model enforcement, Bruening's PhD thesis implements it within DynamoRIO, and SOSP 2009 work on automatically patching errors in deployed software built on its commercial implementation.
booktitle: USENIX Security Symposium (USENIX Security)

author0: Michael I. Gordon and William Thies and Michal Karczmarek and Jeremy Wong and Henry Hoffman and David Maze and Saman Amarasinghe
title: A Stream Compiler for Communication-Exposed Architectures
summary: This technical report (MIT LCS-TM-627) presents the StreamIt compiler for communication-exposed architectures. It describes fission and fusion transformations for adjusting the granularity of a stream graph, a layout algorithm for mapping the graph to a given network topology, and a scheduling algorithm that generates a fine-grained static communication pattern for each computational element, with a backend for the Raw processor. It reports that the compiler's load-balancing optimizations improve performance by up to 145% on the cycle-accurate Raw simulator. The compiler implements the language defined in the CC 2002 paper and targets the Raw machine; Gordon's PhD thesis revisits the same material with updated results for multicore compilation.

title: Searching the World Wide Web in Low-Connectivity Communities
summary: TEK ("Time Equals Knowledge") is a search engine that delivers Web content to low-connectivity communities using only email, trading waiting time for affordability where connection charges make browsing prohibitive. A query travels by email to a server at MIT, which performs the search and filters, ranks, and compresses the retrieved pages into low-bandwidth results; a graphical client and a reliable email transport protocol complete the system. This is the fullest description of the TEK system, built by a large student team at MIT. author0: Libby Levison and William Thies and Saman Amarasinghe
title: Providing Web Search Capability for Low-Connectivity Communities
summary: This ISTAS paper makes the societal case for what it calls Appropriate Information Technology: information systems designed, like appropriate technology in engineering, to suit the limits of their environment. It argues that low-connectivity communities pose challenging technical problems that deserve focused research, and illustrates the approach with the TEK search engine, an email-based system that returns filtered, compressed, low-bandwidth search results to users for whom interactive Web browsing is unaffordable or unreliable. The paper is a companion version of the TEK system papers: the WWW 2002 paper describes the same system in full technical detail, and the Development by Design workshop paper of 2001 is the earliest form of the work.
booktitle: IEEE International Symposium on Technology and Society (ISTAS)

author0: Libby Levison and William Thies and Saman Amarasinghe
title: The TEK Search Engine
summary: This workshop paper introduces the TEK search engine ("Time Equals Knowledge"), which lets users in low-connectivity communities search the Web using only email. A client sends queries by email to a server at MIT; the server searches with existing engines, downloads pages, and returns a ranked, filtered, and compressed subset, remembering what each client has already received so that no page is sent twice. The design targets settings where telephone and ISP fees make online browsing unaffordable. This is the earliest description of the TEK system. The WWW 2002 paper is a later version that gives a fuller account and supersedes this one, and the ISTAS 2002 companion presents the same work for a technology-and-society audience.
booktitle: Development by Design Workshop

author0: Shane Michael Swenson
title: Spatial Instruction Scheduling for Raw Machines
summary: Swenson's M.Eng. thesis studies instruction scheduling for Raw, where instructions must be scheduled in both time and space and the usual division into phases creates a phase-ordering problem. Examining the structure of program scheduling regions, it finds them too diverse for any single simple algorithm. It proposes a scheduler whose internal state is not a fixed assignment but a set of probabilities over assignments of instructions to time and space resources, refined by many small heuristics that iterate cooperatively. A spatial instruction scheduler for Raw built on this technique outperforms existing spatial scheduling systems on average. This is the origin of the probabilistic-preference idea behind convergent scheduling, published at MICRO 2002 with Swenson as an author; that paper supersedes this treatment. The scheduler is integrated with Rawcc's space-time scheduler, targets the Raw machine of Baring it all to Software, and takes its memory disambiguation from Barua's thesis.

author0: Darin Petkov
title: Efficient Pipelining of Nested Loops:  Unroll-and-Squash
summary: Petkov's M.Eng. thesis develops unroll-and-squash, a method for mapping nested loops into hardware and pipelining them efficiently. For kernels whose outer loop is iteration-parallel but whose inner loop carries strong intra- and inter-iteration dependences, it unrolls the outer loop and squashes several iterations through shared inner-loop resources, achieving fine-grained parallelism with a small amount of additional area. The thesis covers the requirements and supporting compiler analyses, the transformation and its algorithmic analysis, and an implementation in the Nimble Compiler environment, evaluated on signal-processing benchmarks where the method achieves up to a 2x increase in area efficiency over the best known techniques.

author0: Mathew Deeds
title: Design and Implementation of a PowerPC and AltiVec Backend with Optimization
summary: Deeds's M.Eng thesis describes the design and implementation of a compiler backend for the PowerPC G4 and its AltiVec multimedia extension, built on MachSUIF. The scalar half works through instruction-set features that complicate code generation: condition registers, limited immediate values, long conditional branches, and the Linux calling convention. The vector half generates AltiVec code from superword-level-parallelism annotations and confronts AltiVec's restriction to aligned loads and stores, contributing code sequences and optimizations for accessing unaligned data. The backend is companion infrastructure to the SLP project: its vector code generation consumes the superword-level parallelism analysis introduced in the PLDI 2000 SLP paper and developed in Larsen's S.M. thesis.

title: Efficient Pipelining of Nested Loops: Unroll-and-Squash
summary: Unroll-and-squash is a loop transformation for pipelining nested loops into hardware. It targets kernels in which an iteration-parallel outer loop traverses a data stream while the inner loop carries strong data dependences — a pattern typical of signal-processing and cryptographic codes such as Skipjack and DES. The transformation unrolls the outer loop and squashes several iterations through shared inner-loop pipeline stages, extracting fine-grained parallelism while sharing hardware resources economically. Implemented in the Nimble Compiler and evaluated on signal-processing benchmarks, it achieves up to a 2x improvement in area efficiency over the best known techniques.

author0: Michael Taylor and Jason Kim and Jason Miller and David Wentzlaff and Fae Ghodrat and Benjamin Greenwald and Henry Hoffman and Jae-Wook Lee and Paul Johnson and Walter Lee and Albert Ma and Arvind Saraf and Mark Seneski and Nathan Shnidman and Volker Strumpen and Matthew Frank and Saman Amarasinghe and Anant Agarwal
title: The Raw Microprocessor: A Computational Fabric for Software Circuits and General Purpose Programs
summary: This IEEE Micro article describes the Raw microprocessor as a computational fabric: 122 million transistors organized as sixteen programmable tiles that together issue sixteen instructions per cycle, control 25 GB/s of I/O bandwidth, and hold 2 MB of distributed on-chip L1 SRAM with 43 GB/s of memory bandwidth. Raw's scalable ISA gives software direct analogues to the gate, wire, and pin resources of the chip, so compilers can orchestrate parallelism and manage wire delay. The article shows how interrupts, caches, context switches, and virtualization carry over, and how the low-latency static network lets software circuits run alongside general-purpose programs. This is the main description of the Raw chip, realizing the architecture proposed in Baring it all to Software. The ISSCC 2003 paper presents the circuit-level implementation, the HPCA 2003 paper the operand network, the ISCA 2004 paper the full evaluation; Taylor's PhD thesis is the most complete treatment.
journal: IEEE Micro

author0: Rajeev Barua and Walter Lee and Saman Amarasinghe and Anant Agarwal
title: Compiler Support for Scalable and Efficient Memory Systems
summary: This IEEE Transactions on Computers article is the journal treatment of Maps, the compiler technology for bank-exposed memory systems: small, decentralized cache banks visible to software, as on Raw. Maps solves bank disambiguation — determining at compile time which bank each memory reference accesses — so data can be placed close to the computation that uses it. Two methods are presented, equivalence-class unification and modulo unrolling, integrated into a compiler that also orchestrates instruction-level parallelism and communication. On sequential codes running on Raw, bank disambiguation improves performance by a factor of 3 to 5 over exploiting ILP alone. This is the journal version of the Maps line: modulo unrolling appeared at HiPC 1998 and the system at ISCA 1999, following a 1998 technical report. Barua's PhD thesis is the most complete treatment; the ILP half of the same compiler is the space-time scheduler.
journal: IEEE Transactions on Computers

author0: Anant Agarwal and Saman Amarasinghe and Rajeev Barua and Matthew Frank and Walter Lee and Vivek Sarkar and Devabhaktuni Srikrishna and Michael Taylor
title: The Raw Compiler Project
summary: This workshop paper lays out the compilation problem posed by the Raw architecture, a mesh of simple RISC-like tiles whose hardware is fully exposed to software. Because Raw provides no hardware for register renaming, dynamic instruction issue, or caching, the compiler and runtime system must take on resource allocation, exploitation of fine-grained parallelism across tiles, communication scheduling, and use of each tile's configurable logic, while the runtime system implements branch prediction, caching, and speculative execution in software. The paper surveys these opportunities and challenges and reports the status of the SUIF-based Raw compiler. The SUIF infrastructure on which the compiler is built is described in a 1994 SIGPLAN Notices paper.
booktitle: SUIF Compiler Workshop

Its authors span the Raw compiler effort and the program analysis needed to partition a program's data and computation across such a fabric; no copy of the report is available on the publications site. The same authors' FCCM 1999 paper, Parallelizing Applications into Silicon, is a later version of this work and supersedes it.

author0: Rajeev Barua and Walter Lee and Saman Amarasinghe and Anant Agarwal
title: Maps:  A Compiler-Managed Memory System for Raw Machines
summary: This 1998 technical report is the earliest write-up of Maps, the compiler-managed memory system for Raw machines. The problem it addresses is preserving unified memory semantics when memory is distributed across processor tiles: the compiler must decide which accesses can be resolved to a known bank and routed over the fast static network, and how the remaining accesses are kept in dependence order over the dynamic network. The report precedes the full evaluation of static promotion and software serial ordering that later versions report. The Maps work is consolidated in a 2001 IEEE Transactions on Computers article and treated most completely in Barua's PhD thesis. This report is the version cited by early users of Maps: the RAWCC space-time scheduler contains Maps as its memory system, and the silicon compiler of Parallelizing Applications into Silicon leverages its static promotion techniques.

author0: Rajeev Barua and Walter Lee and Saman Amarasinghe and Anant Agarwal
title: Memory Bank Disambiguation using Modulo Unrolling For Raw Machines
summary: This technical report, MIT LCS TR-759, presents modulo unrolling, the transformation that makes memory bank disambiguation possible on Raw machines. Because Raw distributes memory across processor tiles, a memory access can use the fast static network only if the compiler knows which tile's bank it touches; modulo unrolling transforms loops so that certain classes of array references each resolve to a single compile-time-known bank, at a relatively small unroll factor. For dense matrix scientific applications, all array references could be accessed on the static network, achieving good speedup on the Raw processor. The modulo-unrolling work was consolidated into a 2001 IEEE Transactions on Computers article, and Barua's PhD thesis gives the most complete treatment.

author0: Rajeev Barua
title: Maps: A Compiler-Managed Memory System for Software-Exposed Architectures
summary: Barua's PhD thesis presents Maps, a compiler-managed memory system for software-exposed architectures. It argues that memory parallelism has lagged instruction-level parallelism because monolithic caches hide the banks that could serve accesses concurrently; in a bank-exposed architecture the compiler sees the banks directly. Maps supplies the enabling analysis, bank disambiguation via equivalence-class unification and modulo unrolling, which distributes program data among banks while proving which bank each reference touches; non-disambiguated accesses are handled through explicit synchronization and software serial ordering. Implemented in the Raw compiler, Maps improves sequential-code performance by a factor of 3 to 5 over ILP alone. This is the most complete treatment of Maps, which progressed from a 1998 technical report through HiPC 1998 and ISCA 1999 to the IEEE Transactions on Computers article. Within the Raw compiler it complements the space-time scheduling of ILP.

author0: Benjamin Greenwald
title: A Technique for Compilation to Exposed Memory Hierarchy
summary: Greenwald's S.M. thesis argues that compiler effort spent compensating for hardware caches is better spent compiling to a memory hierarchy exposed to software, where replacement policy, pollution, and prefetch latency all come under compiler control. Its contribution is C-CHARM (Compiler Controlled Hierarchical Reuse Management), a SUIF-based system that couples compile-time reuse information with array dependence analysis, rewrites loops to occupy a truly minimal amount of local memory, and generates the explicit data-movement operations required by the Raw machine's exposed memory system. C-CHARM compiles to the Raw machine and uses RawCC — the compiler of the space-time scheduling and Maps papers — to parallelize and schedule its output, and it outperforms the dynamic software caching of Hot Pages on its benchmarks. Its address translation draws on modulo optimizations from Amarasinghe's PhD thesis; the strength reduction of division and modulo operations that Greenwald co-authored was later evaluated on C-CHARM-generated code.

author0: Tsvetomir P. Petrov
title: Code Compaction and Parallelization for VLIW/DSP Chip Architectures
summary: This M.Eng. thesis builds a retargetable assembly-code optimizer for VLIW and DSP chips. The tool takes a compact description of a chip's resources, pipeline delay slots, conditional execution, and assembly syntax, together with unoptimized assembly code, and re-arranges — without rewriting — the instructions to exploit the architecture's parallelism. Restricting the problem to reordering keeps it tractable; linear programming and other search-space reductions then seek optimal schedules, achieving performance close to that of native compilers while remaining retargetable, demonstrated on a description of the TI TMS320C6201.

author0: Srikrishna Devabhaktuni
title: Softspec: Software-based Speculative Parallelism via Stride Prediction
summary: This S.M. thesis introduces Softspec, an all-software, speculation-based approach to automatic parallelization. It observes that many loops have stride-predictable memory references, so parallelism can be detected at runtime rather than proved at compile time: predicted access patterns are checked for dependences and loop iterations are executed speculatively in parallel, with no special hardware and no complex interprocedural analysis. A prototype achieves speedup on dense-matrix applications on a symmetric shared-memory multiprocessor, and the thesis shows how applications previously beyond automatic parallelization, among them sparse-matrix codes, can be parallelized the same way. Devabhaktuni's thesis, supervised by Amarasinghe, is the fullest treatment of Softspec; the same work, written up with Bruening, appeared as the published FDDO 2000 paper. The prototype's source-to-source compiler was built in the SUIF infrastructure of Amarasinghe's parallelizing-compiler work.

author0: Vladimir Kiriansky and Derek Bruening and Saman Amarasinghe
title: Secure Execution Via Program Shepherding
summary: This technical report presents program shepherding, monitoring control flow transfers during execution to enforce a security policy: code origin restrictions ensure that malicious code masquerading as data is never executed, shared library code can be entered only through exported entry points, and sandboxing checks placed around program operations cannot be bypassed. Rather than trying to stop the many ways memory can be corrupted, shepherding prevents the final step of an attack — the transfer of control to malevolent code — efficiently, on unmodified IA-32 binaries.

title: StreamIt:  A Language for Streaming Applications
summary: StreamIt is a programming language for streaming applications that targets multicore architectures. It introduces structured stream graphs — filters composed into pipelines, split-joins, and feedback loops — plus control messaging and a natural syntax that make rates and topology visible to a compiler. This is the main language paper of the StreamIt project, which anchored a decade of streaming research at COMMIT. It argues that streaming programs are a distinct and important domain. The companion ASPLOS 2002 paper supplies the compiler story for Raw. Later StreamIt work — phased scheduling, linear analysis — builds on the abstractions defined here. author0: Diego Puppin and Dean Tullsen
title: Maximizing TLP with Loop-Parallelization on SMT
summary: This paper examines how a compiler should parallelize loops for simultaneous multithreading (SMT) processors, where threads share fetch and execution resources every cycle. Puppin and Tullsen tune iteration interleaving, loop fusion, cyclic reduction, loop peeling, loop-invariant code motion, and local accumulation for SMT, and give a compile-time model that picks the most efficient number of threads for each loop. On the Livermore loops the optimizations raise average IPC from 2.72 to 3.97, an average speedup of 1.39 over optimized single-threaded code using up to eight threads.
booktitle: Workshop on Multithreaded Execution, Architecture, and Compilation (MTEAC)

author0: Emmett Witchel and Samuel Larsen and C. Scott Ananian and Krste Asanovic
title: Direct Address Caches for Reduced Power Consumption
summary: A direct addressed cache is a hardware-software design for an energy-efficient data cache. Direct addressing lets software access cache data without a hardware tag check: when the compiler can guarantee an access falls in the same line as an earlier one, it issues tag-unchecked loads and stores through direct address registers, degrading gracefully to ordinary tag-checked accesses otherwise. With support added to the SUIF C compiler and the FLEX Java compiler, the technique eliminates 16-76% of data-cache tag accesses on Mediabench C programs and 18-63% on SPECjvm98, yielding data-cache energy savings of 9-40% and total processor-plus-cache savings of 2-8%.

author0: Samuel Larsen and Emmett Witchel and Saman Amarasinghe
title: Techniques for Increasing and Detecting Memory Alignment
summary: This technical report develops compiler techniques for increasing and detecting the memory alignment of references, a prerequisite for efficient short-vector code. It contributes program transformations that force references to be aligned without interprocedural analysis and with almost no overhead, an analysis that recognizes aligned references, and a profile-based system that recovers global alignment information. The reported results are a five-fold increase in dynamically aligned references, detection of 95% of them, speedups of up to a factor of two on a G4 AltiVec processor, and data-cache energy reductions of as much as 35%. An earlier version of the PACT 2002 paper, which generalizes alignment to memory address congruence, residues modulo an arbitrary bank width, and supersedes this report. The techniques serve the SLP compiler, whose packed loads and stores want aligned addresses, and appear in their most complete form in the alignment chapter of Larsen's PhD thesis.

author0: Gleb A. Chuvpilo and David Wentzlaff and Saman Amarasinghe
title: Gigabit IP Routing on Raw
summary: This workshop paper proposes building a gigabit IP router from the Raw processor, as both network processor and switch fabric. General-purpose architectures had not offered a programmatic interface to enough bandwidth for multi-gigabit routing; Raw's tiled design and software-exposed on-chip networks do. The paper shows that the semi-dynamic communication pattern of a router's switch fabric can be mapped onto Raw's programmatically static interconnect, proposes a rotating crossbar that achieves efficient IP routing on the static network, and argues for folding computation into the fabric itself, for services such as payload encryption. This is the first paper of the Raw router line, building on the Raw processor of Baring it all to Software. Chuvpilo's S.M. thesis completed the design, measuring 26.9 gigabits per second for a 4-port edge router, and a condensed account appeared at ICPP 2003.

author0: Derek Bruening and Evelyn Duesterwald and Saman Amarasinghe
title: Design and Implementation of a Dynamic Optimization Framework for Windows
summary: This workshop paper describes the design and implementation of the dynamic optimization framework for IA-32 Windows that became DynamoRIO. Written as an engineering account for researchers entering dynamic optimization, it explains how a software system maintains complete control over a running application — intercepting exceptions and other abnormal control flow — and details Windows-specific implementation challenges, multiple threads, and code cache management, with performance results quantifying the framework's overheads. This is the earliest DynamoRIO publication, joint work with Evelyn Duesterwald of Hewlett-Packard Labs, whose Dynamo system supplied the starting point. The CGO 2003 infrastructure paper presents the mature system built on this foundation, program shepherding built security enforcement on the same base, and Bruening's PhD thesis gives the most complete treatment.

author0: Elliot L. Waingold and Michael Taylor and Devabhaktuni Srikrishna and Vivek Sarkar and Walter Lee and Victor Lee and Jang Kim and Matthew Frank and Peter Finch and Rajeev Barua and Johnathan Babb and Saman Amarasinghe and Anant Agarwal
title: Baring it all to Software: Raw Machines
summary: The Raw machine is a microprocessor architecture built from replicated tiles, each a simple RISC-like processor with its own instruction and data memory, registers, configurable logic, and programmable switch, joined by a pipelined point-to-point interconnect. Only a minimal set of mechanisms is implemented in hardware; the compiler takes over register renaming, instruction scheduling, and communication routing, and no signal travels more than one tile width per clock cycle. On RawLogic, an FPGA-based prototype, benchmarks ran 10 to 1,000 times faster than a Sparc 20/71 workstation. This IEEE Computer article is the main architecture paper of the Raw project. The compiler agenda it set was carried out by space-time scheduling and Maps, and the fabricated chip was later evaluated in an ISCA 2004 paper.

author0: Matthew Frank and Csaba Andras Moritz and Benjamin Greenwald and Saman Amarasinghe and Anant Agarwal
title: SUDS: Primitive Mechanisms for Memory Dependence Speculation
summary: SUDS, the Software Un-Do System, supplies the primitive mechanisms a Raw machine needs to execute code speculatively when the compiler cannot prove memory references independent. This technical report describes software support for memory dependence speculation: detecting at run time when a speculatively executed memory access has violated a dependence, and checkpointing and rolling back program state so the affected work can be re-executed correctly. Keeping these mechanisms in software preserves the simplicity of the Raw tiles while extending parallelization beyond what fully static orchestration can reach. SUDS targets the Raw architecture and complements the fully static orchestration of the RAWCC space-time scheduler, which requires compile-time knowledge of dependences. Frank's PhD thesis, SUDS: Automatic Parallelization for Raw Processors (2003), gives the most complete treatment of the system.

author0: Csaba Andras Moritz and Matthew Frank and Walter Lee and Saman Amarasinghe
title: Hot Pages: Software Caching for Raw Microprocessors
summary: Hot Pages is a software system that manages the mapping between a program's address space and the on-chip memory distributed across a Raw machine's tiles, providing cache behavior without cache hardware. It combines compile-time and runtime techniques: pointer analysis identifies memory references that can reuse a translated virtual page description, and the translation code is specialized per reference, optimizing the hit case and eliminating translation entirely in some cases. The multi-bank structure lets multiple references proceed in parallel, matching memory bandwidth to the tiles' compute resources; the report presents simulation results for a variety of applications on a prototype Raw system. Hot Pages handles the dynamic references that Maps cannot statically promote, within the RAWCC compiler for the Raw architecture; FlexCache (2000) is a later version of this work. Greenwald's S.M. thesis compares its exposed-memory-hierarchy compiler against Hot Pages.

author0: Walter Lee and Benjamin Greenwald and Saman Amarasinghe
title: Strength Reduction of Integer Division and Modulo Operations
summary: This technical report presents a suite of optimizations for eliminating integer division, modulo, and remainder operations, which are expressive but expensive — on the MIPS R10000 a divide takes 35 cycles against six for a multiply. Beyond algebraic simplifications, the techniques eliminate operations whose arguments are functions of loop induction variables and loop constants, drawing on number theory, integer programming, and loop transformations, in analogy to the strength reduction traditionally applied to multiplication. The operations targeted are those that compiler transformations introduce into address arithmetic: the SUIF parallelizer, the Maps memory system, Hot Pages, and the C-CHARM memory localization compiler all generate division and modulo in transformed array indexes. Implemented as a pass in SUIF, the work was later extended in Sheldon's M.Eng. thesis.

author0: Samuel Larsen and Saman Amarasinghe
title: Exploiting Superword Level Parallelism with Multimedia Instruction Sets
summary: This technical report is the first written account of superword-level parallelism (SLP): the observation that the short SIMD units of desktop processors are best fed not by loop vectorization but by packing independent, isomorphic operations found within basic blocks. It argues that SLP is a distinct form of parallelism, profitable even when parallelism is scarce, unlike the vector parallelism of supercomputers, and describes a simple, robust extraction algorithm that also captures vectorizable loops through unrolling, without loop fission or scalar expansion. The material here was later subsumed into Larsen's PhD thesis, which gives the most complete treatment of the superword-level parallelism work.

author0: William Thies and Michal Karczmarek and Michael I. Gordon and David Maze and Jeremy Wong and Henry Hoffman and Matthew Brown and Saman Amarasinghe
title: StreamIt: A Compiler for Streaming Applications
summary: This technical report is an early account of the StreamIt compiler. It introduces the stream dependence function, a relation between the input channels of two filters that establishes relative time and dependence information across a structured stream graph. Around it the report builds a denotational semantics for validating stream transformations, a fusion transformation that collapses several filters into one, a suite of streaming-domain optimizations, and a phased scheduling algorithm that finds a minimal-latency schedule for a structured stream graph, all realized in a prototype of the StreamIt optimizing compiler. Later work built directly on this report: the ASPLOS 2002 compiler paper draws on its scheduling analysis, and Karczmarek's S.M. thesis builds on its messaging model in developing constrained scheduling.

author0: Mark Stephenson and Johnathan Babb and Saman Amarasinghe
title: Bitwidth Analysis With Application To Silicon Compilation
summary: Bitwise is a compiler analysis that determines the minimum number of bits needed to represent each operand in a program, propagating data-range information both forward and backward through the dataflow graph so that programmers are freed from declaring bitwidth invariants. The savings matter most in silicon compilation, where narrower operands translate directly into less logic, faster clocks, and lower power; this report describes the analysis and its integration with the DeepC silicon compiler, which realizes the full benefit of bitwidth reduction in generated hardware. Bitwise is implemented on the SUIF infrastructure, reusing passes from the Raw compiler of the space-time scheduling paper, and is integrated with the DeepC compiler of Parallelizing Applications into Silicon, whose flow assigns arrays to equivalence classes using Maps. Stephenson's S.M. thesis is a later version of this work and its most complete treatment.
