author0: Derek Bruening and Srikrishna Devabhaktuni and Saman Amarasinghe
title: Softspec: Software-Based Speculative Parallelism
summary: This technical report presents Softspec, an all-software approach to speculative parallelism. Loops whose memory references are stride-predictable are parallelized at runtime: the system predicts access patterns with simple value predictors, performs dependence analysis on the predictions, and detects speculation failures without inter-processor communication, so neither speculation hardware nor complex interprocedural analysis is needed. The report describes the core algorithm, the prototype compiler and runtime, and performance results on a symmetric shared-memory multiprocessor, with examples ranging from while loops with unanalyzable exit conditions to linked-list traversals and sparse-matrix applications. The FDDO 2000 workshop paper presents the same material in published form, pointing back to this report for further details, including extensions to the core algorithm.

author0: William Thies and Frederic Vivien and Jeffrey W. Sheldon and Saman Amarasinghe
title: A Unified Framework For Schedule and Storage Optimization
summary: This technical report is the first writeup of the unified framework for schedule and storage optimization. It formulates the two decisions a parallelizing compiler usually makes separately — the schedule, restricting when statement instances execute, and the storage mapping, restricting where their results are stored — as one system of linear inequalities over affine dependences, and applies occupancy vector analysis to solve for the shortest occupancy vector, so that the tradeoff between parallelism and memory use can be analyzed within a single model. This report is an earlier version of the material published as a TOPLAS 2007 article.

title: StreaMIT: A Language for Streaming Applications

author0: Samuel Larsen
title: Exploiting Superword-Level Parallelism with Multimedia Instruction Sets
summary: Larsen's S.M. thesis is the expanded version of the superword-level parallelism work. Beyond the SLP concept and the packing algorithm, it formulates optimal SLP extraction as a 0-1 integer linear program and measures how close the greedy heuristic comes to optimal on multimedia kernels, describes a simplified vectorizing compiler used for comparison, details the SUIF implementation, and discusses architectural support for SLP. It reports 46% of dynamic instructions eliminated, with speedups from 1.24 to 6.70 on an MPC7400. The compiler was built within the SUIF infrastructure, and the material reached its fullest form in Larsen's PhD thesis. The thesis's SLP pass also served as working infrastructure for two companion M.Eng projects: Deeds's PowerPC/AltiVec backend and Maze's flexible VLIW/SIMD compilation infrastructure.

author0: Mark Stephenson
title: Bitwise: Optimizing Bitwidths Using Data-Range Propagation
summary: Stephenson's S.M. thesis presents Bitwise, a compiler that minimizes the bitwidth — the number of bits used to represent each operand — for both integers and pointers in a program. Bitwise propagates data ranges forward and backward through the program dataflow graph, with loop analyses that solve closed-form bounds for induction sequences, freeing programmers from declaring bitwidth invariants the compiler can infer. Applied to silicon compilation through integration with the DeepC compiler, exploiting bitwidths during architectural synthesis reduces silicon real estate by 15-86%, improves clock speed by 3-249%, and reduces power by 46-73%. The thesis is the fullest treatment of the Bitwise work, which also appeared as a PLDI 2000 paper and a 1999 technical report. Bitwise is built within the SUIF compiler infrastructure, and the DeepC silicon compiler that consumes its analysis appears in an FCCM 1999 paper.

author0: Elliot L. Waingold
title: SIFt: A Compiler for Streaming Applications
summary: SIFt is a stream-aware compiler for the Raw architecture. Waingold's M.Eng. thesis defines an intermediate format for streaming applications — a network of stream transducers with a formal operational semantics — and compilation techniques that map it onto Raw: analysis, placement of transducers onto tiles, communication scheduling, and code generation. A prototype implementation shows that certain applications perform better when compiled with these stream-aware techniques than with ILP-extraction techniques alone, and the thesis outlines three further optimizations needed to realize the maximum throughput of a streaming application. The thesis grew out of the Raw project's search for programming models suited to tiled processors, and it uses space-time instruction scheduling (ASPLOS 1998) as its evaluation baseline and shared infrastructure.

author0: Walter Lee and Rajeev Barua and Matthew Frank and Srikrishna Devabhaktuni and Johnathan Babb and Vivek Sarkar and Saman Amarasinghe
title: Space Time Scheduling of Instruction-Level Parallelism on a Raw Machine
summary: This paper describes RAWCC, the compiler that maps sequential C and Fortran programs onto the Raw machine, whose registers, memory ports, and ALUs are distributed over a two-dimensional mesh. Exploiting instruction-level parallelism there requires spatial instruction partitioning as well as temporal scheduling, and the compiler must explicitly manage all interconnect communication, including global synchronization at branch points. RAWCC orchestrates the parallelism within each basic block through instruction and data partitioning, placement, and event scheduling, and handles control flow with asynchronous global branching and control localization. Measured speedups scale with the number of available functional units. RAWCC targets the Raw architecture and is implemented on the SUIF infrastructure; it contains the Maps compiler-managed memory system (a 1998 technical report) and uses modulo unrolling for bank disambiguation. The Maps ISCA 1999 paper and convergent scheduling later built on it, and Lee's PhD thesis gives the most complete treatment.
booktitle: 8th International Conference on Architectural Support for Programming Languages and Operating Systems (ASPLOS)

author0: Rajeev Barua and Walter Lee and Saman Amarasinghe and Anant Agarwal
title: Memory Bank Disambiguation using Modulo Unrolling for Raw Machines
summary: Modulo unrolling is a code transformation that lets a compiler determine which memory bank an array reference touches on a Raw machine, where memory is distributed across the tiles. Unrolling a loop by a factor derived from the data distribution guarantees that every instance of a reference accesses the bank of one tile known at compile time, so the access can use the fast static network instead of the dynamic one. A relatively small unroll factor suffices, and for dense matrix scientific applications every array reference can be served on the static network, enabling scalable speedups. Modulo unrolling became one of the Maps memory system's two static promotion techniques and is used by the RAWCC space-time scheduler and the silicon compiler of Parallelizing Applications into Silicon. A journal treatment appeared in IEEE Transactions on Computers in 2001, and Barua's PhD thesis gives the most complete account.
booktitle: IEEE International Conference on High Performance Computing (HiPC)

author0: Johnathan Babb and Martin Rinard and Csaba Andras Moritz and Walter Lee and Matthew Frank and Rajeev Barua and Saman Amarasinghe
title: Parallelizing Applications into Silicon
summary: This FCCM 1999 paper compiles sequential C and Fortran programs into custom silicon or reconfigurable architectures. The compiler, built as SUIF passes, analyzes the memory access patterns of pointers and arrays to construct a partitioned system of many small memories; a space-time scheduler assigns instructions to computing elements distributed within the memory array, maximizing locality and statically scheduling the interconnect; the result is emitted as synthesizable Verilog. Specialization improves performance by up to an order of magnitude over a single general-purpose processor, plus parallelization speedups similar to a tightly interconnected multiprocessor. An earlier version circulated as a 1998 technical report, Parallelizing Applications into Smart Memories. The memory compiler leverages the Raw project's compilation algorithms: the space-time scheduler, static promotion from Maps (a 1998 technical report), and modulo unrolling. Bitwidth analysis, in a 1999 Bitwise report and at PLDI 2000, was later integrated with the DeepC compiler.
booktitle: IEEE Symposium on FPGAs for Custom Computing Machines (FCCM)

author0: Rajeev Barua and Walter Lee and Saman Amarasinghe and Anant Agarwal
title: Maps: A Compiler-Managed Memory System for Raw Machines
summary: Maps is the compiler-managed memory system for Raw architectures, which distribute memory across their tiles. The hardware exposes a fast, statically schedulable network and a dynamic network, over which Maps orchestrates all memory accesses while enforcing dependences. Accesses whose bank is known at compile time are promoted to the static network via equivalence class unification and modulo unrolling; the rest are ordered by explicit synchronization and software serial ordering. Static promotion alone yields roughly 20-fold speedup on 32 tiles for regular applications and about 5-fold on 16 or more tiles for irregular ones. Maps works inside the RAWCC space-time scheduler, builds on modulo unrolling and the Raw architecture, and is complemented by Hot Pages software caching for dynamic references. A journal version appeared in IEEE Transactions on Computers (2001), and Barua's PhD thesis gives the most complete treatment.
booktitle: 26th Annual International Symposium on Computer Architecture (ISCA)

author0: Tammy Yap
title: SCAN: A Static Code Analyser for JavaScheme
summary: Yap's MEng thesis builds SCAN, a static code analyzer that examines JavaScheme code fragments without executing them, giving beginning Scheme programmers a debugging tool that complements the standard debugger. The analyzer pinpoints the exact locations of errors: it checks parenthesization and Scheme keyword structure, uses heuristics to call attention to likely typographical errors, and reports undefined variables. Its deepest layer develops and implements set-based analysis to locate potential run-time errors caused by argument type violations, so that a class of failures ordinarily discovered only by running the program is surfaced at analysis time.

author0: Mark Stephenson and Johnathan Babb and Saman Amarasinghe
title: Bitwidth Analysis with Application to Silicon Compilation
summary: Bitwise is a compiler that minimizes bitwidth — the number of bits needed to represent each operand — for every integer and pointer in a program. It propagates static information both forward and backward through the dataflow graph and applies loop analyses that resolve the widths induced by loop-carried arithmetic, freeing programmers from declaring invariants the compiler can infer. Applied to silicon compilation through integration with the DeepC silicon compiler, bitwidth information reduces silicon area by 15-86%, improves clock speed by 3-249%, and reduces power by 46-73% on synthesized hardware. This is the main paper of the Bitwise project; Stephenson's S.M. thesis gives the most complete treatment. The silicon-compilation setting comes from the DeepC work on parallelizing applications into silicon (FCCM 1999); the implementation takes SUIF passes from the Raw compiler and assigns arrays to memory banks with Maps.
booktitle: 21st ACM SIGPLAN Conference on Programming Language Design and Implementation (PLDI)

author0: Csaba Andras Moritz and Matthew Frank and Saman Amarasinghe
title: FlexCache: A Framework for Flexible Compiler Generated Data Caching
summary: FlexCache is a framework for flexible, compiler-generated data caching. It replaces the tag memory and cache-controller hardware with a compiler-managed tag-like data structure, address translation, and tag check, so cache line sizes, associativity, partitioning of the data array, and replacement policies can all be chosen per program. The compiler uses static information to virtualize memory selectively, eliminate tag accesses, and guide replacement of conflicting lines: for the applications studied, more than 90% of cache-tag lookups are eliminated, and even without hardware support FlexCache can outperform fixed hardware caches by removing mapping conflicts and register-spill pollution. An earlier version of this work appeared as the Hot Pages technical report in 1999.

author0: Derek Bruening and Srikrishna Devabhaktuni and Saman Amarasinghe
title: Softspec: Software-based Speculative Parallelism
summary: Softspec is a technique for speculatively parallelizing sequential applications with simple software mechanisms: no interprocedural analysis, no speculation hardware. It targets loops with stride-predictable memory references: value predictors forecast each reference's addresses, dependence analysis runs on the predicted patterns, iterations execute speculatively in parallel, and mispredictions are detected without inter-processor communication. This reaches code static compilers must leave sequential — while loops with unanalyzable exit conditions, linked-list traversals, sparse-matrix applications — demonstrated with a prototype compiler and runtime on a shared-memory multiprocessor. This FDDO 2000 paper is the published form of Softspec, which also exists as Devabhaktuni's S.M. thesis (1999), the fullest treatment of the same work, and as a near-identical technical report carrying extensions to the core algorithm. The compiler was written in the SUIF infrastructure of Amarasinghe's parallelizing-compiler work.
booktitle: ACM Workshop on Feedback-Directed and Dynamic Optimization (FDDO)

author0: Jeffrey W. Sheldon and Walter Lee and Benjamin Greenwald and Saman Amarasinghe
title: Strength Reduction of Integer Divison and Modulo Operations
summary: This LCPC 2001 paper presents a suite of optimizations that eliminate integer division, modulo, and remainder operations, the analogue of strength reduction for multiplication. Using number theory, integer programming, and loop transformations, it removes operations whose arguments are functions of loop induction variables and loop constants, and it handles non-constant denominators, which earlier techniques could not. Implemented as Mdopt, a SUIF pass, the optimizations improve some applications by more than a factor of ten and recover most of the performance lost to low-order interleaving. Mdopt serves compilers whose array transformations introduce division and modulo operations: it plays a correctness role in Rawcc, whose memory front end is Maps; it was integrated into the Hot Pages software caching system; and it was evaluated on code generated by C-CHARM and by the SUIF parallelizing compiler of Amarasinghe's PhD thesis.
booktitle: International Workshop on Languages and Compilers for Parallel Computing (LCPC)

author0: William Thies and Frederic Vivien and Jeffrey W. Sheldon and Saman Amarasinghe
title: A Unified Framework For Schedule And Storage Optimization
summary: This PLDI 2001 paper presents a unified mathematical framework for two decisions a parallelizing compiler usually makes separately: the schedule, restricting when statements execute, and the storage mapping, restricting where their results are stored. Combining affine scheduling with occupancy vector analysis, and handling general affine dependences across statements and loop nests, it shows how to find a good storage mapping for a given schedule, a good schedule for a given storage mapping, and a storage mapping valid for every legal one-dimensional affine schedule — each reduced to an efficiently solvable linear program. A journal version of this work appeared as a TOPLAS 2007 article.

title: A Step Towards Unifying Schedule and Storage Optimization

author0: Samuel Larsen and Saman Amarasinghe
title: Exploiting Superword Level Parallelism With Multimedia Instruction Sets
summary: This paper introduced superword-level parallelism (SLP): short SIMD parallelism found inside basic blocks rather than in vectorizable loops. It contributes a compiler algorithm that packs independent, isomorphic statements into superword operations, seeded by adjacent memory references; loop unrolling turns vector parallelism into SLP, so no loop fission or scalar expansion is required. In its experiments the algorithm eliminated 46% of dynamic instructions, with speedups between 1.24 and 6.70 on an AltiVec processor. This is the main paper of the SLP project. The algorithm was implemented in the SUIF compiler infrastructure, and Larsen's PhD thesis gives the most complete treatment of the work. SLP vectorizers became standard in production compilers, and later COMMIT work built directly on this paper: goSLP optimizes statement packing globally, VeGen generalizes SLP beyond conventional SIMD, and control-flow SLP extends the approach to programs with branches.

author0: Jeffrey W. Sheldon
title: Strength Reduction of Integer Division and Modulo Operations
summary: Sheldon's M.Eng. thesis presents strength-reduction-style techniques that reduce or eliminate integer division and modulo operations, whose hardware implementations are slow relative to other arithmetic. The transformations analyze the values these operations take within for-loops and exploit repeating patterns across iterations — patterns that arise frequently from the data transformations performed by parallelizing compilers — replacing division sequences with cheap arithmetic. The thesis works through the value-range and loop-transformation machinery in detail and reports considerable speedups where divisions account for a sizeable fraction of runtime. The thesis builds on work begun by Amarasinghe, Lee, and Greenwald in a 1999 Raw technical report.

author0: David Maze
title: A Flexible Compilation Infrastructure for VLIW and SIMD Architectures
summary: Maze's M.Eng thesis builds a compiler backend and simulator, based on Machine SUIF, for exploring architectures rather than targeting a fixed one. A single control file describes the machine: in-order, SIMD superword, clustered or unclustered VLIW, or a SIMD/VLIW hybrid, along with its register files, functional units, opcodes, and latencies. Changing that one file retargets both compiler and simulator, which the thesis uses to compare architecture styles directly and to study the effects of register-file size, optimization passes, memory latency, and pipelining. title: A Common Backend for Hardware Acceleration on FPGA
summary: FROST is a common backend that lets DSL compilers target FPGAs. A compiler emits the FROST intermediate representation; a scheduling co-language then gives users control over FPGA-oriented optimizations such as loop pipelining, array partitioning, and vectorization, and over communication with off-chip memory. FROST transforms the AST accordingly and generates C/C++ suitable for high-level synthesis, which the Xilinx SDAccel toolchain implements on the device. Experiments show speedups of up to 15× over O3-optimized CPU implementations of the same algorithms. This ICCD 2017 paper is the first published account of FROST, a collaboration with Politecnico di Milano; the FROST IR is built to accept Halide as a frontend. The ASAP 2018 paper starts from this work and extends it with a fuller system description and an evaluation against a hand-tuned FPGA library.

title: A Unified Backend for Targeting FPGAs from DSLs
summary: This ASAP 2018 paper gives the fuller description of FROST, a unified backend for targeting FPGAs from DSLs. FROST translates an algorithm written in a supported DSL into its intermediate representation, applies transformations driven by a scheduling co-language controlling the generated architecture and level of parallelism, and emits code for high-level synthesis tools. On image processing kernels written in Halide and Tiramisu, FROST matches a hand-tuned FPGA library at the same level of parallelism and surpasses it by 10× when FROST's and the frontends' scheduling commands are combined. title: Gloss: Seamless Live Reconfiguration and Reoptimization of Stream Programs
summary: Gloss is a suite of compiler and runtime techniques for live reconfiguration of distributed synchronous dataflow stream programs. It reconfigures and globally reoptimizes running stateless and stateful programs with no downtime: cluster-wide dynamic recompilation regenerates the whole program for new configurations, concurrent recompilation reduces visible recompilation time to sub-seconds, three reconfiguration strategies transfer program state — the adaptive seamless strategy eliminating downtime entirely — asynchronous state transfer captures stateful filters without checkpointing or distributed consensus, and adaptive merging and resource throttling smooth output rates across the transition. All operations happen in-situ, with no extra hardware. Gloss is implemented in StreamJIT, whose distributed backend appears in Bosboom's S.M. thesis. During dynamic recompilation it keeps all optimizations available, including the task, data, and pipeline parallelism tradeoffs explored in the ASPLOS 2006 parallelization work.

title: A Unified Compiler Backend for Distributed, Cooperative Heterogeneous Execution
summary: Ray's M.Eng. thesis extends the Tiramisu compiler into a unified backend for distributed, cooperative, heterogeneous execution. New scheduling primitives let a programmer, starting from a single algorithm, partition computations across nodes, place work on CPUs and GPUs, and express the data transfers between them; the compiler then generates MPI, CUDA, and combined OpenMP+MPI+CUDA code. The thesis presents this as the first scheduling-language approach to cooperative execution on distributed heterogeneous systems, without hand-composing multiple programming models. The distributed backend built here appears in the CGO 2019 Tiramisu paper, on which Ray is the second author, as the scheduling commands for communication and synchronization; the thesis is her fuller treatment of that part of the system. Its evaluation compares against distributed Halide, whose over-approximated communication its precise polyhedral communication sets avoid, and outperforms it on all benchmarks.

summary: SuperTaco distributes taco-generated sparse tensor algebra kernels across distributed systems. Shinde's M.Eng. thesis contributes a code generation technique that emits Legion programs which partition tensors into blocks, load and store them in a distributed sparse tensor file format, and orchestrate kernel and summation tasks, plus a scheduling language for controlling how the distributed computation is structured. title: Improving performance and security of indirect memory references on speculative execution machines
summary: Kiriansky's PhD thesis addresses indirect memory references, which defeat caches and speculative execution on in-memory databases and graph analytics, and underlie the Spectre side-channel attacks. It combines three systems: milk, a C++ extension whose bulk-synchronous supersteps capture the locality of ideal caches, with up to 4× speedup; Cimple, a DSL whose interleaved coroutines expose instruction- and memory-level parallelism, with up to 6× speedup on index data structures; and DAWG, a secure cache architecture that isolates protection domains to block speculative and non-speculative cache side channels with no overhead beyond Intel's Cache Allocation Technology. This is the most complete treatment of the line, unifying the milk PACT 2016 paper, the Cimple PACT 2018 paper, and the DAWG MICRO 2018 paper under one view of performance and security on speculative machines.

title: Automatic Generation of Efficient Sparse Tensor Format Conversion Routines
summary: This paper shows how to generate routines that convert sparse tensors between disparate formats such as COO, CSR, DIA, and ELL. It decomposes conversion into three phases — coordinate remapping, analysis, and assembly — and contributes a coordinate remapping notation describing how formats group and order nonzeros, an attribute query language for extracting tensor statistics, and an abstract assembly interface, so each format needs one specification rather than a routine per format pair. Generated routines run at 1.00 to 2.01× the performance of hand-optimized SPARSKIT and Intel MKL code and, by avoiding temporaries, outperform both libraries by 1.78 to 4.01× on CSC/COO-to-DIA/ELL conversions. The technique extends the format abstraction of Chou's OOPSLA 2018 paper and is implemented in taco, lowering conversions through the concrete index notation introduced with workspaces. Chou's PhD thesis incorporates this material and gives its most complete treatment.

title: A Unified Iteration Space Transformation Framework for Sparse and Dense Tensor Algebra
summary: Senanayake's M.Eng. thesis develops a transformation framework that lets standard loop optimizations — strip-mining, tiling, collapsing, reordering, parallelization, and vectorization — apply to the irregular loops of sparse tensor algebra. Its central constructs are derived iteration spaces with provenance graphs for recovering coordinates at runtime, and position spaces that tile the contiguous nonzero arrays of compressed tensors to obtain load-balanced parallelism. The prototype extends TACO with a scheduling API and is evaluated on SpMV, SpMM, and MTTKRP against hand-optimized CPU and GPU implementations. The framework extends the iteration graph representation of the Tensor Algebra Compiler, and its parallelization of reductions uses the workspaces of Kjolstad's CGO 2019 paper.

title: A Framework for Computing on Sparse Tensors based on Operator Properties
summary: Henry's M.Eng. thesis extends sparse tensor compilation beyond the (+,×) semiring. It attaches a fill value to every tensor, so data can be sparse over values other than zero (such as ∞ for shortest paths), and derives iteration spaces from declared operator properties — annihilators, identities, idempotence — through a generalized iteration-lattice construction that supports set expressions such as symmetric difference, not just unions and intersections. The prototype in taco lets users define new operators with set notation, and expresses graph algorithms such as BFS, Bellman-Ford, and PageRank, benchmarked against SuiteSparse:GraphBLAS. The OOPSLA 2021 sparse array programming paper is a later version of this material, adding broadcasting and slicing. The framework extends the Tensor Algebra Compiler, and its array index notation extends the tensor index notation formalized in Kjolstad's PhD thesis.

title: Autoscheduling for sparse tensor algebra with an asymptotic cost model
summary: This PLDI 2022 paper presents the first automatic asymptotic scheduler for sparse tensor programs. In sparse code, loop fusion, loop reordering, and format choices change asymptotic complexity, not just constant factors. The paper introduces Protocolized Concrete Index Notation (CIN-P), which specifies loop structure, workspaces, formats, and access protocols; a set-expression cost model that ranks schedules' asymptotic cost over all sparsity patterns; and an autoscheduler that narrows the space to a small Pareto frontier of asymptotically non-dominating kernels, inserting workspaces automatically. Kernels compiled through TACO outperform its default schedules by several orders of magnitude. The work supplies a policy layer for mechanisms defined by the OOPSLA 2017 TACO paper and the CGO 2019 workspaces paper, whose concrete index notation it protocolizes; Looplets later adopted the protocolized notation as its input language.
booktitle: 43rd ACM SIGPLAN International Conference on Programming Language Design and Implementation (PLDI)

author0: Chen, Yishen and Mendis, Charith and Amarasinghe, Saman
title: All You Need is Superword-Level Parallelism: Systematic Control-Flow Vectorization with SLP
summary: This paper introduces SuperVectorization, a framework that generalizes superword-level parallelism (SLP) vectorization to uncover parallelism spanning basic blocks and loop nests, subsuming the roles of inner-loop, outer-loop, and straight-line vectorization while retaining SLP's flexibility. Its core is Predicated SSA, an intermediate representation that replaces the control-flow graph with a flat list of instructions and loops, each carrying a boolean control predicate, so code motion across basic blocks becomes straightforward. A single instance is competitive with, and often better than, LLVM's combined loop and SLP pipeline, including a 3.28× speedup on a volume renderer no tested production compiler vectorizes. The title answers the PLDI 2000 SLP paper, whose superword-level parallelism it extends across control flow. Fine-grained program versioning (MICRO 2024) later built on it, adding runtime dependence checks to the same vectorizer; the work reappears as a chapter of Chen's PhD thesis (2026).

title: Backwards Data-Flow Analysis using Prophecy Variables in the BuildIt System
summary: This arXiv preprint, written with Martin Rinard, proposes using prophecy variables — variables that predict information about the future execution of a program — to drive transformations and optimizations that ordinarily require backwards data-flow analysis. The standard route to such information is to build an intermediate representation and run a backwards analysis that propagates facts against the flow of control to the transformation or optimization site; implemented in the BuildIt staged compilation framework, the prophecy-variable approach eliminates the need for explicit backwards analyses. The approach extends BuildIt (CGO 2021), which constructs next-stage programs by re-executing the input program.
author0: Ajay Brahmakshatriya and Saman Amarasinghe and Martin Rinard
journal: arXiv preprint arXiv:2601.02653

title: Eliminating Hallucination-Induced Errors in LLM Code Generation with Functional Clustering
summary: This arXiv preprint presents functional clustering, a black-box wrapper that eliminates nearly all hallucination-induced errors in LLM code generation. It samples many candidate programs per prompt, executes each on a self-generated test suite, and clusters candidates with identical input/output behavior; the mass of the largest cluster is an exact confidence estimate, and one scalar threshold trades coverage for reliability with exponential guarantees. On LiveCodeBench it preserves baseline pass@1 while cutting the error rate of returned answers from roughly 65% to 2%, and to 0% at a threshold that still answers 15.6% of prompts. Needing only sampling and sandbox execution, the method wraps closed-source APIs unchanged. The preprint condenses Ravuri's M.Eng. thesis (2025), which adds manual error audits tracing residual failures to prompt misinterpretation.
author0: Chaitanya Ravuri and Saman Amarasinghe
journal: arXiv preprint arXiv:2506.11021

title: An Attempt to Generate Code for Symmetric Tensor Computations
summary: This arXiv report documents an attempt to build a compiler-based approach for computations with symmetric tensors. Given a computation and the symmetries of its input tensors, the system derives formulas for random access under a storage scheme that eliminates redundant entries, builds intermediate representations of the loop structure, and translates this information into code through the taco tensor algebra compiler. The framework can reason about a fairly general class of symmetric computations, but the generated code is not performant when the symmetries of different operands are misaligned. The question was later taken up within the Finch project: a 2024 M.Eng. thesis adopted this report's notion of partial symmetry for common tensor kernels, and SySTeC built a symmetric sparse tensor compiler in explicit contrast to the output-oriented approach attempted here.
author0: Jessica Shi and Stephen Chou and Fredrik Kjolstad and Saman Amarasinghe
journal: arXiv preprint arXiv:2110.00186

title: TIRAMISU: A Polyhedral Compiler for Dense and Sparse Deep Learning
summary: This arXiv paper applies the Tiramisu polyhedral compiler to deep learning, demonstrating that one framework can optimize dense, sparse, and recurrent neural networks—sparse and recurrent models being workloads then outside the scope of neural-network compilers. Expressing network operators in Tiramisu's polyhedral representation and scheduling language yields generated code that at least matches Intel MKL-DNN and in some cases outperforms it by 5× on multicore CPUs. The paper extends the CGO 2019 Tiramisu paper beyond image processing, stencils, and linear algebra into neural-network workloads. A deep-learning-based cost model (MLSys 2021) later built on this line, giving Tiramisu an autoscheduler.
author0: Riyadh Baghdadi and Abdelkader Nadir Debbagh and Kamel Abdous and Fatima Zohra Benhamida and Alex Renda and Jonathan Elliott Frankle and Michael Carbin and Saman Amarasinghe
journal: arXiv preprint arXiv:2005.04091

title: The Three Pillars of Machine Programming
summary: The Three Pillars of Machine Programming is a position paper, written by researchers at MIT and Intel, that organizes research on machines that write software into three pillars: intention, giving humans better ways to convey what they want to a computer; invention, creating or refining the algorithms and hardware/software systems that produce programs; and adaptation, using machine-learning-based constructs that autonomously evolve software. Its contribution is the taxonomy itself, a shared vocabulary and agenda for a field spanning programming languages, machine learning, formal methods, and systems.
author0: Justin Gottschlich and Armando Solar-Lezama and Nesime Tatbul and Michael Carbin and Martin Rinard and Regina Barzilay and Saman Amarasinghe and Joshua B. Tenenbaum and Tim Mattson
booktitle: ACM SIGPLAN International Workshop on Machine Learning and Programming Languages (MAPL)

author0: Maydan, Dror E. and Amarasinghe, Saman and Lam, Monica S.
title: Data Dependence and Data Flow Analysis of Arrays
summary: This paper develops a unified mathematical framework for array dependence analysis, showing that dependence levels, direction vectors, and distance vectors are all approximations of one underlying problem, distinguished by how they partition pairs of dynamic accesses into equivalence classes. Within this framework it introduces precise data dependence pairs and data-flow counterparts that determine which write produced the value each read observes, not merely whether two references can touch the same location. The motivating applications are array privatization and code generation for distributed memory machines. The efficient algorithm and the full privatization treatment arrived in the POPL 1993 version of this work, which supersedes it.
booktitle: Workshop on Languages and Compilers for Parallel Computing (LCPC)

author0: Maydan, Dror E. and Amarasinghe, Saman and Lam, Monica S.
title: Array Data Flow Analysis and Its Use in Array Privatization
summary: This POPL 1993 paper extends data-flow analysis, traditionally limited to scalar variables, to individual array elements. It contributes an algorithm exploiting the simplicity of real programs to deliver the precision of Feautrier's parametric integer programming method at practical cost; the Last Write Tree representation, which identifies the exact write instance producing the value seen by each read; and an array privatization algorithm based on data-flow dependence vectors, including the upwards-exposed uses and downwards-exposed definitions needed for initialization and finalization. An earlier version of this work appeared as an LCPC 1992 workshop paper. The Last Write Tree machinery was later built on by the PLDI 1993 communication generation paper and the LCPC 1993 compiler overview, and by Amarasinghe's PhD thesis (1997), whose communication generation rests on Last Write Trees.
booktitle: Twentieth Annual ACM Symposium on Principles of Programming Languages (POPL)

author0: Amarasinghe, Saman and Lam, Monica S.
title: Communication Optimization and Code Generation for Distributed Memory Machines
summary: This PLDI 1993 paper shows how a compiler, given computation and data decompositions, generates an SPMD program with explicit communication for distributed memory. Its central idea is a value-centric approach: rather than deriving communication from data locations and dependences, it uses exact array data-flow analysis to determine which processor produced each value another processor reads. Decompositions and communication are represented as systems of linear inequalities and solved by polyhedral projection, a model supporting elimination of redundant messages, message aggregation, overlap of communication with computation, local storage allocation, and global-to-local address translation. The array data-flow analysis comes from the companion POPL 1993 paper, whose Last Write Trees drive the communication generation. The framework was later built on by the LCPC 1993 compiler overview and the SIAM 1995 overview, whose communication generation uses the machinery here. Amarasinghe's PhD thesis (1997) gives the most complete treatment of this work.
booktitle: ACM SIGPLAN '93 Conference on Programming Language Design and Implementation (PLDI)

author0: Amarasinghe, Saman and Anderson, Jennifer M. and Lam, Monica S. and Lim, Amy W.
title: An Overview of a Compiler for Scalable Parallel Machines
summary: An overview of the parallelizing compiler the SUIF group built to translate sequential dense matrix programs into efficient code for scalable parallel machines, both distributed address space (Intel iPSC/860) and shared address space (Stanford DASH). It organizes compilation into three phases: precise array data-flow analysis that identifies the producer of the value read by each access; allocation of computation and data to processors to exploit parallelism while minimizing communication, trading away excess parallelism to eliminate communication; and code generation managing multiple address spaces. A simple example is walked through the entire pipeline. This LCPC 1993 overview stitches together the line's companion papers: the array data-flow analysis from POPL 1993 and communication generation and optimization from PLDI 1993. The compiler described here was later built on by Amarasinghe's PhD thesis (1997), which implements its data transformation algorithm on this infrastructure.
booktitle: Workshop on Languages and Compilers for Parallel Computing (LCPC)

author0: Wilson, Robert P. and French, Robert S. and Wilson, Chris S. and Amarasinghe, Saman and Anderson, Jennifer M. and Tjiang, Steve and Liao, Shih-Wei and Tseng, Chau-Wen and Hall, Mary W. and Lam, Monica S. and Hennessy, John
title: SUIF: A Parallelizing and Optimizing Research Compiler
summary: SUIF (Stanford University Intermediate Format) is a compiler infrastructure for research on high-performance systems, released for community use. It consists of a small, documented kernel that defines the intermediate representation and the interface between passes, plus a toolkit: C and Fortran front ends, a loop-level parallelism and locality optimizer, an optimizing MIPS back end, compiler development tools, and support for teaching. The paper describes the design and the research the platform had carried, from dependence analysis and loop transformations to software prefetching and instruction scheduling. This SIGPLAN Notices article is the infrastructure paper of the SUIF project, and the infrastructure was later built on across the corpus: the interprocedural parallelizer is implemented as SUIF passes, and at MIT the system hosted the Raw compiler and the superword-level parallelism work.
journal: ACM SIGPLAN Notices

author0: Amarasinghe, Saman and Anderson, Jennifer M. and Lam, Monica S. and Tseng, Chau-Wen
title: An Overview of the SUIF Compiler for Scalable Parallel Machines
summary: An overview of the SUIF automatic parallelizer arguing that the compiler techniques needed to generate correct and efficient code are largely common across scalable parallel machines, whether the address space is shared or distributed. It describes the compiler's structure — symbolic analyses such as constant propagation, induction variable recognition, and reduction recognition, followed by parallelism and locality analysis, communication and synchronization analysis, and code generation — targeting distributed address space machines such as the Intel Paragon and IBM SP2 alongside shared address space machines such as Stanford DASH and the KSR-1. The compiler described is built on the SUIF infrastructure; its communication generation applies the Fourier-Motzkin projection machinery of the PLDI 1993 paper, and the interprocedural version of its symbolic analyses is the design-and-experience system presented at the same meeting.
booktitle: Seventh SIAM Conference on Parallel Processing for Scientific Computing
venue: Seventh SIAM Conference on Parallel Processing for Scientific Computing

author0: Hall, Mary W. and Murphy, Brian R. and Amarasinghe, Saman
title: Interprocedural Analysis for Parallelization: Design and Experience
summary: A design-and-experience account of the interprocedural analysis system built for parallelization in the Stanford SUIF compiler. It explains how the analyses a parallelizer needs — scalar and array data-flow analysis, privatization, reduction recognition, symbolic analysis of subscripts — were restructured to work across procedure boundaries, obtaining precision close to full inlining without its cost, and illustrates the machinery on an excerpt from a Fortran benchmark. The integrated suite locates coarse-grain parallelism in scientific benchmarks that earlier interprocedural systems missed. The system combines the Fiat analysis tool with the Stanford SUIF compiler. The Supercomputing '95 paper builds on the machinery described here, adding the full empirical evaluation across the Spec92fp, NAS, and Perfect suites, and Amarasinghe's PhD thesis (1997) uses its algorithms. The TOPLAS 2005 article is the archival version of this work.
booktitle: Seventh SIAM Conference on Parallel Processing for Scientific Computing
venue: Seventh SIAM Conference on Parallel Processing for Scientific Computing

author0: Anderson, Jennifer M. and Amarasinghe, Saman and Lam, Monica S.
title: Data and Computation Transformations for Multiprocessors
summary: This PPoPP 1995 paper presents a compiler that automatically parallelizes sequential programs and also restructures their array layouts to fit the memory hierarchy — by the paper's account, the first system to do both. The algorithm has two steps: choose the parallelization and the assignment of computation to processors so that synchronization and true sharing are minimized, then transform data layouts in the shared address space using a new data transformation framework that attacks false sharing and poor spatial locality. Applications compiled this way and measured on the Stanford DASH multiprocessor show parallelism and memory system performance being optimized together. The algorithms are implemented in the SUIF compiler system. The data transformations were later built on by the ICS 1995 unified compilation study and by the assembled system of IEEE Computer 1996.
booktitle: Fifth ACM SIGPLAN Symposium on Principles and Practice of Parallel Programming (PPoPP)

author0: Tseng, Chau-Wen and Anderson, Jennifer M. and Amarasinghe, Saman and Lam, Monica S.
title: Unified Compilation Techniques for Shared and Distributed Address Space Machines
summary: This ICS 1995 paper argues that compilers for shared and distributed address space machines converge: the analyses a distributed-memory compiler performs because correctness demands them — data decomposition, communication analysis — pay off as locality and synchronization optimizations on shared-memory machines, where hardware makes them optional but performance makes them valuable. Using profiling and simulation to identify memory access and synchronization costs as the chief obstacles to scalable speedup, the authors adapt these distributed-memory techniques inside the SUIF compiler and measure case-study applications on the Stanford DASH multiprocessor, showing substantial improvements from compiler-managed locality and reduced barrier synchronization. The optimizations are implemented in the SUIF compilation system, and the data layout transformation applied once decompositions are known comes from the companion PPoPP 1995 paper.
booktitle: International Conference on Supercomputing (ICS)

author0: Amarasinghe, Saman and Anderson, Jennifer M. and French, Robert S. and Hall, Mary W. and Lam, Monica S. and Liao, Shih-Wei and Murphy, Brian R. and Tseng, Chau-Wen and Wilson, Chris S. and Wilson, Robert P.
title: Hot Compilers for Future Hot Chips
summary: A presentation to the computer architecture community at Hot Chips VII, making the case that parallelizing compiler technology had matured enough to shape chip and system design. It surveys three SUIF thrusts: interprocedural pointer analysis for C programs; detection of coarse-grain parallelism through interprocedural array privatization and reduction recognition; and global optimizations that eliminate barriers and cache traffic between parallel loops, with speedups shown for NAS benchmarks on an SGI Challenge and applications on Stanford DASH. It closes by arguing that multiprocessors built from superscalar processors are more cost-effective than ever-wider superscalar designs. Every result in the talk is produced by the SUIF compiler; the coarse-grain parallelism section presents the Supercomputing '95 interprocedural system and the optimization section the data and computation transformations of PPoPP 1995. An IEEE Micro 1996 article is the article version of this talk.
booktitle: Hot Chips VII

author0: Hall, Mary W. and Amarasinghe, Saman and Murphy, Brian R. and Liao, Shih-Wei and Lam, Monica S.
title: Detecting Coarse-Grain Parallelism Using an Interprocedural Parallelizing Compiler
summary: This Supercomputing '95 paper is an empirical evaluation of the interprocedural parallelizer built in the Stanford SUIF system. The compiler integrates privatization and reduction recognition for both scalar and array variables with symbolic analysis of array subscripts, in an interprocedural framework nearly as precise as full inlining without its costs. It parallelizes loops spanning numerous procedures and hundreds of lines, achieving parallelism coverage above 80% on 8 of 10 Spec92fp programs and 7 of 8 NAS sample benchmarks, with speedups on all of the high-coverage Spec92fp programs. The analysis is implemented in the Stanford SUIF compiler and builds on the design described in the SIAM 1995 case study and an LCPC 1995 companion. The system was later built on by IEEE Computer 1996, which reports a SPECfp95 ratio of 63.9 on an eight-processor AlphaServer, and the TOPLAS 2005 article is the archival version of this work.
booktitle: Proceedings of Supercomputing '95

author0: Hall, Mary W. and Murphy, Brian R. and Amarasinghe, Saman and Liao, Shih-Wei and Lam, Monica S.
title: Interprocedural Analysis for Parallelization
summary: This LCPC paper reports early results from the fully interprocedural automatic parallelization system built in the Stanford SUIF compiler. The system integrates dependence analysis, privatization, and reduction recognition for both scalar and array variables, supported by interprocedural symbolic analysis, all constructed with the FIAT analysis-building tool. The framework is designed to give results as precise as full inlining while managing analysis complexity, and the implemented system parallelized, completely automatically, loops containing hundreds of lines of code — supporting an early empirical demonstration that interprocedural analysis measurably advances automatic parallelization on standard benchmark suites. The Supercomputing '95 paper presents the same system's coarse-grain parallelism results in full, and a TOPLAS 2005 article is the most complete version of this material. Amarasinghe's PhD thesis builds on the analyses, detailing the array side of the system.
booktitle: Workshop on Languages and Compilers for Parallel Computing (LCPC)

author0: Amarasinghe, Saman and Anderson, Jennifer M. and Wilson, Chris S. and Liao, Shih-Wei and French, Robert S. and Hall, Mary W. and Murphy, Brian R. and Lam, Monica S.
title: Multiprocessors from a Software Perspective
summary: This IEEE Micro article addresses computer architects, arguing that parallelizing-compiler technology had matured enough to change how multiprocessors should be designed and evaluated. It surveys the Stanford SUIF work — interprocedural array analysis that finds outer-loop parallelism, pointer analysis extending parallelization from Fortran to C, and locality optimizations for multiprocessor caches — and reports SPEC experiments on an eight-processor Digital AlphaServer 8400: SUIF raised the SPEC92fp ratio from 506 to 1,016 and the SPEC95fp ratio from 12.2 to 38.4. The article is a version of the group's Hot Chips VII talk, Hot Compilers for Future Hot Chips. The parallelization results rest on the interprocedural system presented at Supercomputing '95 and the data and computation transformations of PPoPP 1995.
journal: IEEE Micro

author0: Hall, Mary W. and Anderson, Jennifer M. and Amarasinghe, Saman and Murphy, Brian R. and Liao, Shih-Wei and Bugnion, Ed and Lam, Monica S.
title: Maximizing Multiprocessor Performance with the SUIF Compiler
summary: This Computer article is the summary overview of the SUIF compiler, which automatically parallelizes and optimizes sequential programs for shared-memory multiprocessors. It presents the two capabilities the authors found essential: locating coarse-grain parallelism through interprocedural analysis, array privatization, and reduction recognition, and optimizing multiprocessor memory behavior against false sharing and poor locality. The techniques significantly affected half of the NAS and SPECfp95 benchmark suites, yielding speedups on more than three-fourths of the programs and a SPECfp95 ratio of 63.9 on an eight-processor Digital AlphaServer, the highest reported at the time. The article condenses the analyses presented at Supercomputing '95 and the memory optimizations of PPoPP 1995. A reprint with an added status section appeared in the Digital Technical Journal in 1998, and a TOPLAS 2005 article gives the complete account of the analyses. The results later served as a case study in a CGO 2005 keynote.
journal: Computer

author0: Hall, Mary W. and Anderson, Jennifer M. and Amarasinghe, Saman and Murphy, Brian R. and Liao, Shih-Wei and Bugnion, Ed and Lam, Monica S.
title: Maximizing Multiprocessor Performance with the SUIF Compiler (Digital Technical Journal reprint)
summary: This Digital Technical Journal article reprints, for Digital's engineering audience, the Computer 1996 overview of SUIF's automatic parallelization: interprocedural analyses that locate coarse-grain parallelism and memory optimizations that together yielded speedups on three-fourths of the NAS and SPECfp95 benchmarks, measured on Digital AlphaServer multiprocessors. It adds a new section, 'The Status and Future of SUIF', recording the release of the SUIF-parallelized SPECfp95 benchmarks through SPEC, predicated array data-flow analysis for run-time parallelization, the connection of SUIF to Compaq's GEM compiler, and SUIF's selection for the National Compiler Infrastructure. An expanded reprint of the Computer 1996 article, which remains the primary version of this material. The underlying parallelization system is the one presented at Supercomputing '95, and the memory optimizations come from PPoPP 1995.
journal: Digital Technical Journal

author0: Taylor, Michael and Kim, J. and Miller, Jason and Wentzlaff, David and Ghodrat, Fae and Greenwald, Benjamin and Hoffman, Henry and Johnson, Paul and Lee, Walter and Saraf, Arvind and Shnidman, Nathan and Strumpen, Volker and Amarasinghe, Saman and Agarwal, Anant
title: A 16-issue multiple-program-counter microprocessor with point-to-point scalar operand network
summary: This ISSCC paper presents the Raw chip to the circuits community: a 16-issue microprocessor with multiple program counters, built as a 4-by-4 array of tiles joined by four full-duplex 32-bit on-chip networks. The static router serves as a point-to-point scalar operand network with single-cycle-per-hop latency, and the networks are register-mapped directly into the compute processor's bypass paths, cutting ALU-to-network latency by as much as 4 cycles. Implemented in IBM's SA-27E six-level copper ASIC process on a 331 mm2 die with a 1,657-pin package, the chip taped out in August 2002 at a worst-case frequency of 225 MHz. This is the implementation companion to the IEEE Micro article describing the chip and to the HPCA 2003 paper that defines scalar operand networks; the compile-time assignment of operations to tiles comes from space-time scheduling. Taylor's PhD thesis gives the most complete treatment.
booktitle: IEEE International Solid-State Circuits Conference (ISSCC)

author0: Rabbah, Rodric and Thies, William and Gordon, Michael I. and Sermulins, Janis and Amarasinghe, Saman
title: High-Productivity Stream Programming for High-Performance Systems
summary: An extended abstract accompanying an HPEC presentation that surveys the StreamIt language and compiler as a route to high-productivity, high-performance stream programming. It organizes the compiler effort into three thrusts: domain-specific DSP optimizations, which recognize linear computations and move them to the frequency domain when profitable, for an average 4.5x speedup on a Pentium 3; backends for tiled, multicore, and cluster targets, achieving a 16x average speedup on a 16-tile Raw machine over a single tile; and cache aware optimizations yielding a 249% average speedup on a StrongARM 1110. The abstract stitches together results published separately: linear analysis (PLDI 2003) and state space analysis (CASES 2005), the communication-exposed backend (ASPLOS 2002), cache aware optimization (LCTES 2005), and the graphical development environment (P-PHEC 2005), all built on the StreamIt language (CC 2002).
booktitle: Ninth Annual High Performance Embedded Computing Workshop (HPEC)

author0: Hall, Mary W. and Amarasinghe, Saman and Murphy, Brian R. and Liao, Shih-Wei and Lam, Monica S.
title: Interprocedural Parallelization Analysis in SUIF
summary: This TOPLAS article is the complete archival description of the automatic parallelization system in the Stanford SUIF compiler. It documents the full suite of interprocedural analyses — array privatization, array reduction recognition, and scalar data-flow analyses including symbolic analysis — that collaborate to find coarse-grain parallel loops that run on multiple processors without cross-processor synchronization or communication. The system parallelized interprocedural loops of over a thousand lines completely automatically; on four benchmark suites, a third of the programs spend more than half their execution time in computations these techniques parallelize. This is the most complete version of work reported earlier at LCPC 1995, in a companion SIAM 1995 paper, and at Supercomputing '95, with performance results shared with the Computer 1996 article; Amarasinghe's PhD thesis gives a more detailed treatment of the array analyses.
journal: ACM Transactions on Programming Languages and Systems (TOPLAS)

author0: Perkins, Jeff H. and Kim, S. and Larsen, Samuel and Amarasinghe, Saman and Bachrach, J. and Carbin, Michael and Pacheco, C. and Sherwood, F. and Sidiroglou, S. and Sullivan, Gregory and Wong, Weng-Fai and Zibin, Y. and Ernst, Michael D. and Rinard, Martin
title: Automatically patching errors in deployed software
summary: ClearView is a system that automatically patches errors in deployed software, operating on stripped Windows x86 binaries without source code, debugging information, or human intervention. It learns invariants that characterize normal executions, detects failures with monitors for out-of-bounds writes and illegal control transfers, identifies invariants whose violation correlates with failure, generates candidate patches that enforce them in the running application without restarts, and keeps the patches that continued observation shows to work. In a DARPA Red Team exercise on Firefox, ClearView blocked all ten code-injection attacks, and its patches corrected the underlying error for seven of the ten exploits. ClearView detects illegal control transfers with Determina's Memory Firewall, a commercial descendant of program shepherding, and patches running binaries through the runtime code manipulation of DynamoRIO, described most fully in Bruening's PhD thesis; its invariant learning is based on the Daikon system.
booktitle: ACM SIGOPS 22nd Symposium on Operating Systems Principles (SOSP)

author0: Amarasinghe, Saman and Campbell, Dan and Carlson, W. and Chien, Andrew and Dally, Bill and Elnozahy, Mootaz and Hall, Mary W. and Harrison, R. and Harrod, William and Hill, K. and Hiller, Jon and Karp, S. and Koelbel, C. and Koester, D. and Kogge, Peter and Levesque, J. and Reed, Dan and Sarkar, Vivek and Schreiber, Rob and Richards, M. and Scarpelli, A. and Shalf, John and Snavely, A. and Sterling, Thomas
title: ExaScale Software Study: Software Challenges in Extreme Scale Systems
summary: This report presents the findings of the DARPA Exascale Software Study, conducted in 2008-2009 with Amarasinghe among its two dozen contributors. Surveying operating systems, runtimes, compilers, libraries, languages, and tools, it identifies concurrency and energy efficiency as the defining software challenges of extreme-scale systems — machines needing 1000x more application concurrency while memory-to-compute ratios fall toward a hundredth of a byte per operation — and argues for a rebuilt software stack based on software-hardware co-design, deconstructed operating systems, and self-aware resource management.

author0: Ceryen Tan
title: A Hybrid Static/Dynamic Approach to Scheduling Stream Programs
summary: Tan's MEng thesis addresses a rigidity in StreamIt's execution model: the compiler analyzes data dependencies at compile time and emits a static schedule fixing where and when each actor runs, which costs nothing at run time but cannot adapt when cores turn out to be unavailable or static work estimates load-balance the machine badly. The thesis contributes a hybrid static/dynamic scheduler that keeps the static schedule as the baseline and layers lightweight dynamic load-balancing on top, adjusting actor placement to run-time conditions and correcting load imbalances while adding very little overhead. The work extends the StreamIt scheduling line of the ASPLOS 2006 paper toward run-time adaptivity.

author0: Lerer, A. and Ward, M. and Amarasinghe, Saman
title: Evaluation of IVR Data Collection UIs for Untrained Rural Users
summary: This paper evaluates whether untrained rural users can operate interactive voice response (IVR) interfaces, using a deployment that collected feedback from teachers in rural Uganda. Automated survey calls were delivered to over 150 teachers over several months, with the interface revised throughout the study in response to user interviews and call transcripts. Task success varied from 0% to over 75% across interface designs, and most participants could not use a touchtone or touchtone-voice hybrid interface without prior training. The paper closes with design recommendations for IVR data collection. The study builds on the ICTD 2009 comparison of forms, SMS, and voice, which found voice dictation to a live operator more accurate than electronic entry, and asks whether an automated system can replace the operator.
booktitle: First ACM Annual Symposium on Computing for Development (DEV)

author0: Palkar, Shoumik and Thomas, James J. and Narayanan, Deepak and Thaker, P. and Palamuttam, R. and Negi, P. and Shanbhag, Anil and Schwarzkopf, Malte and Pirk, Holger and Amarasinghe, Saman and Madden, Sam and Zaharia, Matei
title: Evaluating End-to-End Optimization for Data Analytics Applications in Weld
summary: This PVLDB paper turns the Weld vision into a measured system. It designs an automatic adaptive optimizer for Weld applications that eliminates the overheads of composing imperative libraries like Pandas and NumPy, using lightweight runtime measurements to make data-dependent decisions in ad-hoc workloads with sub-second overhead. The evaluation asks which optimizations matter in practice and whether Weld can be adopted incrementally: data science workloads accelerate by up to 23× on one thread and 80× on eight threads, adaptive optimization adds up to 3.75× over rule-based optimization, and porting just 4–5 operators of a library already yields benefits. The paper builds on the CIDR 2017 vision paper, which introduced Weld's intermediate representation and lazy runtime API.
journal: Proceedings of the VLDB Endowment (PVLDB)

author0: Lugato, David and Kjolstad, Fredrik and Chou, Stephen and Amarasinghe, Saman and Kamil, Shoaib
title: Taco: compilation et génération de code d'expressions tensorielles
summary: A French-language article in AVANCÉES, the review of CEA-DAM, presenting taco to the simulation community. Written with CEA's David Lugato, it explains how taco generates parallel kernels for tensor algebra expressions on dense and sparse operands: per-dimension format descriptors (CSR as dense-then-sparse), iteration graphs over nonzeros, and merge lattices that turn additions and multiplications into disjunctions and intersections of sparse iteration. Benchmarks against MKL, OSKI, and Eigen show generated kernels competitive with hand-optimized libraries, and the article describes the three-layer tool suite: C++ library, command-line tool, and web interface. A digest for a general scientific readership rather than new research: the material condenses the OOPSLA 2017 tensor algebra compiler paper and the ASE 2017 tool paper, both of which supersede it technically.
journal: AVANCÉES
